Corn Market Deep Dive

WASDE Update: USDA raised 2025/26 U.S. corn production to 16.814 billion bushels on a record 90
million harvested acres and a yield of 186.7 bu/acre, the largest crop since the 1930s. Traders had
expected around 16.5 billion and 186.1 bpa, so the result was a bearish surprise. Ending stocks climbed
to 2.11 billion bushels versus expectations near 2.01 billion, a seven-year high that lifted the stocks-to-
use ratio to 13.1 percent. The farm price was left at $3.90/bu, down from $4.30 last year, underscoring a
burdensome balance sheet. Demand categories were unchanged, so the larger crop translated directly
into higher carryout

Global Balance: World corn production was trimmed 2 MMT to 1,286.6 MMT, while ending stocks fell 1.1
MMT to 281.4 MMT. Smaller crops abroad offset record U.S. output, keeping global supply comfortable but
fractionally tighter. Brazil’s crop was steady at 131 MMT, and exports were kept at 43 MMT, trimming
carryout to 3.4 MMT. EU production edged up to 55.3 MMT, with imports lifted to 23 MMT and exports cut
to 1.8 MMT, confirming Europe’s reliance on outside origins. In China, USDA lowered beginning and ending
stocks by about 1 MMT, signaling continued reliance on state reserves rather than higher imports

Futures & Spreads: Corn futures dipped immediately after the report but recovered to close firmer, with
December ending near $4.30/bu, about ten cents higher on the day. The limited reaction underscored the
balance between record supply and stronger export demand. Wide carries remain a defining feature,
reflecting abundant supply

Funds & positioning: Managed money funds remain heavily net short, keeping rallies capped but leaving
scope for covering if yields fall short of USDA’s 186.7 bpa projection. Analysts noted that futures had already
gained nearly 25¢ into the report, reflecting expectations that supply might already be peaking

Trade flows: USDA raised exports by 100 million bushels to a record 2.975 billion, the only demand
category revised in the September update. Strong early sales and competitive offers were highlighted as
the main offset to burdensome supply

Short-Covering: The latest CFTC Commitments of Traders report for the week ending September 9
showed managed money expanding its net short position to nearly 100,000 contracts, as reductions in long
positions outweighed cuts on the short side. Commercials, including elevators and end-users, slightly
reduced their overall net long while still adding both longs and shorts to layer in coverage ahead of harvest.
Open interest rose by more than 10,000 contracts on September 17, underscoring that forward selling
remains the dominant trend, consistent with storage hedging in the face of record supply.

U.S. Cash Market & Basis:The U.S. corn market is showing the classic early-harvest split between
pressured export channels and steadier inland demand. Country bids softened seasonally as new-crop
bushels moved into the pipeline, while CIF corn held in a tighter band with freight still elevated. Weekly
export inspections reached 56.8 million bushels (1.44 MMT), a strong pace that validates USDA’s record
export forecast, with Mexico and Japan again the leading buyers. Interior ethanol plants and feeders in
the Western Corn Belt maintained firm bids to secure coverage, tempering the broader decline.

International Futures & Trade: Global corn production was cut 2 MMT to 1,286.6 MMT, while stocks
slipped 1.1 MMT to 281.4 MMT. Brazil’s exports was kept at 439 MMT, EU production edged higher with
imports lifted to 23 MMT, and China’s beginning and ending stocks were each trimmed by ~1 MMT.
These changes leave world supply comfortable but emphasize the U.S. as the heaviest source of balance
sheet pressure

So what: The September WASDE confirmed a supply-heavy outlook for corn. Record acreage and a near-
record yield pushed U.S. production and stocks to multi-year highs, locking futures into a carry structure
that rewards storage. The U.S. balance sheet is now defined by abundant supply and weaker prices, with
harvest pressure set to weigh further. Globally, smaller foreign crops only partly offset the U.S. surge,
leaving the U.S. with the heaviest balance sheet pressure. The key risk is whether final harvest results
validate USDA’s yield, or come in lower, which could force a shift in sentiment

Soybean Market Deep Dive

WASDE Update: USDA’s September report trimmed U.S. soybean production to 4.30 billion bushels,
down from August on slightly lower harvested acreage and yield now pegged at 53.5 bu/acre, versus
analyst expectations closer to 4.35 billion and 53.7 bpa. Exports were cut to 1.685 billion bushels, the
lowest in six years (analysts had looked for 1.72 billion), reflecting China’s continued reliance on Brazilian
supplies. Crush was raised to a record 2.555 billion bushels, leaving ending stocks at 300 million bushels
and the stocks-to-use ratio at 12.5 percent, tighter than the ~340 million expected. The season-average
farm price was lowered 10¢ to $10.00/bu, underscoring a more comfortable balance sheet.

Global Balance: USDA’s September WASDE made only marginal changes to the world soybean balance
sheet. Global production was trimmed slightly to 425.9 MMT, with ending stocks down 1.0 MMT to 123.0
MMT. The main driver was Argentina, where crush was raised by 0.6 MMT, tightening ending stocks to
23.9 MMT and reinforcing strong demand for meal and oil. Brazil’s balance sheet was largely steady, with

production and exports unchanged and only a minor upward tweak in carryout to 37.3 MMT. China’s
outlook was also left stable, with imports and ending stocks holding at 21 and 43.4 MMT, respectively.
The global soybean outlook tightened only at the margins, with Argentina’s higher crush the key change.
Ample Brazilian supplies and steady Chinese demand keep the world balance sheet comfortable, but the
shift in Argentina underscores firm product demand that could support meal values even as weak U.S.
exports weigh on beans.

Futures & Spreads: Soybean futures continue to stall under abundant supply and weak export pull. After
multiple failed pushes into the mid-$10.50s, November slid back toward $10.40 support and is hovering
near five-year lows. Ratings context helps explain the tone: late-August conditions were near 68% G/E,
but by mid-September they’ve eased to roughly 63–64%, with harvest ~5% and just getting started in the
South. The curve stays firmly in carry/contango: Nov/Jan holds a 12–13¢ carry (~55–60% of full carry),
and by late August the expiring Sep ’25 sat ~21¢ under Nov, one of the widest end-of-summer carries in
decades—signaling comfortable near-term supply and strong incentives to store rather than lift nearby.

Funds & positioning: Managed money was net short as of Sep 9, in line with the bearish tone. By mid-
August, outright shorts had swelled above 125k contracts (≈59% of open interest on the short side). That
concentration has capped rallies but also loads the spring: a sharper-than-expected U.S. yield cut, a
China buying burst, or policy shifts could force fast short-covering. Absent a catalyst, funds remain
comfortable leaning short into harvest.

Export commitments: U.S. soybean export sales remain well behind last year at this point, with new-crop
bookings concentrated in Mexico and “unknown.” The absence of China remains the defining feature. China
has already covered roughly 95% of its October import needs with South American origin and has recently
paid about a $1/bu premium for Brazilian soybeans over U.S. Gulf values, leaving U.S. exporters sidelined.
USDA’s weekly data showed sales of 19.9 million bushels and inspections of 16.6 million for the week
ending September 18, consistent with sluggish demand compared to Brazil’s aggressive program.

U.S. Cash Market & Basis: Cash soybean markets remain sharply divided between weak export demand
and firm domestic crush. Export corridors stayed heavy — CIF soy near +50 to +55¢ vs November — while
processors paid up to secure beans on still-favorable margins. Brazil’s program continues to siphon
Chinese demand. Weekly inspections were only 16.6 million bushels (0.45 MMT), highlighting sluggish
shipments versus Brazil’s dominant export program.

So what: Soybeans remain stuck in balance: strong crush demand and record meal exports provide
support, but the absence of Chinese buying and Brazil’s dominance cap rallies. Speculative positioning is
heavily skewed short — net short as of September 9, with mid-August levels showing more than 125,000
contracts short (about 59% of open interest). That weight has kept futures subdued near five-year lows, yet
it also sets the stage for volatility. A meaningful surprise — whether weaker-than-expected harvest yields,
a burst of Chinese buying, or policy easing — could trigger sharp short covering and a fast rally. Absent
that, soybeans are likely to chop sideways in the $10.00–10.30 band as commercials carry supply and
processors remain the key demand anchor.

Wheat Deep Dive

WASDE Update: USDA’s September report left U.S. wheat production unchanged at 1.927 billion bushels,
in line with expectations, but raised exports by 25 million to 900 million versus analyst ideas near 875
million, trimming ending stocks to 844 million bushels, tighter than the 860 million projected. The season-
average farm price was lowered 20¢ to $5.10/bu, consistent with a burdensome domestic balance sheet.
Global Balance: USDA also introduced several global adjustments. Russia’s crop was raised 1.5 MMT to
85.0, while Australia’s output climbed 3.5 MMT to 34.5 and EU production rose 1.9 MMT to 140.1. Russian
exports were trimmed to 45.0 MMT, lifting ending stocks by nearly 2 MMT, while EU stocks slipped as

imports were revised down. Globally, production increased to 816.2 MMT and ending stocks rose to 264.1
MMT, up 4 MMT from August, reinforcing an abundant world balance sheet. These changes lifted world
production to 816.2 MMT and raised ending stocks by 4 MMT to 264.1, underscoring a looser global balance
sheet than August.

Futures & Spreads: Wheat futures extended weakness after the report, with December CBOT SRW
slipping to $5.18/bu and Kansas HRW easing to $5.09/bu. Prices have tested fresh multi-year lows near
$5.00; the early-September pop was mostly short-covering and faded quickly. Wide carries persisted, with
the Dec–Mar spread steady near 18¢, about 75 percent of full carry, underscoring strong incentives for
storage. Carry structures were near full commercial levels across all wheat classes, confirming that
abundant supplies are being pushed forward in time rather than rationed nearby.

Trade Flows & Basis: Russian exports remained heavy, with FOB 12.5 percent protein wheat offered
slightly lower at $228–230/MT, maintaining pressure on global values. EU shipments continue to lag,
running more than 40 percent below last year, while Australia’s improved crop outlook adds to global
supply weight. U.S. basis was steadier but lower than earlier suggested: USDA data placed CIF SRW
Gulf bids at +45 to +55¢ vs December, up modestly from the prior week but well below the +100¢ implied
earlier. FOB SRW premiums for 10.5% protein held around +90¢. HRW protein premiums were mixed:
Gulf FOB HRW was unchanged near +110¢, but delivered 14.5 percent HRW into Chicago fell by 20¢ on
September 17, showing uneven demand.

Speculative positioning: Managed money funds remain heavily net short across SRW, HRW, and
spring wheat futures, leaving the market vulnerable to sharp but temporary rallies if export sales surprise
or if geopolitics disrupt Black Sea flows. Chicago net short positions have recently been running above
90,000 contracts, a coiled base that could fuel squeezes but has so far kept rallies capped. Commercial
hedgers extended coverage into modest rallies, further limiting recovery attempts.

So what: The September WASDE reaffirmed wheat’s bearish outlook. Larger global crops in Russia,
Australia, and the EU pushed world supplies higher, reinforcing burdensome stocks and intensifying
competition for U.S. exports. Futures have already pressed to fresh multi-year lows near $5.00, and the
brief early-September bounce was little more than short covering before sellers reasserted control. Wide
carries across all classes continue to reward storage and discourage nearby rallies, keeping the market
range-bound and defensive. Still, the heavy speculative short base — Chicago net short above 90k
contracts — leaves scope for sharp but fleeting squeezes if Russian exports falter, Australian weather
turns unfavorable, or U.S. sales surprise. Until then, wheat remains a buyer’s market anchored by
comfortable global supply.

U.S. Cash Market & Basis

The U.S. corn market is showing the classic early-harvest split between pressured export channels and
steadier inland demand. At the Gulf, CIF bids for #2 Yellow Corn were quoted at +78 to +79¢ over
December futures as of September 16, well below the +90–95¢ implied earlier. Weekly export inspections
reached 56.8 million bushels (1.44 MMT) in the week ending September 18, a strong pace that validates
USDA’s record export forecast, with Mexico and Japan again the leading buyers. Interior basis softened
seasonally as new-crop bushels moved into the pipeline, though ethanol plants and feeders in the
Western Corn Belt maintained firm bids to secure coverage. Nationally, harvest pressure and river freight
constraints continue to weigh on values, but inland users are tempering the decline.

Cash soybean markets remain sharply divided between weak export demand and firm domestic crush.
CIF Gulf bids for #1 Soybeans were quoted at just +50 to +55¢ over November on September 16,
reflecting heavy barge freight and limited Chinese demand. Weekly inspections were only 16.6 million

bushels (0.45 MMT), highlighting sluggish shipments versus Brazil’s dominant export program. In
contrast, processor bids stayed steady-to-strong, underpinned by crush margins above $2.00/bu. The
September WASDE lifted U.S. crush to a record 2.555 billion bushels, reinforced by robust soymeal
exports, which continue to support domestic demand even as exports falter.

Wheat basis reflected the same global pressures weighing on futures. CIF SRW Gulf bids were quoted at
+45 to +55¢ over December as of September 16, modestly higher than the prior week but well below the
+100¢ previously implied. FOB SRW premiums for 10.5% protein held steady near +90¢, while HRW
premiums softened, with delivered 14.5% HRW to Chicago reported down 20¢ on September 17. Weekly
inspections totaled 15.6 million bushels, while export sales were 11.2 million, underscoring how
aggressive Black Sea competition continues to cap U.S. export opportunities. Domestic millers remain
adequately covered, with demand shifting to opportunistic breaks or any tightening in protein supplies.

So what: Basis patterns continue to mirror the broader market structure. Corn shows wide carries and
seasonal harvest pressure, but strong inspections keep Gulf bids supported. Soybeans are the clearest
divergence: exporters struggle with weak Chinese demand and high freight, while processors bid
aggressively to secure coverage. Wheat basis remains two-speed, steady in SRW export channels but
softer in HRW country, with Black Sea competition still setting the ceiling. For merchandisers, corn and
wheat favor storage strategies to capture carry and later basis appreciation, while soybeans tilt toward
prompt movement into processors to monetize strong nearby bids.

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Brazil’s soybean program remains the centerpiece of global flows. ANEC lifted its September
projection to 7.43 MMT, a sharp increase from last week’s 6.75 MMT and well above last year. That pace
has clogged ports, with beans taking precedence and slowing the movement of corn despite a record
safrinha. Domestic corn values in Mato Grosso hovered near R$60/bag, reflecting oversupply, but exporters
have struggled to clear stocks quickly. This bottleneck has temporarily opened the door for U.S. corn into
some Asian destinations, even as Brazil retains the advantage on soybeans into China.

Argentina: Argentina remains the cheapest nominal origin, with Upriver corn offers holding near $175–
180/MT, but very little is moving. Farmers continue to hoard grain as a hedge against inflation ahead of
October elections, and exporters have been reluctant to register new forward sales under the DJVE system.
Even with favorable weather lifting crop prospects, political and currency risks are keeping Argentina’s
participation in world trade muted.

Black Sea: Russia raised its wheat export duty to $1.67/tonne, which has slowed the pace of sales despite
a record crop. FOB 12.5% wheat values slipped to $228–230/MT, keeping Russian offers the cheapest into
key Middle East and North African tenders. Ukraine’s new 10% levy on oilseed exports has triggered
confusion at customs, with vessels delayed and sales effectively frozen. Together, these measures highlight
how government intervention, not production, is dictating the pace of Black Sea exports.

European Union: Europe remains stuck on the defensive. Wheat exports are running ~40% below last
year, with French offers consistently undercut by Russia. At the same time, drought damage has pulled
EU corn production down to 57–58 MMT, driving import needs up toward 18–21 MMT, the largest in three
years. The bloc has shifted from exporter to buyer, with Brazilian and U.S. corn expected to capture share
once Brazil’s logistical logjam eases.

China: China continues to bypass U.S. origins despite an 80–90¢/bu FOB discount on American
soybeans. August arrivals were about 12.3 MMT, almost entirely Brazilian, while tariffs and negative
crush margins kept U.S. beans unworkable. Sorghum imports from the U.S. collapsed 97% year-on-year,

replaced by Brazilian origin. Yet downstream demand for protein is still firm: Dalian soymeal futures rose
to ¥3,580/MT (~$492/MT) on steady hog consumption, underscoring the divergence between weak raw
bean demand and resilient meal usage.

Other origins: Canada is advancing with wheat and canola harvests, though prairie heat capped canola
yields. Australia’s crop outlook was boosted to 34.5 MMT, though El Niño risks remain in play. South Africa
raised its corn export forecast to 3.5 MMT, adding to regional competition. In India, domestic wheat prices
have surged well above government support levels, prompting speculation about a potential reduction in
the 40% import duty — a policy change that could redraw wheat flows later this year.

So what: This week underscored the disconnect between production and availability. Brazil has more grain
than ever but can’t move it all at once. Russia has wheat to spare but is taxing exports. Ukraine has crops
in storage but customs bottlenecks keep them from moving. The EU suddenly needs corn, while China
won’t touch U.S. supplies. Rising freight costs (BDI at 2,154) add another constraint. For the U.S., the
immediate opening is Europe’s import gap, but the bigger swing factor will be policy decisions — whether
India lowers its wheat duty or China eases its freeze on U.S. farm goods.

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Sep 11 – Sep 17)

USDA WASDE (September): USDA projected U.S. corn production at 16.8B bu on a record yield of
186.7 bu/acre, the largest harvest since 1933. Ending stocks climbed to a seven-year high of 2.11B bu,
with the season-average farm price held steady at $3.90/bu. Soybean production was trimmed to 4.30B
bu on slightly smaller harvested area and yield pegged at 53.5 bu/acre. Exports were cut to a six-year low
of 1.685B bu, while crush was raised to a record 2.555B bu, leaving ending stocks at 300M bu. The
season-average soybean price was lowered 10¢ to $10.00/bu. Wheat exports were raised to 900M bu,
cutting ending stocks to 844M bu, and the farm price was reduced 20¢ to $5.10/bu.

Crop Progress (USDA NASS, week ending Sep 14): U.S. corn condition slipped one point to 67%
good/excellent. Harvest reached 7%, equal to the five-year average, while maturity advanced to 41%.
Soybean condition eased to 63% good/excellent. Harvest stood at 5%, ahead of the five-year average of
3%, with 41% dropping leaves. Weather stayed favorable overall, though dryness in the western Corn
Belt continued to pressure stalk quality.

Export Inspections: For the latest week, corn inspections were reported at 56.8M bu (1.44 MMT),
soybeans at 16.6M bu (0.45 MMT), and wheat at 15.6M bu (0.42 MMT). Corn shipments remained strong,
led by Mexico and Japan, while soybeans lagged with China largely absent. Wheat flows stayed capped
by Black Sea competition.

Export Sales: Weekly export sales data showed 21.3M bu of corn, 19.9M bu of soybeans, and 11.2M bu
of wheat. The soybean figure remained light without major Chinese buying, while corn sales validated
USDA’s raised forecast.

Ethanol Production & Stocks (EIA, week ending Sep 12): Ethanol output averaged 1.055M bpd,
higher than the prior week. Stocks fell to 22.6M barrels. Plants continued to run with positive margins,
though no official implied corn-use figures were reported.

NOPA Crush (August, reported Sep 16): NOPA members processed 189.8M bu, a record for the
month. Soymeal demand was strong, while soyoil stocks came in below expectations, consistent with
steady renewable diesel use.

Flash Sales: USDA confirmed multiple daily sales during the week: 225,000 MT of corn to Mexico (Sep
15), another 106,680 MT of corn to Mexico, 22,000 MT of soybean oil to South Korea, and 123,000 MT of
soybeans to unknown destinations earlier in September.

International Reports:

Brazil – ANEC Exports: ANEC revised its September soybean export forecast higher to 7.43 MMT, up
from 6.75 MMT projected the week prior, reinforcing Brazil’s dominance in China’s nearby coverage.
Heavy soybean loadings have strained port capacity, slowing corn flows despite a record safrinha crop.
FOB Paranaguá soy offers held near $545/MT, about $20/MT below U.S. Gulf values, keeping Brazilian
origin the clear choice for Chinese crushers. Santos corn offers stayed near $205/MT for October
shipment, leaving U.S. Gulf corn largely sidelined.

Argentina – Rosario Board of Trade (BCR): Farmer selling remained muted despite corn FOB Upriver
values near $175/MT, the cheapest globally. A wide gap between the official and parallel peso rates
continues to encourage on-farm hoarding ahead of October elections. Export registrations (DJVE) were
minimal, as exporters wait for policy clarity before committing forward sales.

China – Customs: China imported 12.3 MMT of soybeans in August, almost entirely Brazilian, while corn
arrivals were limited to 0.25 MMT. Domestic crush margins stayed negative, curbing new demand, while
state reserve auctions met nearby needs. The Ministry of Agriculture maintained its 2025 corn output
forecast at 280 MMT, though weather issues in the northeast were flagged as a risk. Dalian soymeal
futures firmed on steady hog demand, underlining resilience in downstream feed use even as soybean
imports slow.

European Union – MARS / IGC: The EU’s crop monitoring service cut maize yields to 7.2 t/ha, pegging
2025 corn output at just 57.6 MMT, the smallest since 2018. The International Grains Council now
projects EU corn imports at 21 MMT for 2025/26, making the bloc the world’s second-largest buyer.
France and other exporters continue to lag into North Africa, as Black Sea origins undercut EU
offers.Global – FAO Food Price Index (Sep 6): The FAO’s August food price index fell again, with the
cereal sub-index down on ample harvest supplies.

Global – FAO Food Price Index: The FAO’s August food price index was broadly steady, though the
cereal sub-index eased by 0.8% on large harvests in the EU and Russia. World maize prices firmed on
stronger U.S. demand, while rice markets stayed volatile under India’s export restrictions. The Baltic Dry
Index climbed to 2,205 on Sep 18, extending its recent uptrend and signaling rising freight costs that
could erode exporters’ margins in coming weeks.

Weather & Crop Conditions

Crop Progress & Rainfall: Mid-September weather remained broadly harvest-friendly, with warm, dry
conditions accelerating maturity. As of September 14, the corn harvest was 7% complete, equal to the five-
year average, while soybeans were 5% complete, ahead of the 3% average. National crop ratings slipped
by one point to 67% good/excellent for corn and 63% for soybeans. Moisture continued to split east and
west: recent showers in Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio improved topsoil and aided pod fill, while Iowa,
Minnesota, and the Dakotas stayed dry, raising concern over stalk integrity and late-season beans.

Temperatures: Highs held in the upper 70s°F to low 80s°F, with lows mostly in the 50s°F. A patchy frost
brushed North Dakota and northern Minnesota, with some readings dipping into the 30s°F. Damage was
limited and localized, as most crops were already mature or near maturity.

Outlook (6–10 days): NOAA projects continued above-normal warmth and below-normal precipitation
across the Plains and western Corn Belt, favoring rapid harvest progress. A slow-moving system may bring
1–2 inches of rain to parts of the Midwest, briefly slowing harvest but improving soil profiles for winter wheat
establishment along the Mississippi corridor.

South America: Conditions are steadier than previously feared. In Brazil, farmers in Mato Grosso and
Goiás await the onset of consistent pre-monsoon rains, but soil moisture is rated satisfactory to favorable,
and seasonal planting should begin on time if rains arrive in late September. Southern Brazil (Rio Grande
do Sul) remains on watch for wheat quality risks under dry pockets. In Argentina, late-August rains improved
the northern Pampas, but the central and southern Pampas remain dry enough to raise concern as corn
and soybean planting approaches in October.

Global: Europe’s summer drought left EU corn output pegged near 55–57 MMT, the lowest since 2018,
setting up import demand of around 21 MMT in 2025/26. Canada’s Prairies continued to struggle with
drought, curbing canola and wheat yields. Australia’s outlook, by contrast, has improved: USDA raised its
wheat production forecast by 3.5 MMT to 34.5 MMT, and ABARES signaled stronger winter crop potential
after timely rains. India’s monsoon finished below normal (~8% deficit), tightening prospects for rice and
vegetable oils despite a late-season recovery.

So what: U.S. weather no longer presents significant yield risk — harvest is confirming USDA’s outlook,
with attention shifting to harvest pace, stalk integrity, and basis behavior as supplies enter the pipeline.
Internationally, Brazil’s monsoon onset remains the key watch for soybean planting; delays could briefly
extend U.S. competitiveness. Elsewhere, Europe’s corn shortfall is already priced in, while Australia’s
improved wheat outlook and Canada’s drought stress pull global balances in opposite directions.

Synthesis & Outlook

Markets have moved beyond the WASDE print and into harvest reality, where early yield checks and
barge logistics are steering sentiment more than paper values. Corn and soybeans are maturing quickly
under warm, dry weather, and combines are starting to test USDA’s high yield bar. Futures remain range-
bound, but cash tells the sharper story: inland processors keep bids firm while river markets sag under
heavy freight and muted export pull. Wheat stays governed by Black Sea pricing and a swelling global
balance sheet, even as domestic stocks tightened modestly. Macro signals — a softer dollar, steady
crude, and firmer freight costs — leave a mixed but mostly neutral backdrop. The base case remains
range-trade with carries intact; upside requires yield disappointments or a surprise from China, while
downside builds if harvest runs smoothly and Brazil’s planting window opens on schedule.

Base case: Harvest pace quickens and validates USDA’s neutral-to-bearish posture. December corn
consolidates in a $4.10–4.20 range, November soybeans hold around $10.00–10.30, and December
wheat drifts between $5.00–5.20. Wide carries in corn and wheat continue to reward storage hedges,
while strong processor demand keeps soybeans supported despite sluggish exports.

Bullish triggers: A consistent pattern of below-trend field yields — 5–10 bpa lighter for corn or soybeans
slipping under 53 bpa — could push December corn toward $4.40 and November soybeans back to
$10.80–11.00. A burst of Chinese buying, or Mexico extending heavy corn purchases, would reinforce
rallies. For wheat, a sharper slowdown in Russian shipments or weather setbacks in Australia could spark
short covering from the heavily net-short fund base.

Bearish triggers: If favorable harvest weather holds and yields confirm USDA’s high projections, funds
may lean back into shorts. December corn could slip to $3.80–3.90, soybeans test $9.70–9.80, and wheat
retest $4.80. A timely monsoon in Brazil would accelerate soybean planting and cap any U.S. export
window. Rising freight costs or a firmer U.S. dollar would add pressure to basis and spreads.

Watchlist for Sep 17–Sep 24: (1) USDA Crop Progress on Sep 22 — first detailed read on harvest pace
and early yield reports; (2) USDA weekly export sales on Sep 19 — soybeans remain the focus for any
Chinese activity, while corn demand from Mexico and Japan stays key; (3) Brazil weather — timing of

monsoon onset in central states will dictate soybean planting progress; (4) Black Sea exports — Russian
duties and Ukraine’s new oilseed levy continue to disrupt flows; (5) Macro drivers — dollar direction,
crude oil stability, and Baltic Dry Index levels shaping competitiveness.

grains and oilseeds enter late September with a neutral-to-bearish tilt. Abundant U.S. supply keeps
spreads wide and flat prices capped, while Brazil’s export pace and Russia’s wheat shipments dominate
global trade flows. The hinge now is harvest truth: if yields validate USDA, the downside bias persists; if
not, early disappointments could spark fund covering and give soybeans, in particular, a short-term rally
window before Brazil’s new crop gains traction.

Ethanol for America Act

The major barrier to a higher Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) is the fuel versus food debate. Now is the
perfect time to move to E15. Corn prices are extremely low, and the latest USDA WASDE reported a record
crop and a record crop expansion.

USDA WASDE forecast corn production at 16.7 billion bushels, with the yield at 188.8 bushels per acre and
ending stocks at 2.1 billion. The season-average corn price dropped 30 cents to $3.90 a bushel. Most
importantly, 202526 crop year is expected to have 1.8 billion more bushels than 2024/25.

With current ethanol production consuming 5.6 billion bushels, a 10 percent increase in consumption would
consume an additional 560 million bushels. The reality is that year around E15 would add approximately
50 million bushels and regulatory streamlining would add another 50 million bushels. At some point over
the next ten years, the additional corn consumption could be 2.8 billion bushels minus lower fuel
consumption resulting from electric vehicles. The ethanol corn consumption increase is likely to be more
of a S curve as new compacity comes online.

With Brazil and the U.S. corn and soybean production increasing, 100 million bushels of ethanol corn
consumption will barely move the needle. The ethanol production capacity expansion that would be three
to four years from now is when the corn consumption impact to the corn market would be felt.

Executive Summary

Corn – Export Sales to Mexico Offset Harvest
Pressure
CME corn futures (Dec ’25) were nearly unchanged, slipping
0.6 percent to $4.24/bu by September 24. Two USDA flash
sales to Mexico totaling about 443,000 MT supported
values, alongside weekly inspections of 1.33 MMT, which
were 12 percent below the prior week but still 12 percent
ahead of last year. Funds covered shorts, lifting open
interest, while commercials added new hedges as harvest
advanced. Basis was mixed: Gulf bids weakened under high
barge freight costs, while processors and ethanol plants bid
firmly, leaving the national index near 22¢ under December.
The Dec/Mar spread widened slightly to 19¢ (about 61
percent of full carry), signaling routine storage incentives

Soybeans – Argentine Tax Suspension Pressures Futures and U.S. Basis
November soybeans dropped 3.3 percent to $10.09/bu as Argentina suspended export taxes through
October, spurring heavy farmer selling and cheapening global offers. Chinese crushers booked about 10
Argentine cargoes, sidelining U.S. origin. Export inspections plunged 40 percent week-on-week to

Wheat – Abundant Global Supply Keeps Futures Defensive

CBOT December wheat fell 1.7 percent to $5.19/bu as large crops in Russia, Canada, and the EU
reinforced heavy world supply. U.S. inspections of about 0.85 MMT were solid compared with last year,
but exports remain uncompetitive against Black Sea offers. SRW Gulf basis held firm near 80¢ over
December, while HRW FOB Texas Gulf improved by roughly 14¢ to about 78¢ under December as
exporters covered needs. The December–March spread near 18¢, about 50 to 55 percent of full carry,

Crude oil held steady between $63 and $64 per barrel, sustaining favorable ethanol and biodiesel
margins, while U.S. Treasury yields slipped below 4.1 percent, trimming grain storage costs.

Weather

U.S. harvest benefitted from warm, dry conditions across much of the Midwest, accelerating corn and
soybean maturity while leaving subsoil deficits severe in the western Corn Belt. A light frost in North
Dakota and northern Minnesota caused minor, localized damage. In South America, Brazil’s soybean
planting awaited consistent rains in central regions, while dryness in southern Brazil raised wheat
concerns. Argentina remained moisture-limited across the Pampas despite some showers, leaving
planting conditions less than ideal.

What’s Next (Sep 25 – Oct 1):

U.S. Government Funding: A potential federal shutdown by Oct 1 could disrupt USDA reporting and
grain inspections.

Quarterly Data: Sept 30 USDA Grain Stocks and Small Grains Summary will finalize old-crop carryout
and update wheat production.

Export Sales: Sep 25 report will confirm whether Argentina’s surge is displacing U.S. corn and soy;
China’s absence from U.S. purchases remains a key risk.

Logistics: Critically low Mississippi River levels keep barge freight inflated – any rains or Army Corps
measures could ease pressure.

South America: Brazil needs consistent rains by early October to accelerate soybean planting, while
Argentine sowing hinges on financing and weather after the tax holiday.

Black Sea & Policy: Russian export pace and Argentina’s campaign rhetoric will shape global trade
flows, alongside any movement on Chinese tariffs.

Corn Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: December 2025 corn futures were stable this week, settling at $4.24/bu on
September 24, down just 2¢ from the prior week. The market traded quietly, with five-day realized
volatility near 11 percent, reflecting a balance between harvest pressure and steady demand. Calendar
spreads widened modestly, with Dec ’25–Mar ’26 at +19¢ (61 percent of full carry) versus 17¢ a week
earlier, signaling normal commercial storage incentives without tipping into surplus-driven maximum
carry. Options activity was subdued, with implied volatility near 20 percent and skew narrowing as traders
anticipated rangebound trade.

Positioning & Money Flow: Short covering helped support values. CFTC Commitments of Traders data
(as of September 16, published September 19) showed managed money trimming net shorts to roughly –
81,500 contracts, the least bearish stance since May. Commercials simultaneously added hedges as
new-crop corn filled elevators, lifting total open interest by about 50,000 contracts. This mix reflects
commercials locking in storage carries while funds eased off heavy shorts, leaving the market less
vulnerable to downside momentum but also lacking speculative buying power.

U.S. Cash & Basis: Cash corn showed a split pattern. At the Gulf, CIF premiums for September loadings
firmed to +79¢ over December, but high barge freight costs forced FOB offers lower, easing to about
+99¢ over December ($243/MT) from +105¢ the prior week. Interior river elevators tracked the freight
pinch, with Mid-Mississippi and Ohio Valley bids falling 5–10¢ as drafts were cut and loadings delayed.
By contrast, ethanol plants and feeders held firm: Indiana and Ohio processors stayed near even to +5¢
over December, while western Corn Belt plants paid –20¢ to –10¢, historically strong for harvest. The
national corn basis index averaged –22¢ under December, near seasonal norms.

Export Flows: Exports remain supportive. Weekly inspections (week ending September 18, reported
September 22) reached 1.329 MMT, down 12 percent from the prior week but 12 percent above last year.
USDA confirmed two flash sales to Mexico totaling 443,000 MT, highlighting Mexico’s role as a consistent
buyer. New-crop export sales (week ending September 18, reported September 25) totaled about

641,000 MT, led by Mexico and Japan, with total U.S. commitments at 14.5 MMT, well above last year’s
pace.

International Trade: Brazil’s FOB Paranaguá corn stayed around $215–220/MT, about $10 below U.S.
Gulf offers, keeping Brazil competitive into Asia and the Middle East. The stronger real (R$5.30/$) slowed
farmer selling, but ANEC raised September exports to 7.12 MMT, matching last year’s record. Argentina’s
government suspended export taxes on corn through October, triggering a rush of sales; exporters
registered over 5 MMT of shipments within 48 hours, with FOB Up-River values near $205/MT,
undercutting both Brazil and the U.S. Russia offered corn near $205/MT FOB, adding to global supply
competition, while Ukraine shipped 2.1 MMT in August–September via Danube and rail, though still well
below normal.

Fundamentals & Reports: Crop Progress (week ending September 21, published September 22)
showed corn harvest at 11 percent, in line with the five-year average, with crop condition ratings at 66
percent good/excellent (down one point from the prior week). Ethanol production (EIA, week ending
September 20, published September 20) averaged 1.055 million barrels/day, down 50,000 from the prior
week but still +0.6 percent year-on-year, with stocks at 22.6 million barrels, the lowest since January.
Margins remained positive, around $0.20/gal, supporting firm processor bids.

So What? Corn markets are transitioning smoothly into harvest. Futures stability and modest carry
expansion show commercials content to store grain, while basis highlights the split between pressured
river/export channels and firm processor demand. Strong Mexican buying and steady ethanol grind are
cushioning downside risks, while aggressive Argentine sales and cheaper Brazilian FOBs cap upside.
With funds no longer heavily short, the market is balanced but lacks speculative buying. Rangebound
trade around $4.20 looks likely into the September 30 Quarterly Stocks report, which is the next catalyst
for direction.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: November 2025 soybean futures fell sharply this week, losing 34¾¢ (–3.3 percent)
to settle at $10.09/bu on September 24. The selloff was triggered by Argentina’s surprise suspension of
export taxes through October, which sent a wave of farmer selling onto the market. Chinese crushers
immediately booked an estimated 10 Argentine cargoes, sidelining U.S. origin and pushing U.S. export
inspections down more than 40 percent week-on-week to 484,000 MT. The futures curve weakened
modestly, with the Nov ’25–Jan ’26 spread widening to 14–15¢ (60–65 percent of full carry). This
structure reflects heavy early harvest deliveries offset by strong crush demand, preventing a collapse into
maximum carry.

Fundamentals & Trade: The tax holiday in Argentina, combined with a collapsing peso, made Argentine
soybeans and products the cheapest globally, undercutting both U.S. and Brazilian offers. Soymeal FOB
Rosario fell $25/MT below U.S. Gulf, while whole beans on Matba-Rofex surged as exporters rushed to
register shipments before duties return. In Brazil, FOB Santos premiums rose to +250¢ over November
as competition shifted toward Argentine meal and oil, leaving more bean demand to Brazil. In the U.S.,
Gulf bids softened 5–10¢ under the weight of barge freight costs and South American competition. The
national soybean basis averaged –43¢ under November futures, among the weakest harvest-time levels
in years, though processors continued to pay premiums thanks to robust crush margins.

Positioning & Money Flow: Managed money funds responded to the policy shock by liquidating longs,
with open interest in soybeans falling about 10,000 contracts as speculators pulled back. Unlike corn,
where funds reduced shorts, soybeans saw outright long liquidation. Commercial hedgers added shorts
as harvest pressure mounted and basis weakened. Implied volatility climbed modestly (realized vol near
15 percent), underscoring uncertainty about whether Argentina’s export surge is a temporary shock or a
structural shift.

So What? The soybean market has transitioned abruptly from a demand-driven equilibrium into one
dominated by South American supply shocks. With Argentina flooding the market during its tax holiday,
U.S. futures and basis are under pressure despite robust domestic crush demand. The risk is asymmetric:
should Argentina’s policy end on schedule in late October, U.S. and Brazilian beans could regain share,
tightening spreads and firming futures. Until then, U.S. soy remains trapped in a weak export
environment, with November futures anchored near $10. Short-term direction hinges on whether China
steps in for U.S. purchases despite tariffs or continues to lean entirely on Brazil and Argentina.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: CBOT December 2025 wheat futures extended their slide, losing 8¾¢ (–1.7
percent) to close at $5.19½/bu on September 24. The downtrend reflects persistent global oversupply,
with ample production from Russia, Canada, and the EU offsetting any regional concerns. While rallies
remain shallow and fleeting, spreads suggest an orderly market rather than one in distress. The Dec ’25–
Mar ’26 carry widened slightly to 18¢, equal to 50–55 percent of full carry. This level signals adequate
commercial hedging activity and comfortable storage returns, but not the burdensome surpluses that
would push spreads toward maximum carry.

Global Supply & Demand: Large Northern Hemisphere crops continue to weigh on futures. Russian
export offers remain aggressive, with 12.5 percent protein wheat holding near $255/MT FOB, keeping
pressure on U.S. HRW and SRW in key tenders. Canada and the EU both raised crop estimates, while
Australia’s crop prospects steadied despite dryness. Together, these upgrades reinforce the global
abundance theme. U.S. export inspections were 0.85 MMT for the week, solid compared with last year,
but still insufficient to offset stiff Black Sea competition.

Cash & Basis: In the U.S. cash market, SRW Gulf basis stayed firm near +80¢ over December as
traders covered prior sales, while HRW FOB Texas Gulf strengthened by 14¢ to ~78½¢ under December,
reflecting exporter buying after harvest. Interior basis was steady, with mills largely covered for fall needs.
Quality concerns linger in some spring wheat regions, but with global supplies so heavy, they have not
materially altered trade flows.

Speculative Positioning: Managed money remains heavily net short across wheat contracts, with
Chicago SRW attracting the bulk of bearish exposure. The persistence of this large short base is both a
weight on prices and a latent source of volatility. Funds have consistently re-established shorts on rallies,
confident that abundant global supply caps upside. Yet this short exposure leaves the market primed for
sharp squeezes on any bullish catalyst, whether logistical disruption, weather shock, or geopolitical event.
Commercial hedgers have taken the other side, steadily layering in forward sales. As a result, open
interest has crept higher while the forward curve remains in carry, underscoring the dominance of
commercial storage hedging.

So What? Wheat markets remain trapped in a bearish fundamental backdrop, but event-driven volatility is
a clear risk. On one hand, abundant supply, with Russia, Canada, and the EU all flush with exportable
wheat, suggests rallies will be sold and futures will stay defensive near the $5.20 area. On the other,
prices are now low enough to stimulate incremental demand: U.S. exports are running ahead of last year,
and cheaper wheat is drawing into feed channels. This value-driven buying places a floor under the
market, limiting downside. For now, expect wheat to grind in a narrow range with occasional sharp rallies
when shorts are forced to cover. The key is that futures are no longer trading on weather or crop size
alone, instead, the battle is between entrenched bearish supply expectations and slowly improving
demand. Until a fundamental tightening materializes, wheat will remain rangebound, with risk skewed
toward choppy, event-driven price action.

U.S. Cash Market & Basis

Corn basis showed a split pattern this week. At the Gulf, CIF barge corn premiums firmed to +79¢ over
Dec for September loadings, reflecting the scramble for barge capacity amid record freight costs. Yet the
high transportation expense forced FOB Gulf offers lower, easing to about +99¢ over Dec ($243/MT)
versus +105¢ the prior week. This dynamic left exporters passing freight burdens back to farmers through
weaker basis. Interior river elevators tracked the freight pinch, with some bids in the Mid-Mississippi and
Ohio valleys falling 5–10¢ as barge drafts were cut and loadings delayed. In contrast, ethanol plants and
feeders in the interior maintained relatively firm bids: Indiana and Ohio processors held steady near even
to +5¢ over Dec, and some western Corn Belt plants were paying –20¢ to –10¢, historically strong for
harvest. The cmdtyView national corn basis index averaged –22¼¢ under Dec, slightly firmer than the
prior week but near seasonal norms.

Soybean basis weakened broadly on harvest pressure and export softness. The Gulf basis slipped 5–10¢
as U.S. offers lost ground to Argentina’s heavily discounted beans after the tax holiday. Nationally,
soybean basis averaged –43¢ under November futures, among the weakest early-harvest levels in years.
River locations were especially pressured by the freight spike, with Upper Mississippi elevators cutting
bids sharply. By contrast, domestic processors maintained firm bids thanks to strong crush margins:
board crush values stayed historically high, and some Western Corn Belt crushers paid up to +10¢ over
Nov to secure supplies even as harvest deliveries expanded. This divergence underscores the tension
between robust domestic demand and weak export competitiveness.

Wheat basis showed modest firmness in select channels. Gulf SRW remained relatively strong near +80¢
over Dec, reflecting traders covering prior export commitments. HRW FOB Texas Gulf improved by ~14¢
on the week, now quoted at 78½¢ under Dec, as exporters replenished nearby coverage after harvest.
Interior basis was steady, with mills largely covered for fall needs.

So What? The cash market is reflecting the same themes evident in futures spreads. Corn and wheat are
in carry, with exporters hedging forward and elevators capturing storage returns, while soybeans are
under immediate pressure from Argentina’s surge. Merchandisers face weak export basis but firm
domestic demand in both corn and soy, creating a fragmented market where processors and feeders are
better buyers than exporters. For producers, corn and wheat economics favor storage and hedging into
deferred months, while soybeans may warrant quicker sales into strong domestic crusher bids rather than
holding grain amid weak river values.

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Brazil’s corn exports remain heavy, with ANEC raising its September forecast to 7.12 MMT,
matching last year’s record pace. Shipments are moving primarily to China, Iran, Spain, and Egypt. FOB
Santos corn held steady around $215–220/MT, about $10 cheaper than U.S. Gulf offers, while
Paranaguá premiums were near +105¢ over December. A firmer real (R$5.30/$) has slowed farmer
selling, with interior Mato Grosso prices even ticking up slightly to R$50/60kg, though exporters are still
able to pull supplies. First-crop corn planting in Center-South Brazil is 25 percent complete, well ahead of
average after early rains in Paraná. On soybeans, Brazil is nearly sold out of old-crop stocks, with
September exports pegged near 7.5 MMT. Chinese crushers continue to source mostly Brazilian beans,
with premiums rising late in the week as Argentine meal and oil competed for demand.

Argentina: A dramatic shift occurred after Argentina’s government suspended export taxes on soybeans,
corn, and wheat through October 31. Levies were cut from 26 percent to zero on soybeans and from 9.5
percent to zero on corn and wheat, triggering a rush of farmer sales. Exporters registered over 5 MMT of
shipments within 48 hours, with corn FOB Up-River values near $205/MT, still a $10 discount to Brazil
and the U.S. Gulf. Importers including Vietnam, Malaysia, and Egypt quickly booked Argentine corn, while
soymeal FOB Rosario fell $25/MT below U.S. Gulf values. Domestic corn and soybean prices in pesos

collapsed, offset by the peso’s steep devaluation to 1,412/USD official (1,475 parallel). The surge may
front-load Argentina’s exports, leaving a potential lull later this year once the tax holiday ends.

Black Sea: Russia continues to dominate wheat exports, offering 12.5 percent protein wheat near
$255/MT FOB. Corn exports remain modest but competitive, with offers near $205/MT. Ukraine shipped
2.1 MMT of corn in August–September via Danube and rail routes, but overall exports remain 40 percent
below normal with the Black Sea corridor still closed and EU transit restrictions in place. New Ukrainian
duties on oilseeds have effectively halted raw soybean exports, redirecting some crush demand back to
the Americas, though in limited volumes.

Other Origins: EU wheat exports are lagging sharply versus last year, while corn imports remain brisk
from Brazil and Ukraine. Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan booked corn cargoes from both U.S. and South
America at $255–265/MT C&F. Mexico remained the key U.S. buyer, highlighted by flash sales totaling
443,000 MT this week. Sorghum also saw renewed Chinese interest, with a few U.S. cargoes reportedly
booked for feed. South Africa raised its corn export outlook to 3.5 MMT, with flows directed toward Asia.

So What? Global grain flows this week underline the competitive headwinds facing U.S. exporters.
Brazil’s corn remains the cheapest option for many destinations, while Argentina’s tax holiday triggered a
flood of cheap offers that displaced U.S. soybeans and meal in Asia. Black Sea wheat is still the most
aggressive supplier, capping U.S. export prospects. Yet cracks are visible: Brazil’s farmer selling has
slowed under a strong real, and Argentina’s export surge is temporary, likely exhausting volumes by
November. For U.S. corn, steady Mexican demand provides a floor, while soybeans remain hostage to
Chinese buying decisions, delayed so far but potentially supportive once harvest lows are reached. The
balance of trade flows favors end-users today, but the risk of sudden shifts in South America or the Black
Sea keeps the outlook volatile heading into Q4.

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Sep 18 – Sep 24)

Crop Progress (USDA NASS, published Sep 22 for week ending Sep 21): U.S. corn harvest was 11
percent complete, matching the five-year average but two points behind last year’s pace. Soybean
harvest reached 9 percent, equal to the five-year average but three points behind last year. Crop maturity
was broadly on track, though condition ratings edged lower: corn at 66 percent good/excellent (from 67)
and soybeans at 61 percent (from 63). A light frost in North Dakota and Minnesota caused minor,
localized damage but with most crops already at or near maturity, the impact was limited.
So what: The favorable weather window accelerated maturity and aided harvest, reinforcing expectations
for a large crop, though dryness in the western Corn Belt raised concerns about stalk integrity and late-
season losses.

Export Inspections (USDA FGIS, week ending Sep 18, reported Sep 22): Corn inspections were
1.329 MMT, down 12 percent from the prior week but still 12 percent ahead of last year. Soybean
inspections slumped to 484,000 MT, more than 40 percent below the prior week, as Chinese buying
shifted to Argentina during its tax holiday. Wheat inspections were 0.85 MMT, solid relative to last year,
reflecting steady SRW shipments but still constrained by Black Sea competition.
So what: Corn exports remain a bright spot, underpinned by Mexico and other Western Hemisphere
buyers, while soybeans face acute pressure from South American competition. Wheat exports are
adequate but continue to struggle against aggressive Russian offers.

Export Sales (USDA FAS, week ending Sep 18, reported Sep 25): Net new-crop corn sales were
641,000 MT, led by Mexico and Japan, with two flash sales to Mexico (totaling 443,000 MT) confirming
strong demand from the U.S.’s top buyer. Soybean new-crop sales were muted, with China absent and

Argentine supplies dominating. Wheat sales were modest, with U.S. offers undercut in global tenders.
So what: Corn’s forward sales remain seasonally strong, with total commitments at 14.5 MMT (well
above last year), while soybeans continue to lag badly, signaling further downside risk if China remains
sidelined.

Ethanol Production & Stocks (EIA, week ending Sep 20, published Sep 20): Ethanol output averaged
1.055 million barrels/day, down 50,000 from the prior week due to plant maintenance but still 0.6 percent
above last year. Stocks fell to 22.6 million barrels, the lowest since January, confirming that demand is
absorbing supply. Positive margins (about $0.20/gal) and firm DDGS values provided further incentive for
processors to run hard.
So what: The corn grind for ethanol remains solid, supporting basis near plants even as harvest
expands.

NOPA Crush (published Sep 16 for August data): The U.S. soybean crush reached 167.8 mbu in
August, up 6 percent year-on-year, while soybean oil stocks fell 6.7 percent year-on-year.
So what: Strong crush margins are incentivizing processors to bid aggressively for beans, even as export
demand weakens, cushioning the downside in cash markets.

So What? The data this week reaffirmed a split market: corn fundamentals remain resilient on strong
export and ethanol pull, soybeans are under heavy export pressure despite robust crush, and wheat
holds steady but lacks a demand spark. With harvest advancing smoothly and spreads paying
commercials to store grain, the near-term focus will be on the Sept 30 Quarterly Stocks report for
confirmation of old-crop carry and any surprises in wheat production.

International Reports:

Brazil – ANEC & Planting Pace: Brazil’s corn exports remain torrid, with ANEC raising its September
forecast to 7.12 MMT, matching last year’s record pace. Lineups are concentrated on China, Iran, Spain,
and Egypt. FOB Santos corn held near $215–220/MT, about $10 below U.S. Gulf offers, while Paranaguá
premiums were steady at +105¢ over Dec. Interior prices in Mato Grosso firmed slightly (~R$50/60kg) as
the stronger real slowed farmer selling. First-crop corn planting in Center-South Brazil is 25 percent
complete, well ahead of average after timely rains in Paraná. Soybeans are essentially sold out of old-
crop stocks, with September exports projected at 7.5 MMT. Chinese imports in August were 85 percent
sourced from Brazil, underscoring its continued dominance in the soybean trade.

Argentina – Export Surge Post-Tax Holiday: Argentina’s government suspended export taxes on
soybeans, corn, wheat, and products through October 31, cutting levies from 26 percent (soybeans) and
9.5 percent (corn, wheat) to zero. The move triggered a flood of sales, with exporters registering more
than 5 MMT of shipments within 48 hours. Corn FOB Up-River (Rosario) values settled near $205/MT,
roughly a $10 discount to U.S. and Brazilian offers, and buyers from Vietnam, Malaysia, and Egypt
quickly booked cargos. Soymeal FOB Rosario collapsed relative to the U.S. Gulf, undercutting by
$25/MT. The peso’s collapse (official 1,412/USD, parallel 1,475) amplified farmer selling.
So what: Argentina’s surge is a short-term bearish shock, likely front-loading exports into Oct–Nov and
leaving fewer volumes available later in the season once the tax holiday ends.

Black Sea – Abundant Supplies: Russia remains the most aggressive wheat exporter, offering 12.5
percent protein wheat near $255/MT FOB. Corn exports are smaller but competitive at $205/MT. Ukraine
shipped 2.1 MMT of corn in Aug–Sep via Danube and rail, though overall exports are still 40 percent
below normal with the Black Sea corridor closed and EU restrictions in place. New Ukrainian export duties

on oilseeds (10 percent on soy, rapeseed, sunflower seed) effectively halted raw bean exports,
redirecting some EU crush demand toward Brazil and the U.S., though in small volumes.

Other Origins – EU, Asia, South Africa: EU corn imports remain strong, driven by Brazil and Ukraine,
while wheat exports are sluggish compared to last year. Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan booked corn
tenders at $255–265/MT C&F from both U.S. and South America. Mexico continues to anchor U.S. corn
demand, highlighted by USDA flash sales this week. Chinese buyers focused on Argentina for soybeans
and stayed absent from U.S. purchases, consistent with tariffs. South Africa raised its corn export forecast
to 3.5 MMT (from 2.5), adding some competition into African and Asian markets.

So What? International flows reflect heavy competition from South America and the Black Sea, leaving
the U.S. as the residual supplier for now. Brazil’s record corn exports and Argentina’s tax-driven flood of
soy and corn are pressuring U.S. values short term. Still, both dynamics carry caveats: Brazil’s farmer
selling is slowing under a strong real, and Argentina’s tax holiday ends in October, potentially tightening
availability. For wheat, Russia remains the price leader globally, while U.S. exports rely on incremental
value buying. Net effect: global trade remains oversupplied for now, but the structure is fragile, hinging on
South American policy shifts and Black Sea logistics.

Weather & Crop Conditions

United States: Conditions shifted toward a harvest-friendly pattern. Warm, dry weather across much of
the Midwest accelerated corn and soybean maturity, keeping national harvest progress near the five-year
average. Dryness persisted in the western Corn Belt, leaving subsoil deficits severe and raising concerns
about stalk integrity and lodging risk as harvest advances. A light frost touched northern North Dakota
and Minnesota, with lows in the 30s°F, but most crops were mature enough to avoid material damage.
Scattered rains in the central and eastern Corn Belt provided some short-term soil moisture relief for
winter wheat planting, but not enough to lift critically low Mississippi River levels.

South America: Brazil’s planting season is about to ramp up, but central regions (Mato Grosso, Goiás)
remained dry under El Niño influence, delaying widespread soybean seeding until consistent rains arrive.
Southern Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul) also trended dry, adding stress to the wheat crop at a sensitive
stage, with implications for both yield and quality. In Argentina, soil moisture remained limited across the
Pampas despite some showers in northern provinces, leaving conditions less than ideal ahead of October
corn and soybean planting. The temporary removal of export taxes spurred farmer sales, but the incentive
to accelerate planting still hinges on improved rainfall and access to inputs.

Global Weather Issues: Canada’s spring wheat and canola crops were revised higher after favorable
late-season rains, while Russia and the EU both lifted grain production estimates, reinforcing global
abundance. In contrast, dryness in southern Brazil and Argentina remains a watchpoint, particularly for
wheat yields and upcoming corn and soybean planting. Australia’s outlook stayed dry under El Niño,
weighing on wheat prospects, while Ukraine’s late-summer rains improved soil conditions for winter
sowing.

So what: Weather has transitioned from being a yield risk to shaping harvest pace and logistics in the
U.S., with dryness now a factor for river flows and basis rather than production. The light frost scare
confirmed that major yield threats are mostly behind. Globally, the focus shifts south: delays in Brazil’s
soybean planting or persistent dryness in Argentina could tighten early 2026 export availability and add
risk premium back into soybean and corn markets later this fall. For now, favorable U.S. harvest weather
is slightly bearish for prices, while South American uncertainty provides the next potential catalyst.

Synthesis & Outlook

Synthesis & Outlook

This week marked the clear shift from weather risk to harvest reality. Futures and cash markets are
aligned: modestly wider carries in corn, soy, and wheat correspond with ample but orderly supply
expectations, while cash basis patterns reinforce the split between weak river/export values and firm
domestic processor demand. The market is not signaling surplus panic, spreads remain well below full
carry, but harvest pressure is evident, especially in soybeans where Argentina’s tax holiday added an
external supply shock.

Speculative positioning also reflects this transition. Funds have cut shorts in corn and wheat, reducing
downside momentum, while soybeans saw outright long liquidation. This leaves markets in a balanced
but sensitive posture: with fewer heavy shorts, a fresh rally will require a true fundamental catalyst (such
as disappointing yield reports or unexpected export demand), while the absence of such catalysts could
see the trade lean bearish again.

Base case: Rangebound trade is the most likely near term. December corn is expected to hover between
$4.10–$4.40, November soybeans around $10.00, and December wheat near $5.20. Spreads are likely to
hold at 50–65% of full carry as commercials continue to hedge storage, and basis should stay bifurcated
firm at processors, weak along the river.

Bullish triggers: A surprise in next week’s Sept 30 Quarterly Stocks or early October WASDE, such as a
lower-than-expected corn yield (175 bpa or below) or a sharp trim to soybean output, could tighten
balance sheets and spark short-covering. Any significant Chinese soybean purchase, or a continuation of
Mexico’s large-scale corn buying, would add fuel. On wheat, any sign of Russian export restriction could
trigger a short squeeze given heavy fund shorts. Improvements in Mississippi River levels would also
allow exports to flow more freely, supporting Gulf basis and narrowing spreads.

Bearish triggers: Conversely, if harvest conditions remain ideal and early yield results trend better than
feared, markets could resume their grind lower. In corn, a strong harvest pace and yields near USDA’s
current 177.5 bpa would pull Dec futures back toward the $4.00 area. For soybeans, continued Argentine
and Brazilian competition paired with ongoing Chinese absence could pressure Nov futures toward
$9.70–$9.80. A prolonged U.S. government shutdown after Oct 1 that halts USDA reports and
inspections could also sap confidence. Macro risks, such as a firmer U.S. dollar or weaker global equity
sentiment, would likewise weigh on futures.

Watchlist (Sep 25 – Oct 1):

Quarterly Stocks & Small Grains Summary (Sep 30): Final old-crop corn and soybean carry-in, plus
updated wheat production.

USDA Export Sales (Sep 25): Monitor for any Chinese demand in soybeans or additional corn flash
sales to Mexico.

Mississippi River logistics: Critically low levels continue to inflate freight and weaken Gulf bids; any
rainfall or Army Corps measures could improve flows.

South American weather: Brazil needs consistent rains by early October to accelerate soybean planting;
Argentina’s planting pace depends on both moisture and financing post-tax holiday.

Macro signals: Government shutdown risk, crude oil direction, and currency moves (USD, BRL, ARS) all
remain market shapers.

In summary: The grain complex enters late September with a neutral-to-bearish tilt. Supplies are ample
enough to weigh on flat prices, yet not burdensome enough to trigger distressed selling. Commercials are
content to carry grain at profitable spreads, while end-users benefit from weak export basis and firm
processor bids. The pivot from weather to harvest means that yield reports, stocks data, and export flows

will now set direction. With speculative shorts reduced, rallies require fresh bullish fuel — absent that, the
market will likely remain rangebound into early October.

Ethanol for America Act

The major barrier to a higher Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) is the fuel versus food debate. Now is the
perfect time to move to E15. Corn prices are extremely low, and the latest USDA WASDE reported a record
crop and a record crop expansion.

USDA WASDE forecast corn production at 16.7 billion bushels, with the yield at 188.8 bushels per acre and
ending stocks at 2.1 billion. The season-average corn price dropped 30 cents to $3.90 a bushel. Most
importantly, 202526 crop year is expected to have 1.8 billion more bushels than 2024/25.

With current ethanol production consuming 5.6 billion bushels, a 10 percent increase in consumption would
consume an additional 560 million bushels. The reality is that year around E15 would add approximately
50 million bushels and regulatory streamlining would add another 50 million bushels. At some point over
the next ten years, the additional corn consumption could be 2.8 billion bushels minus lower fuel
consumption resulting from electric vehicles. The ethanol corn consumption increase is likely to be more
of a S curve as new compacity comes online.

With Brazil and the U.S. corn and soybean production increasing, 100 million bushels of ethanol corn
consumption will barely move the needle. The ethanol production capacity expansion that would be three
to four years from now is when the corn consumption impact to the corn market would be felt.

U.S. Corn Production (Billion Bushels)

Source: USDA

For example:

The National Corn Growers Association (NCGA) is intensifying its call for action from Congress
and the administration after the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s latest World Agriculture and
Supply and Demand Estimates report projected a record 16.7-billion-bushel corn crop this year,
further threatening the livelihood of farmers already facing record-low corn prices.

“Corn growers are already marketing their corn for extremely low corn prices, and this massive
projected corn supply without market-based solutions to increasing corn demand is already
causing corn prices to fall further,” said Illinois farmer and NCGA President Kenneth Hartman Jr.

Executive Summary

Corn – Stocks Surprise Pushes Futures Lower,
Demand Offers Cushion
USDA’s quarterly Grain Stocks delivered the biggest shock
of the week, placing Sep 1 U.S. corn inventories at 1.53
bbu, nearly 200 mbu above trade expectations, which reset
supply perceptions and pressured December futures two
percent lower to $4.165/bu, their weakest in a month.
Spreads reflected the bearish tone, with Dec/Mar near 16¢,
or roughly three-quarters of full carry, rewarding commercial
storage. Harvest basis collapsed in river markets as
Mississippi barge freight spiked to record levels, dragging
Gulf bids lower. Still, export demand proved resilient:
inspections hit 1.53 MMT, up nearly 30 percent from last

year, and sales of 1.9 MMT included almost 0.9 MMT to Mexico. That steady flow kept U.S. corn values
competitive into Latin America and Japan despite Brazil’s lingering presence in world markets.

Soybeans – Argentine Policy Distorts Trade, U.S. Basis Softens
Soybeans traded defensively, with November futures slipping one percent to $10.13/bu despite slightly
tighter Sep 1 U.S. stocks at 316 mbu, down eight percent from last year 344 mbu. Argentina’s abrupt
suspension of export taxes unleashed a wave of farmer selling, prompting China to secure roughly 2.7
MMT of Argentine soy at steep discounts and sidelining U.S. origin. U.S. export inspections, at just 0.59
MMT, remained well below average, though sales of 0.72 MMT offered modest relief with Egypt and
Mexico leading buyers. High freight costs weighed on basis, with the national average near 43¢ under
November, among the weakest early-harvest levels in years. Crush margins narrowed to $1.10/bu as
soymeal lost ground and soy oil’s early-week rally stalled. Futures spreads remained near full carry, with
Nov/Jan at 19¢, underscoring comfortable pipeline supplies and weak nearby demand.

Wheat – Rising Stocks and Production Confirm Bearish Tone

The wheat complex slid to fresh lows as the Grain Stocks and Small Grains reports reinforced global
surplus. U.S. Sep 1 wheat stocks reached 2.12 bbu, about 80 mbu above expectations, while USDA raised
the 2025 crop to 1.985 bbu on better yields in HRW and HRS areas. December Chicago wheat fell 2.5
percent to $5.09/bu, with Dec/Mar spreads stretching to 18¢ (roughly 50–65 percent of full carry). Export
demand was lackluster, with cumulative inspections only modestly above last year’s depressed pace.
Global supply pressure remained acute: Russia continued aggressive exports near $230/MT FOB, Poland
and Ukraine expanded wheat output, and Argentina’s new crop was pegged sharply higher at 22 MMT.
Heavy fund shorts persisted, keeping the market on the defensive absent a geopolitical shock.

Macro/Policy – Softer Dollar, Divergent South American Currencies Shape Trade

Macro conditions offered no relief. The U.S. Dollar Index hovered near one-year highs (97.68) as
Treasury yields climbed toward four percent, raising carrying costs and challenging U.S. export
competitiveness. Crude oil pulled back, trimming biofuel optimism, while equities softened on broader
risk-off sentiment. Argentina’s late-September suspension of export taxes on corn, soy, and wheat briefly
unleashed a surge of farmer selling and distorted global flows, most notably diverting Chinese soybean
purchases away from the U.S. Logistics compounded the strain: critically low Mississippi River levels
drove barge freight to multiples of average costs, further eroding interior basis and export margins. The
U.S. government shutdown that began October 1 has halted updates to USDA data releases, including
Crop Progress and Export Sales, adding a new layer of uncertainty to near-term market signals .

Weather

U.S. weather was broadly supportive of harvest, with warm and dry conditions accelerating crop maturity
and harvest progress (corn 18 percent, soybeans 19 percent harvested by Sep 28). Crop ratings held
steady, confirming no late-season damage. The Plains remained dry, raising concerns for HRW wheat
establishment, though early October rains in forecasts could improve stands. In South America, Brazil’s
soybean planting just began, but is off to a slow start as farmers wait for consistent rains in Mato Grosso
and Goiás, while southern Brazil dried out after earlier excess moisture. Argentina benefited from late-
September rains across the Pampas but forecast dryness in early October could again challenge corn
planting and wheat recovery.

What’s Next (Oct 2 – Oct 8):

USDA Export Sales (Oct 3): will confirm whether Mexico remains the key U.S. corn buyer and if China
reappears in soybeans.

Harvest Pace: watch for corn and soybean harvest acceleration toward the 50 percent mark by mid-
October.

WASDE Setup: traders position for Oct 9 USDA report, balancing higher carry-in against yield
speculation.

River Logistics: rainfall in the Ohio/Tennessee basins could ease barge freight, but absent relief, Gulf
basis levels may weaken further.

Brazil Planting: forecast rains in early October critical for Mato Grosso soybean sowing; delays would
inject risk premium.

Black Sea & Policy: monitor Russian export pace and Argentina’s volatile policies ahead of elections as
potential price drivers.
