Corn Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: December 2025 corn futures slumped to $4.165/bu on Oct 1, down 9¢ (two percent)
from the prior week and marking a one-month low. The sell-off accelerated on Sept 30 after USDA’s
quarterly Grain Stocks pegged Sep 1 inventories at 1.53 bbu, roughly 190 mbu above trade expectations.
The bearish surprise reset supply perceptions and pushed Dec futures through key support near $4.20.
Spreads remained steep: Dec ’25–Mar ’26 closed around +16¢ carry, about 75 percent of full carry,
offering elevators roughly 5¢/mo to store grain. Implied volatility picked up after the report but settled near
21 percent, signaling more two-sided trade but no panic.

Funds & Positioning: CFTC data through Sept 23 showed managed money net short near 150,000
contracts, and open interest rose modestly in the days following the stocks report, suggesting fresh short
positions entered the market. Commercials extended hedges, taking advantage of profitable carry. The
net result is a market tilted structurally bearish, funds pressing shorts, commercials storing, with little
speculative buying to counter the move.

U.S. Cash & Basis: Interior basis weakened sharply where river logistics dominate. Illinois River bids fell
to 30 to 40¢ under Dec, and Memphis bids collapsed to 70¢ under as Mississippi barge freight spiked to
around $19.53/ton, more than double normal levels in some corridors. Gulf CIF corn eased accordingly,

weighing on export elevators. By contrast, ethanol plants and feeders kept bids relatively firm: Iowa
processors paid near parity to Dec, and Plains feedlots continued to bid premiums as local supplies
stayed tight. Nationally, the corn basis index averaged about 22¢ under December futures, consistent
with the seasonal harvest pressure but not yet signaling distress.

Export Flows: Export demand provided support for prices despite the shock of USDA’s higher-than-
expected old-crop carryout estimate. Weekly inspections reached 1.53 MMT (up 30 percent YoY), led by
Mexico (0.5 MMT) and Japan. Sales totaled 1.92 MMT, with Mexico booking nearly 0.9 MMT alongside
notable interest from Colombia and Spain. That volume helped keep U.S. Gulf corn competitive, even as
Brazil continued to dominate Asia with cheaper offers.

International Trade: Brazilian FOB corn out of Santos traded near $205/MT ($5.20/bu), maintaining a
$25–30 discount to U.S. Gulf offers and limiting U.S. exporters’ reach into Asia. Argentina briefly undercut
prices from both rival sources during its zero-duty export window, with Up-River FOB near $200–205/MT,
but the bulk of the “competitively priced” supply has already been flushed through the system. China
remained absent from U.S. corn books, working through state reserves and favoring domestic feed
grains. Dalian Jan ’26 corn futures hovered around ¥2,500/MT ($6.50/bu), still above import parity, but
tariffs and politics continue to block U.S. flows

So What? Corn is firmly in a storage-driven phase. The surprise in USDA stocks added immediate weight
to futures, but robust Latin American demand is keeping a floor under Gulf values. Wide carries and weak
river basis signal commercials are comfortable hedging and holding grain, while inland processors seize
opportunities from cheap harvest supplies. For now, futures appear anchored in the mid-to-low $4s, with
the path of least resistance slightly lower if harvest yields validate USDA’s high expectations. The bearish
structure leaves funds in control, but the set up also leaves futures prices vulnerable to short covering
should yields disappoint or export demand accelerate.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: November 2025 soybean futures eased one percent this week, settling at
$10.13/bu. The move came despite slightly tighter-than-expected U.S. Sep 1 stocks at 316 mbu, which
were modestly below trade expectations. Futures spreads remained steep: the Nov ’25–Jan ’26 spread
closed near +19¢, about 85 percent of full carry, underscoring abundant nearby supply and muted
urgency from buyers. Board crush margins narrowed to roughly $1.10/bu, down from earlier levels as
meal softened and a rally in soybean oil lost steam.

Funds & Positioning: Speculators responded to the Argentine policy shock by pulling back. Managed
money trimmed exposure, with longs liquidated on the shift in trade flows away from the U.S.
Commercials expanded short hedges into harvest, consistent with a carry market and weaker Gulf basis.
Implied volatility rose modestly, reflecting heightened uncertainty over how long South America’s
competitive advantage will persist.

Cash & Basis: U.S. basis weakened across river markets. CIF Gulf premiums slipped under the
combined weight of high barge freight and harvest supplies, while interior bids in the Midwest fell as
elevators struggled to move grain. In contrast, domestic crushers kept bids relatively firm, though even
processor basis eased slightly as plants gained coverage. Nationally, basis patterns aligned with the
futures carry: nearby demand is soft, while commercials capture storage returns by rolling grain forward.

Trade Flows: Export inspections were subdued at 594,000 MT, well below last year’s pace and
underscoring limited global demand for U.S. beans. Weekly sales totaled 0.72 MMT, led by Egypt,
Taiwan, and Mexico. Crucially, China was absent. Instead, China booked an estimated 2.7 MMT of

Argentine soybeans during the brief zero-tax window, diminishing the prospects for U.S. shipments to the
world’s largest buyer as harvest ramps up in the Corn Belt. This diversion highlighted how policy shifts
abroad can dictate near-term U.S. export performance.

International Competition: Argentine supplies dominated headlines after the government suspended its
hefty export tax (roughly 30 percent of the value), making Argentine soybeans, soybean meal and
soybean oil the cheapest globally. That advantage allowed China to secure large volumes at a $2.15–
$2.30/bu premium to CBOT November futures yet, still undercutting U.S. and even Brazilian offers after
tariffs and logistics. Brazil’s FOB Gulf remained steady but less active, as much of its old crop is sold.
Meanwhile, U.S. Gulf basis eased further, reflecting shrinking competitiveness into world markets.

So What? Soybeans remain caught in a tug-of-war: modestly supportive U.S. stocks and firm crush
demand at home versus severe headwinds from South American competition abroad. The futures curve
near full carry and weakening harvest-time basis signal that commercials prefer to store beans rather
than chase exports. The competition from Argentina has since dissipated, as the temporary tax holiday
ended abruptly in late September upon reaching the $7 billion export cap in just two to three days,
allowing U.S. values to regain some footing. Without China returning to the U.S. book, futures are likely to
hover near $10.10 , with rallies capped by high U.S. inventories and pre-booked South American offers.
The asymmetric risk is that until U.S. tariffs are addressed, China’s prior purchases will keep U.S.
soybeans stuck in a structurally weak export environment through the prime harvest season.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: December 2025 CBOT wheat futures fell 2.5 percent this week to $5.09/bu, setting
fresh contract lows as heavy supply weighed on sentiment. The Dec–Mar spread widened to 18¢ carry,
roughly 50–65 percent of full carry, underscoring how comfortable the supply situation has become.
Implied volatility firmed into the low 20s, reflecting the sharp move lower but still within the band of orderly
trade.

Global Supply & Demand: The bearish tone was cemented by USDA’s Grain Stocks and Small Grains
Annual Summary reports. Sep 1 U.S. wheat stocks were pegged at 2.12 bbu, about 80 mbu above trade
expectations and six percent higher than last year. At the same time, 2025 production was revised up to
1.985 bbu, with larger HRW and HRS crops than previously thought. Abroad, production estimates
moved higher too, assessments of Poland’s crop rose to 13.4 MMT, Ukraine expanded winter plantings,
and Argentina’s new crop is forecast at 22 MMT vs 18.6 MMT last year. Together, these adjustments
loosened the global balance further, keeping pressure on U.S. FOB values.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets echoed the futures weakness. HRW, SRW, and HRS stocks all exceeded
analyst expectations, leaving domestic pipelines flush. U.S. FOB offers softened: SRW near $250/MT and
HRW 11.5% around $270/MT, undercut by French and Russian values. Russian 12.5% protein wheat
held near $228–230/MT FOB Black Sea, continuing to set the global floor. Basis levels at the Gulf
remained pressured as exporters struggled to attract fresh sales despite lower board prices.

Trade Flows: Export demand remains sluggish. Weekly sales totaled 0.54 MMT, led by the Philippines
and Italy, but the cumulative program is still only 15 percent ahead of last year’s depressed pace.
Inspections reached 9.54 MMT YTD, a modest gain versus 2024 but far below what is needed to offset
the heavy carry-in. With Russia dominating global tenders and EU wheat also available, U.S. exports
remain a residual supplier.

Speculative Positioning: Managed funds remain entrenched in heavy short positions across all U.S.
wheat classes. The combination of bearish fundamentals and wide carries makes wheat an attractive
short, and rallies have been consistently sold into. However, the size of the net short leaves the market
exposed to sharp bouts of short covering should a bullish catalyst emerge, for instance, a disruption in
Black Sea flows or weather setbacks in Australia.

So What? Wheat is firmly in a supply-heavy phase. Larger-than-expected U.S. stocks and an upward
production revision reinforced bearish sentiment, while aggressive Russian exports continue to cap world
values. Futures now trade near levels that could stimulate incremental demand, but without a material
tightening in global supply or a geopolitical disruption, rallies are likely to be shallow and fleeting. The
market structure, full carry spreads, heavy speculative shorts, and weak FOB values, reflects a trade
dominated by surplus management. Until demand improves or competitors falter, wheat futures are likely
to grind sideways at depressed levels, with volatility driven more by positioning squeezes than by
fundamental tightening.

U.S. Cash Market & Basis

Corn: Harvest pressure and strained logistics weighed heavily on corn basis. Interior river bids fell
sharply as Mississippi barge freight surged to well above average levels, with spot freight costs doubling
in some corridors. Lower Mississippi elevators saw basis collapse as exporters passed the freight burden
back to farmers, leaving CIF Gulf values under pressure. In contrast, ethanol plants and feed mills in the
Eastern Corn Belt reported steadier bids, trimming only modestly as processors maintained demand. The
national average corn basis ended the week near 22¢ under December futures, underscoring the split
between weak river markets and firmer inland demand.

Soybeans: Soybean basis weakened across most export channels. CIF Gulf premiums slipped as
harvest deliveries met expensive river freight, while the national average soybean basis was around 43¢
under November, one of the weakest harvest-time levels in recent years. The softness was amplified by
the absence of China from the U.S. program and the diversion of demand toward Argentine beans during
Buenos Aires’ brief tax holiday. By contrast, domestic crush plants continued to pay up, though margins
narrowed from earlier highs. Eastern Corn Belt crushers reported only modest basis slippage, supported
by slow farmer selling and steady product demand, while Pacific Northwest export basis held relatively
firm given limited pipeline supplies. The net result was a two-speed market: weak at river and Gulf, but
firmer at processors.

Wheat: Wheat basis softened in line with the bearish tone of the Grain Stocks report. With HRW, SRW,
and HRS inventories exceeding expectations, exporters struggled to maintain premiums. FOB Gulf offers
eased, with HRW 11.5 percent around $270/MT and SRW near $250/MT, still well above Russian values.
Domestic mills held bids largely steady, covered for nearby needs, but lacked incentive to chase
additional volume with abundant supply confirmed.

So What? Cash markets are validating the futures carry. Corn and soybeans show sharp basis weakness
where river logistics bite, but interior processors and feeders continue to anchor demand. Wheat basis
mirrors the global oversupply theme, slipping under competitive pressure from Russia and Europe. For
merchandisers, the strategy remains straightforward: store grain where possible to capture carry, sell
soybeans into crushers rather than export channels, and wait for potential relief in river freight or South
American demand before export basis recovers.

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Brazil remained the price leader in global corn and soybean trade. FOB Santos corn held near
$205/MT, keeping a $25–30 discount to U.S. Gulf offers and sustaining strong demand into Asia and the
Middle East. Soybean old-crop availability is now minimal, but forward premiums remain competitive,
particularly with Argentina’s temporary surge now fading. Farmer selling slowed under currency strength,
leaving exporters to rely on pipeline stocks to keep shipments moving.

Argentina: The short-lived suspension of export taxes on corn, soybeans, and wheat triggered a wave of
registrations and front-loaded sales. Within days, exporters booked more than 5 MMT of shipments, with
corn FOB Up-River offers near $200–205/MT, briefly undercutting Brazil and the U.S. Meal and oil also
priced aggressively into Asia, pushing U.S. values out of contention. With taxes reinstated, Argentina’s
competitiveness has already receded, leaving open the possibility of a quieter export program into year-
end.

China: China capitalized on Argentina’s tax holiday, securing roughly 2.7 MMT of soybeans and multiple
product cargoes at steep discounts. U.S. beans were left sidelined despite slightly tighter domestic
stocks, while Brazil supplied the balance of China’s September arrivals. With domestic crush margins still
weak, China’s forward buying strategy remains opportunistic, chasing the cheapest origin rather than
building a steady U.S. program.

Black Sea: Russia continued to dominate wheat exports, with 12.5 percent protein wheat offered near
$228–230/MT FOB, the cheapest globally. Ukraine’s exports remain constrained, about 40 percent
behind last year, as volumes move mainly via Danube and rail routes. Corn shipments totaled around two
MMT since August, keeping Ukraine relevant in EU feed demand but leaving Russia as the central force
in world wheat pricing.

European Union: EU wheat production was revised higher, with Poland’s crop boosted to 13.4 MMT.
Corn imports remain brisk, with Ukraine and Brazil supplying most of the flow to cover Europe’s shortfall.
EU exporters remain largely uncompetitive in wheat tenders compared with Russia, reinforcing the global
abundance narrative.

Other Origins: Mexico remained the standout U.S. corn buyer, taking nearly 0.9 MMT in last week’s
sales alongside strong inspections. Japan and Spain also booked U.S. corn cargoes, though at smaller
scale. In wheat, North African and Middle Eastern tenders were dominated by Russia, while Argentina’s
short burst of offers diverted some Asian demand away from the U.S.

So What? Global flows underscore how U.S. exports remain the residual supplier. Brazil continues to
anchor corn values into Asia, while Argentina’s tax holiday injected a temporary flood of beans and
products that displaced U.S. offers in China. Russian wheat remains the benchmark, capping upside for
U.S. FOB prices. Yet cracks are visible: Brazilian farmer selling has slowed, and Argentina’s
competitiveness is already fading. For U.S. exporters, Mexico’s steady corn demand provides a floor, but
broader opportunities hinge on shifts in South American supply or a disruption in Black Sea flows. Until
then, world buyers enjoy abundant choice at prices that undercut U.S. Gulf offers.

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Sep 25 – Oct 1)
Government Shutdown: The inability to agree on a continuing resolution left the U.S. government closed
as of the writing of the report. Given the current position of both sides, this shutdown could last longer
than a couple of days, but it may also be resolved by the end of the day. However, until the government
reopens, USDA will not publish reports. Whether the reports are released later is unclear. Prior

shutdowns that lasted several weeks resulted in interpolation for the missing data points in the affected
reports, which were never released after reopening. Still, most shutdowns only last for a couple of days
and ultimately the shutdown will not impact world grain and oilseed market fundamentals.

Quarterly Grain Stocks (USDA, published Sep 30): The September 1 corn stocks estimate came in at
1.53 billion bushels, nearly 190 million above analyst expectations and 12 percent higher than last year.
The surprise increase reflected larger on-farm holdings and implied stronger feed and residual use earlier
in the summer, resetting perceptions of the carryout path. Soybean stocks were reported at 316 million
bushels, a touch below expectations but still comfortably above last year’s 268 million. For wheat, Sep 1
inventories reached 2.12 billion bushels, about 80 million higher than trade guesses and six percent
larger year-on-year, reinforcing the weight of abundant supply heading into 2025/26.

Small Grains Annual Summary (USDA, published Sep 30): USDA revised U.S. wheat production for
2025 to 1.985 billion bushels, up from the previous 1.927 billion, as higher HRW and HRS yields more
than offset minor reductions elsewhere. The increase not only added to domestic stocks but also
underscored the global abundance theme, particularly as Russia, Canada, and South America are all
projected to expand output. This revision reinforced the bearish tone already established by the Grain
Stocks report.

Crop Progress (USDA NASS, published Sep 29 for week ending Sep 28): Corn harvest advanced to
18 percent complete, slightly ahead of the 15 percent five-year average, while soybean harvest reached
19 percent versus the 16 percent norm. Crop ratings held steady at 66 percent good/excellent for corn
and 63 percent for soybeans, with no late-season deterioration. HRW wheat planting stood at 26 percent,
behind the 29 percent average pace, reflecting dryness across parts of the Southern Plains. Overall, the
data suggest a smooth U.S. harvest, with ample supplies moving into the pipeline, though concerns
remain for wheat stand establishment in the Plains.

Export Inspections (USDA FGIS, week ending Sep 25, reported Sep 29): Weekly corn inspections
totaled 1.53 MMT, a solid performance that was up 30 percent from last year, led by consistent shipments
to Mexico and Japan. Soybean inspections, at 594,000 MT, were well below seasonal averages, with
China absent from the U.S. program as Argentine beans captured demand. Wheat inspections reached
0.66 MMT, steady compared with last year’s pace, but not enough to offset competition from Russia and
the EU. The inspection data underscored the split dynamic: strong corn exports, weak soybeans, and
steady but underwhelming wheat shipments.

Export Sales (USDA FAS, week ending Sep 18, reported Sep 25): Net corn sales surged to 1.92 MMT,
highlighted by nearly 0.9 MMT sold to Mexico, confirming Mexico’s continued role as the cornerstone of
U.S. demand. Soybean sales were 0.72 MMT, led by Egypt and Mexico but with China again absent.
Wheat sales came in at 0.54 MMT, a modest volume that reflected limited competitiveness in global
tenders. Together, the sales data showed how corn remains in demand, soybeans continue to
underperform, and wheat struggles to find traction against cheaper Black Sea origins.

Ethanol Production & Stocks (EIA, weekending Sep 27, reported Oct 1): Ethanol output averaged
1.024 million barrels per day, down slightly from the prior week’s 1.055 million barrels per day, while
stocks rose to 23.456 million barrels, up from 22.602 million. Implied corn use for ethanol held steady,
reflecting solid processor margins supported by gasoline demand near nine mbpd and blending
economics still positive. The data confirms that ethanol remains a consistent source of corn demand
during harvest, offsetting some of the bearish supply-side signals from the USDA stock estimate.

So What? The fundamental reports this week reinforced a bearish tilt for corn and wheat, with larger-
than-expected stocks and upward production revisions outweighing steady domestic demand. Soybeans
provided only minor relief, with stocks slightly tighter than expected but still burdened by poor exports and
competition from Argentina. Corn exports and ethanol use remain bright spots, keeping some resilience in
the balance sheet, while wheat continues to face overwhelming global competition. The key hinge
remains Chinese buying — without renewed demand, harvest pressure will dominate soybeans into
October, while corn and wheat remain defined by heavy supplies and storage-led market structures.

International Reports:

Brazil – Exports & Farmer Selling: Brazil remained the anchor for global corn trade, with FOB Santos
offers near $205/MT, roughly $25–30 below U.S. Gulf levels and keeping Brazil dominant into Asia and
the Middle East. Old-crop soybean availability has largely dried up, but forward premiums remain
competitive. A stronger Real slowed farmer selling, leaving exporters more reliant on pipeline supplies to
sustain shipments.

Argentina – Tax Holiday Fallout: Argentina temporarily suspended export taxes on soybeans, corn,
wheat, and products in late September, triggering an immediate wave of registrations exceeding five
MMT. Corn FOB Upriver values printed at $200–205/MT, briefly undercutting Brazil and the U.S., while
China secured an estimated 2.7 MMT of soybeans during the window and meal/oil moved at steep
discounts. The move front-loaded exports: once duties return, Argentina’s competitiveness is expected to
fade into late Q4.

China – Opportunistic Buying: Chinese crushers capitalized on Argentina’s brief tax holiday, sidelining
U.S. origin by booking multiple soybean and product cargoes at steep discounts. Despite slightly tighter
U.S. soybean stocks, China maintained its absence from the U.S. export program, while Brazil covered
the balance of arrivals. With domestic crush margins still weak, Chinese buying remains opportunistic and
price-driven rather than steady.

Black Sea – Russian Dominance Continues: Russia extended its dominance in wheat trade, offering
12.5 percent protein at $228–230/MT FOB, the cheapest globally. Ukraine’s exports remained
constrained, still running about 40 percent behind last year, with shipments mainly redirected through
Danube and rail routes. Corn exports totaled around two MMT since August, keeping Ukraine relevant for
EU feed demand but leaving Russia as the primary price-setter in wheat.

European Union – Larger Crops, Steady Imports: EU wheat production was revised higher, with
Poland’s crop lifted to 13.4 MMT. At the same time, corn import demand remains brisk, primarily covered
by Brazil and Ukraine. EU exporters continue to struggle for competitiveness in global tenders, especially
against Russian wheat.

Other Origins – Mexico & Asia: Mexico was again the standout U.S. buyer, booking nearly 0.9 MMT of
corn last week alongside strong inspections. Japan and Spain also took U.S. corn cargoes, though at
smaller scale. In wheat, North African and Middle Eastern tenders remained dominated by Russia, while
Argentina’s short-lived surge diverted some Asian demand away from the U.S.

So What? International trade flows this week reinforced the headwinds facing U.S. exporters. Brazil
continues to undercut U.S. corn into Asia, while Argentina’s temporary tax holiday displaced U.S. beans
in China. Russian wheat remains the cheapest origin, limiting U.S. opportunities in global tenders. Yet
these competitive pressures carry limits: Brazil’s farmer selling is slowing under currency strength, and
Argentina’s surge was temporary. U.S. corn maintains a strong foothold in Mexico, but broader market
share gains will hinge on shifts in South America or disruptions in the Black Sea.

Weather & Crop Conditions

United States
Crop Progress & Rainfall: Warm, dry conditions accelerated fieldwork and kept harvest moving
smoothly. By Sept 28, corn harvest reached 18 percent (vs 15 percent avg) and soybeans 19 percent (vs
16 percent avg). Crop ratings held steady at 66 percent G/E for corn and 63 percent G/E for soybeans.
Dryness remained most acute across the western Corn Belt, where subsoil deficits kept stalk
integrity/lodging risk elevated. Winter wheat planting advanced to 26 percent complete (vs 29 percent
avg), with parts of the Southern Plains looking for timely moisture to firm stands.

Temperatures: A broadly warm, harvest-friendly pattern prevailed. No widespread frost threat
materialized, preserving late-season yield potential and allowing steady dry-down. Heat wasn’t excessive
but combined with dryness continued to sap subsoil moisture in western Belt areas and did little to relieve
low river levels that are feeding into barge logistics stress.

Outlook (6–10 days): Early-October guidance in the summary points to a continued bias toward
warm/dry for rapid harvest, with attention on any Ohio/Tennessee basin rains that could ease barge
freight and modestly support Gulf basis. In the Plains, showers will help HRW establishment if they verify;
otherwise, stand risk lingers into mid-October.

South America: Brazil’s soybean planting is beginning, but central areas (Mato Grosso, Goiás) still need
consistent rains to scale up; southern Brazil has turned drier, adding stress to wheat at a sensitive stage.
In Argentina, late-September showers aided northern areas, yet the Pampas remain moisture-deficient
heading into October corn/soy planting. The early-October rain setup is pivotal: timely coverage would
unlock fieldwork; continued patchiness would push planting later and tighten the forward calendar.

Global: Late-season improvements lifted Canada (spring wheat/canola) and prompted a wheat upgrade
in the EU (notably Poland), while Russia stayed on track under favorable conditions—together reinforcing
an abundant global supply backdrop. Australia remained dry under El Niño, trimming wheat potential as
filling progresses. Ukraine picked up late-September rains, improving soil conditions for winter sowing.

So What? In the U.S., weather has shifted from yield risk to pace/quality/logistics: fast harvest adds near-
term supply pressure and keeps river-linked basis weak. The next meaningful swing factor sits in South
America, if central Brazil rains lag or Argentina stays dry, early-season planting delays could add risk
premium back into beans (and to a lesser extent corn) later in October. For now, the U.S. pattern is
modestly price-bearish, while South American uncertainty is the key wildcard.

Synthesis & Outlook

This week underscored the pivot from harvest-friendly U.S. weather and steady demand in corn to acute
export headwinds in soybeans and a still-burdensome global wheat supply. Futures and cash are broadly
aligned: corn is anchored by strong Mexican demand and firm ethanol grind, soybeans are weighed down
by Argentina’s temporary export surge, and wheat remains capped by Russia’s dominance. Spreads in all
three markets are in carry, but not at burdensome extremes, signaling orderly commercial hedging rather
than distressed selling. Basis shows the same split: exporters under pressure from freight and South
American competition, while domestic processors keep bids firm.

Speculative positioning reflects this mixed setup. Funds trimmed shorts in corn and wheat, reducing
downside momentum, while soybeans saw outright long liquidation as Argentina’s tax holiday flooded the
market with cheap offers. The balance of positioning leaves markets sensitive: with fewer shorts to
squeeze, rallies will need true catalysts, disappointing yield reports, tighter stocks data, or fresh export

demand. Without such triggers, the path of least resistance remains sideways to slightly lower into early
October.

Base case: December corn holds in a $4.10–$4.35 band, November soybeans hover near $10.10, and
December wheat trades around $5.00–$5.20. Carries remain at 55–65 percent of full storage, reflecting
ample but orderly supply. Processor basis continues to anchor soybeans and corn domestically, while
river markets stay pressured by freight costs and weak export competitiveness.

Bullish triggers: USDA’s Grain Stocks surprise tightened the soybean balance sheet modestly but
added weight to corn and wheat; any further Chinese soybean purchase or continued flash sales of U.S.
corn to Mexico would reinforce rallies. On wheat, a sudden Russian export policy shift remains the
clearest upside spark, given the heavy fund shorts. Even modest Mississippi River relief would help firm
Gulf basis and narrow spreads.

Bearish triggers: With harvest weather ideal and yield results meeting USDA’s high expectations,
futures could grind lower. December corn risks drifting back to $4.05, November soybeans could retest
$9.80–$9.90 under Argentina’s and Brazil’s export dominance, and wheat could soften if Russia
continues to undersell globally. A firmer dollar or weaker crude would add downside pressure.

Watchlist (Oct 3 – Oct 9):

USDA Export Sales (Oct 3): Confirm whether Mexico remains the key U.S. corn buyer and if China
reappears in soybeans.

Harvest Pace: Watch for corn and soybean harvest acceleration toward the 50% mark by mid-October.

WASDE Setup: Traders position for Oct 9 USDA report, balancing higher carry-in against yield
speculation.

River Logistics: Rainfall in the Ohio/Tennessee basins could ease barge freight, but absent relief, basis
may weaken further.

Brazil Planting: Forecast rains in early October critical for Mato Grosso soybean sowing; delays would
inject risk premium.

Black Sea & Policy: Monitor Russian export pace and Argentina’s volatile policies ahead of elections as
potential price drivers.

In summary: The grain complex closes September with a neutral-to-bearish tilt. Ample U.S. supply and
South American competition keep rallies capped, but the market is not in distressed surplus, spreads and
basis point to orderly storage and selective demand. For commercials, corn and wheat favor carry
capture, while soybeans favor quick movement into crushers. The key swing factors lie in the recent Sept
30 stocks report and ongoing South American weather. Without a bullish surprise in either, markets are
likely to stay rangebound.

Ethanol for America Act

The major barrier to a higher Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) is the fuel versus food debate. Now is the
perfect time to move to E15. Corn prices are extremely low, and the latest USDA WASDE reported a record
crop and a record crop expansion.

USDA WASDE forecast corn production at 16.7 billion bushels, with the yield at 188.8 bushels per acre and
ending stocks at 2.1 billion. The season-average corn price dropped 30 cents to $3.90 a bushel. Most
importantly, 202526 crop year is expected to have 1.8 billion more bushels than 2024/25.

Corn Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: December 2025 corn consolidated after the late-September break, settling at $4.22
on Oct 8 (+6¢ w/w). The USDA Grain Stocks shock (larger-than-expected Sep 1 stocks, published Sep
30) kept a bearish overhang, but follow-through selling faded as the market marked time into WASDE.
The Dec ’25–Mar ’26 spread held near +17¢ carry on Oct 8, roughly two-thirds of full carry on seven
percent interest + $0.05/bu/month storage/insurance, continuing to reward hedge-and-store programs.
Realized vol eased from the post-report spike as ranges tightened.

Pre-WASDE Expectations: Consensus centers on a U.S. corn yield of 184.5-185.0 bpa and production
of 16.5-16.6 bbu, with 2025/26 U.S. ending stocks at 2.2 bbu. On the global balance sheet, world corn
ending stocks are 281-283 MMT. For South America benchmarks prior to this window, USDA
(September) predicted the Brazilian corn crop at 131.0 MMT and forecast Argentinian production at 53.0
MMT, while CONAB’s most recent projection expected Brazilian corn production to total 139.7 MMT.

Funds & Positioning: With CFTC’s Commitments of Traders report suspended during the shutdown, the
CFTC published the last report available on Sep 26 covering positions as of Sep 23, showed managed
money net short 95,000 corn contracts, with commercials largely on the other side. Open interest rose
into month-end, consistent with fresh shorting after the stocks surprise; the heavy speculative short keeps
the market sensitive to any bullish nudge.

U.S. Cash & Basis: Harvest pressure plus river logistics kept basis soft in the barge markets. Illinois
River bids commonly 35–45¢ under Dec; Mid-South/Lower Mississippi locations 70–80¢ under, reflecting
draft limits and barge surcharges that persisted through this week (late-September quotes around
$19.53/ton, roughly 53¢ per bushel, remained indicative). CIF Gulf eased accordingly, weighing on export
elevators. By contrast, ethanol plants and Plains feeders held comparatively firmer bids (many near parity
but quite a few bids just under the Dec contract), pulling grain away from export channels. Nationally, the
corn basis index averaged 40¢ under Dec, consistent with seasonal harvest pressure but not yet
signaling distress.

Export Flows: With USDA’s weekly updates paused, the last official prints guide the view. The FAS
Export Sales report for the week ended Sep 18 and published on Sep 25 totaled 1.92 MMT, including
0.88 MMT to Mexico. FGIS export inspections (week ended Sep 26; published Sep 29) were 1.53 MMT;
FGIS operations continued into the week ended Oct 2, indicating ongoing loadings even as barge costs
stayed high. Pre-blackout cadence, led by Mexico and Japan, helped keep Gulf values nominally viable
despite competitively priced supplies from Brazil.

International Trade: Brazil remained the low-cost anchor; FOB Santos near $205/MT ($5.20/bu
equivalent) preserved a $25–30/MT edge over typical U.S. Gulf offers into Asia. Argentina briefly
undercut both during its late-September tax holiday (Up-River $200–205/MT) before the window closed
and offers firmed. China stayed largely absent from US books; domestic coverage and alternative origins
filled nearby needs. In the futures market, Dalian Jan corn held a premium to import parity, but

policy/biotech constraints continued to limit US access.

So What? Corn remains storage-driven: wide carries and weak river-linked basis encourage commercials
to own time, while interior demand (ethanol/feed) quietly supports floor values near $4.22. The heavy
speculative short and steady pre-blackout export cadence (Mexico/Japan) argue for range-bound trade
into WASDE, with direction hinging on the potential US yield update and any relief in Mississippi logistics.
However, if the government does not reopen, traders will continue to rely on anecdotal reports for yield
estimates. The increase in uncertainty due to the information gap during the shutdown means that
speculative traders are unlikely to make large, directional bets until USDA releases its next assessment of
US production.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: November 2025 soybeans recovered modestly from the late-September drop,
ending $10.29/bu on Oct 8. The curve stayed wide, with Nov ’25–Jan ’26 at a 19¢ carry, about three-
quarters of full carry based on the following assumptions, seven percent interest + $0.05/bu/month
storage cost. The wide but steady spreads are consistent with ample nearby supply and limited urgency
from exporters.

Pre-WASDE Expectations: Consensus looks for a U.S. soybean yield of 53.1 to 53.2 bpa (down slightly
from prior estimates), production of 4.26 to 4.27 bbu, and 2025/26 US ending stocks of 0.290 bbu. On the
global balance sheet, traders expect USDA to report new-crop world soybean ending stocks at 124 MMT.
In the September WASDE, USDA’s analysts predicted the Brazilian crop at 175.0 MMT and Argentinian
production at 48.5 MMT, while CONAB’s latest estimate prior to Oct 8 has Brazil at 177.6 MMT.

Products & Crush: Board crush margins improved slightly to $1.485/bu as of October 8, supported by
steadier meal and a firmer soybean oil prices after September weakness. The Dec CME board crush
contract dropped from a recent high of more than $2.25 in early August to almost $1.40/bu in late
September. Positive crush economics helped keep processor bids comparatively firmer than river-
exposed elevators and maintained a stable domestic offtake into early October.

Funds & Positioning: With the Commitments of Traders reporting suspended during the shutdown, the
last available report (as of Sep 23; published Sep 26) showed managed money near flat to slightly short (-
29,000 contracts) after covering shorts into month-end. Commercial hedging remained aligned with a
carry structure; speculative participation was light into the report week.

Cash & Basis: The barge market weighed on river basis levels with CIF Gulf premiums of +70–100¢ for
Nov, down from roughly +140¢ a month earlier amid elevated barge costs and harvest inflows. Midwest
elevators trimmed bids as farmer movement increased, while processors stayed firmer relative to futures
given positive crush economics; Eastern Corn Belt crushers continued to pay +50–70¢ vs. Nov.
Nationally, an average basis near 78¢ under Nov sits among the weaker early-harvest prints in recent
years and is consistent with the low water levels and constrained export pull.

Trade Flows: The last official USDA prints before the blackout showed export sales during the week
ended Sep 18 of 0.72 MMT (led by Egypt, Taiwan, Mexico) and export inspections for the week ended
Sep 26 at 0.59 MMT. China remained largely absent from the US market as heavy late-September buying
from Argentina during its short-lived zero-duty window diverted demand just as the US harvest
accelerated.

International Competition: Argentina’s temporary suspension of export taxes triggered Chinese bargain
hunting, allowing buyers to secure up to 2.1 MMT of Argentine soybeans at steep discounts. After the

window closed, Argentina’s advantage faded, but Brazil remained the global price setter: FOB Santos
$440-470/MT ($10.20/bu) versus US Gulf $495/MT, while Argentine Up-River normalized near $480/MT
after the tax holiday ended. That pricing stack kept US offers at a disadvantage into Asia even as
crushers supported domestic demand.

So What? Currently the soybean market is harvest- and storage-driven: a wide nearby carry and weak
barge markets encourage commercials to own time, while positive crush margins keep processors
bidding and provide a domestic floor near $10.30/bu. Export headwinds persist given Brazil’s FOB
advantage and September’s Argentine sales to China; near-term price discovery hinges on realized US
yields, the continuity of central-Brazil planting rains, and any sign of Chinese buying returning to US
origin.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: The Dec wheat contract traded quietly during the week ending Oct 8 with prices
remaining close to $5.00, consolidating after the late-September decline. The Dec/Mar spread held near
an 18¢ carry on Oct 8, roughly 80 percent of full carry under a 7 percent interest + $0.05/bu/month
assumption, consistent with abundant nearby supply and a market still rewarding storage. Implied
volatility stayed firm but orderly as participants awaited new balance sheet guidance.

Pre-WASDE Expectations: Trade consensus anticipates USDA will predict US 2025/26 ending-stocks at
875 million bushels, with world wheat ending stocks near 265-266 MMT. Traders do not expect a
significant yield revision, though analysts will watch for adjustments to exports and feed use after the
increased carry in suggested in the September Grain Stocks report. Internationally, attention centers on
whether USDA analysts trim the Russian export forecast, currently near 51 MMT, or adjusts Australian
output following recent dryness.

Global Supply & Demand: The tone remains shaped by USDA’s Grain Stocks and Small Grains – 2025
Summary assessments. Sep 1 U.S. wheat stocks of 2.12 bbu and 2025 production of 1.985 bbu
confirmed a larger-than-expected supply base. Abroad, Russian exporters continue to ship grain at a
record pace, EU and Black Sea output are ample, and Argentinian new crop, estimated near 21 MM,
adds further weight to global availability heading into 2025/26.

Cash & Basis: Physical markets mirrored the board’s weakness. US FOB SRW near $250/MT, HRW
11.5 percent, near $270/MT, while Russian 12.5 percent protein wheat held near $230/MT FOB Black
Sea, keeping a lid on US competitiveness. Gulf basis stayed under pressure as exporters struggled to
generate fresh demand, and domestic mill bids softened in line with ample stocks.

Trade Flows: With USDA weekly series paused, the last official readings guide sentiment. US export
sales during the week ended Sep 18 totaled 0.54 MMT, while inspections through week ended Oct 2 left
cumulative shipments modestly above last year’s depressed pace but still insufficient to absorb the higher
carry-in. Russia’s continued dominance in world tenders and steady EU participation keep the US as a
residual supplier.

Speculative Positioning: With CFTC Commitments of Traders report suspended during the shutdown,
the last available report published on Sep 26 showed managed money heavily net short. As of Sep 23,
the CFTC estimated the net fund position short 98,000 contracts of SRW and 43,000 HRW contracts. The
entrenched short bias has capped rallies, but its size leaves the market exposed to abrupt short covering
– if a trigger appears.

So What? The wheat market remains well supplied, rewarding storage. Ample domestic and global
inventories, persistent Black Sea competition, and wide carries continue to define trade. Futures appear
locked in the low-$5 range until demand improves or a weather or geopolitical shock alters export flows.
Near-term volatility will likely stem more from positioning shifts than from any immediate tightening in
fundamentals.

U.S. Cash Market & Basis

Corn: Harvest and logistics continued to weigh on corn basis across river markets. Illinois River bids
ranged from 35¢ to 45¢ under December, while Lower Mississippi levels slipped to 70–80¢ under,
reflecting persistent draft limits and elevated barge tariffs that carried over from late September. CIF Gulf
premiums eased modestly, and export elevators reported slower spot movement as high freight costs
erased much of the nominal advantage from lower board prices. In contrast, ethanol plants and feeders
kept bids comparatively firm, with several processors paying near parity to December futures amid strong
margins and seasonal grind demand. Nationally, the corn basis index averaged roughly 41¢ under
December, consistent with harvest-season pressure but not yet signaling distress.

Soybeans: Soybean basis remained under pressure where river freight dominates. CIF Gulf bids
hovered near +50–75¢ vs. November, down from roughly +140¢ a month earlier, while Midwest elevators
trimmed bids to manage heavy harvest inflows. Processors maintained stronger premiums, particularly in
the Eastern Corn Belt, where crushers continued to bid as much at -151¢ under the November contract
(in the southeastern market) as ample supplies and recovering crush margins sustained domestic buying
interest. Nationally, basis levels near 79¢ under November are among the weakest early-harvest readings
in recent years, consistent with a futures curve near full carry and subdued export pull following the
Argentine sales surge in late September.

Wheat: Cash wheat markets softened alongside futures as exporters struggled to generate fresh
demand. HRW 11.5% FOB Gulf hovered near $270/MT, while SRW offers slipped toward $250/MT,
undercut by Russian 12.5% protein wheat near $230/MT FOB Black Sea. Basis levels at the Gulf
remained weak, reflecting both the larger-than-expected carry-in and competitive global offers from
Russia, France, and Ukraine. Domestic mill bids in the southern Plains stayed steady but offered little
counterweight to soft export margins.

So What? Cash markets across all major grains continue to reflect a bifurcated structure: export corridors
remain the weak link, pressured by costly barge freight and intense global competition, while processors
and inland consumers maintain comparatively firmer bids supported by strong crush and ethanol
economics. The wide carry across futures curves reinforces commercial storage behavior, keeping grain
in the interior and limiting Gulf recovery until freight normalizes or export demand materially improves.

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Brazil remained the global price setter in soybeans and a key low-cost origin for corn. FOB Santos
soybeans were indicated near $440/MT ($11.97/bu), keeping a clear advantage over US Gulf offers
($403/MT) into Asia. FOB Santos corn held around $205/MT ($5.20/bu equivalent), preserving a $25–
30/MT edge versus typical US Gulf corn into long-haul destinations. With Brazil’s old-crop soy program
largely pre-sold, nearby liquidity focused on spot beans and meal/oil parcels; the price leadership
persisted nevertheless, limiting US optionality in Asia and pressuring Gulf differentials despite harvest-
season board weakness.

Argentina: The late-September temporary suspension of export taxes triggered a burst of farmer selling
that allowed China to secure roughly two million tonnes of soybeans at steep discounts. That policy
window has since closed, and Up-River (Rosario) soy FOB normalized near $406/MT, erasing most of the
extreme discount versus Brazil/US For corn, Up-River FOB briefly printed $200–205/MT during the zero-
duty window before firming after the reinstatement of taxes. The quick policy swing diverted near-term
Chinese demand away from US origin just as US harvest accelerated, and while the price advantage
from Argentine supplies faded after the tax-holiday window closed, some of that nearby business will
work through lineups into early Q4.

China: Chinese buyers remain largely absent from the US soybean market instead opportunistically
sourcing soybeans from Argentine suppliers during the tax holiday. On feed grains, Dalian Jan corn near
¥2,143/MT ($7.76/bu) continued to sit above US import parity, but policy/biotech constraints and tariff
structure kept US corn exporters from translating that theoretical advantage into actual flows. The net
effect for early October was a soft US export pull in soybeans driving US shippers continued reliance on
Western Hemisphere demand (Mexico/Japan) to keep US corn loadings moving.

EU / Black Sea: Russian 12.5 percent protein wheat FOB Black Sea hovered in the low $230s/MT,
anchoring global wheat pricing and undercutting US SRW/HRW FOB (roughly $250/MT and $270/MT,
respectively). Competitive EU offers (France/Poland) and steady Black Sea availability kept US wheat
largely residual in discretionary tenders, even as CBOT printed fresh lows. The same pricing stack also
constrained US corn and soymeal into North Africa and the Mediterranean, where Black Sea/EU origins
filled a significant share of nearby demand.

Other Origins: The pre-blackout US corn export cadence remained centered on Mexico and Japan, as
shown by the 1.92 MMT sales total for the week ended Sep 18 (including 0.88 MMT to Mexico) and 1.53
MMT inspections for the week ended Sep 26, with FGIS activity continuing into Oct 2. That pattern helped
Gulf corn stay nominally competitive within the Americas even as Brazil held the edge into Asia. US
soybeans, by contrast, faced sub-0.6 MMT inspections (week ended Sep 26) and a sales slate led by
Egypt/Taiwan/Mexico, reflecting the Argentine diversion and Brazil’s ongoing price leadership.

So What? The global pricing stack this week was unchanged in direction: Russia sets the floor in wheat,
Brazil sets the pace in soy and remains aggressive in corn, and Argentina’s tax-holiday cargoes
temporarily diverted China away from U.S. beans. With U.S. Gulf soybean offers still at a premium to
Brazilian sources in the Asian markets and Black Sea wheat more competitive than US supplies, export
demand remains the weak link for US values even as domestic processors and hemisphere demand
(Mexico/Japan) provide a floor. Until relative FOB spreads narrow, or freight/logistics ease enough to
improve netbacks, US export share in key tenders will lag, keeping basis weaker at the Gulf and
reinforcing the carry-and-store incentives signaled by CME spreads.

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Oct 2 – Oct 9)

Government Shutdown: Federal agencies remained partially closed through this writing. Until the
government reopens, USDA does not publish its slate of weekly reports (Export Sales, Crop Progress),
and CFTC has suspended Commitments of Traders updates. Historically, brief shutdowns see data being
backfilled quickly; longer ones have resulted in gaps that are not retro released, with agencies
interpolating time series after the fact. The market impact remains more about near-term signal loss than
fundamentals: cash and global price relationships continue to transmit the key information.

Quarterly Grain Stocks (USDA, published Sep 30): No change from last week’s release. Sep 1 corn
stocks: 1.53 bbu (+190 mbu vs. expectations, +12% y/y), soybeans: 316 mbu (below expectations, above
last year’s 268 mbu), wheat: 2.12 bbu (+80 mbu vs. expectations, +six percent y/y). These levels remain
the anchor for pre-WASDE positioning in this blackout window. Small Grains Annual Summary (USDA,
published Sep 30): No new update this week. U.S. wheat production for 2025 at 1.985 bbu (up from 1.927
bbu prior), driven by larger HRW/HRS crops. This continues to frame the wheat market’s supply heavy
bias into October.

Crop Progress (USDA NASS, not published Oct 2–Oct 9): Latest available is week ending Sep 28
(published Sep 29): corn 18 percent harvested (vs. 15 percent 5-yr avg), soybeans 19 percent (vs. 16
percent), ratings steady (corn 66 percent G/E, soy 63 percent G/E). With warm/dry Oct 2–8 conditions,
harvest likely advanced further, but we anchor to the last official print.

Export Inspections (USDA FGIS, fee-funded operations continued): Last consolidated official totals
pre-blackout: week ending Sep 26 (published Sep 29), corn 1.53 MMT, soybeans 0.59 MMT, wheat 0.66
MMT. FGIS operations continued into the week ending Oct 2, indicating ongoing loadings, but we do not
introduce new unaudited totals.

Export Sales (USDA FAS, not published Oct 2–Oct 9): Latest available week ending Sep 18
(published Sep 25), corn 1.92 MMT (incl. 0.88 MMT to Mexico), soybeans 0.72 MMT
(Egypt/Taiwan/Mexico; China absent), wheat 0.54 MMT (Philippines/Italy among buyers). These remain
the reference points for demand into the shutdown.

Ethanol Production & Stocks (EIA, week ending Oct 3): Production increased w/w to 1.07 mbpd, with
stocks down slightly to 22.72 mb; margins remained positive enough to keep processor bids
comparatively firm versus river-exposed bids. For context, the last pre-window print was week ending Sep
27 (reported Oct 1) at 1.024 mbpd production and 23.456 mb stocks.

CFTC Commitments of Traders (publication suspended): Latest available snapshot as of Sep 23
(published Sep 26), managed money net short corn 95k, near flat/slightly short soy (-29k), heavily short
wheat (−98k SRW, −43k HRW). No new official positioning this week.

So What? With USDA weekly’s dark this week, the balance-sheet narrative is unchanged from late
September: corn retains support from Mexico/Japan shipments and steady ethanol runs, soybeans face
persistent export headwinds after Argentina’s late-September sales and Brazil’s FOB advantage, and
wheat remains constrained by Black Sea price leadership. Futures curves advertising carry, plus weak
river basis and relatively firmer processor bids, continue to direct grain toward storage and domestic use
rather than the export channel until either freight normalizes or relative FOB spreads move decisively in
the U.S. favor.

International Reports:

Brazil – CONAB Crop Outlook: No new CONAB bulletin emerged in the October 2–8 window; the next
is slated for October 14. The latest available prior to this period predicted Brazil 2025/26 corn crop at
139.7 MMT and soybeans at 177.6 MMT, reflecting upward revisions from prior estimates on improved
yields in key regions like Mato Grosso. Absent fresh volume guidance, cash prices continue to reflect
burdensome nearby world supply with soybean prices around $440/MT and corn values close to
$205/MT, sustaining pressure on US offers into Asia despite harvest-season board weakness.

Brazil – ANEC Export Lineups: ANEC figures for October 1–7, project soybean exports of 7.12 MMT for
the full month, up sharply from 4.44 MMT in the same period last year amid robust Chinese demand. The
strong October lineup reinforces the price signal, with Santos the most competitive source and the price
level there the operative guide for near-term flows. Brazilian competitiveness has limited US optionality in
long-haul destinations even as the calendar suggests US shipments should start to dominate world flows.

Argentina – Government Policy: The zero-duty window ended in late September, with the surge of
sales during that period including two million tonnes of soybeans to China at steep discounts. Post-
window, Up-River (Rosario) soy FOB normalized near $406/MT, erasing most of the extreme discount
versus Brazil/US origins; corn had briefly printed $200–205/MT during the tax holiday before firming after
reinstatement. Those late-September purchases continued to shape early-October executions, leaving
US soy exports at a disadvantage despite harvest availability, though the resumption of traditional
Argentine export taxes opens a modest window for US recovery if Chinese buying rotates back to the
northern hemisphere sources.

China – Exchange Context (DCE): Market monitoring noted Dalian Jan corn near ¥2,225/MT ($7.88/bu)
during the window. Domestic Chinese values remained above import parity, but policy/biotech constraints
continued to limit translation into U.S. corn flows, keeping reliance on Western Hemisphere demand like
Mexico/Japan to sustain loadings.

Black Sea – Public FOB Indications (Russia 12.5%): Indications held in the low $230s/MT FOB Black
Sea. Russia continued to cap world wheat values, undercutting US SRW ($250/MT) and HRW 11.5
percent ($270/MT) and keeping US wheat the residual supply in world tenders, amid ample EU/Black Sea
availability.

Global – IGC / AMIS / FAO Multilateral Balances: AMIS published the October edition of its monthly
Market Monitor report on October 3; no new IGC or FAO last week. In the absence of new supply and
demand data markets keyed off late-September national releases and spot FOBs/logistics as the primary
signals, reinforcing the abundant supply backdrop.

So What? International reports this week highlighted persistent US export challenges, with Chinese
buyers sourcing soybeans almost exclusively from South America, compounded by the Argentine tax-
holiday, resulting in one of the slowest starts to a US export season that was not a non-drought year. In
addition, Black Sea wheat shipments have also remained more competitive than US sources. While the
wheat market reflects a more traditional competitive landscape, the distortions of Chinese trade flows due
to political tension continues to erode US market share in oilseed trade. The AMIS update added no
major shifts, leaving trade keyed to spot dynamics where US Gulf offers trail competitors into key
destinations. Yet, Brazil's slowing farmer sales and Argentina's aggressive tax policy moves suggest that
cracks may be forming in the pressure and US suppliers could play a larger role in world shipments in the
coming months. Currently, US corn remains competitive into Mexico, but broader share of world trade
flows hinge on South American pacing or Black Sea hiccups, keeping basis weaker at Gulf while and
widening the carry.

.

Weather & Crop Conditions

United States
Crop Progress & Rainfall: Warm, dry conditions dominated the central U.S. through Oct 8, accelerating
harvest progress and field dry-down. With USDA data suspended during the shutdown, the last official

figures (week ending Sep 28) showed corn 18 percent harvested (vs 15 percent avg) and soybeans 19
percent (vs 16 percent avg), while winter wheat planting stood at 26 percent (vs 29 percent avg). Field
reports and weather data imply further advancement this week under clear skies. Dryness remained most
pronounced across the western Corn Belt, where subsoil deficits continued to stress stalk integrity and
raise lodging risk. The Plains saw scattered early-week showers that aided HRW emergence in some
areas, though additional moisture is still needed for uniform stands.

Temperatures: A broadly warmer-than-normal, harvest-friendly pattern prevailed. No widespread frost
threat materialized, preserving yield potential and allowing rapid natural dry-down. Heat was moderate
but, paired with the ongoing dryness, continued to sap subsoil moisture in the western Corn Belt and did
little to relieve the low Mississippi River levels constraining barge drafts.

Outlook (6–10 days): Forecasts issued during the window point to a continued warm/dry bias favoring
harvest completion across the Midwest. Limited rainfall in the Ohio and Tennessee basins could bring
some incremental improvement to river stages but is unlikely to remove navigation restrictions
immediately. In the Plains, showers, if realized, would help HRW establishment; otherwise, stand risk will
persist into mid-October.

South America: Early-October rains improved soil moisture across central Brazil, allowing soybean
planting to accelerate after a delayed start, particularly in Mato Grosso and Goiás. Southern Brazil, which
had been excessively wet earlier, turned more balanced, improving conditions for fieldwork. In Argentina,
the Pampas trended drier again after late-September relief; wheat is filling under marginal moisture, and
early corn planting is proceeding slowly while producers wait for more consistent precipitation. The next
ten days will be critical for soil recharge before full soybean sowing begins later in the month.

Global: No major weather deviations were reported in other key origins. Russia and the EU maintained
favorable late-season conditions supporting large crops, while Australia remained dry under El Niño,
trimming wheat yield potential as filling advanced. Ukraine continued to benefit from late-September rains
that improved soil conditions for winter sowing.

So What? In the United States, weather remains harvest-friendly and price-neutral to bearish, adding
supply to the pipeline while leaving river-linked basis under pressure. The focal risk now shifts south:
central Brazil’s rains must stay consistent to sustain planting momentum, while Argentine dryness
threatens early-season crop establishment. Until those patterns diverge meaningfully, the U.S. backdrop
stays supply-heavy, and South American rainfall remains the key wildcard for grain and oilseed price
direction into mid-October.

Synthesis & Outlook

This week underscored the pivot from harvest-friendly US weather and steady demand in corn to acute
export headwinds in soybeans and a still-burdensome global wheat supply. Futures and cash are broadly
aligned: corn is anchored by strong Mexican demand and firm ethanol grind, soybeans are weighed down
by the lack of demand for US exports, and wheat remains capped by competitive Russian sources.
Spreads in all three markets are in carry, but do not reflect burdensome extremes, due to the robust
domestic demand, signaling orderly commercial hedging rather than distressed selling. Basis shows the
same split: exporters under pressure from freight and South American competition, while domestic
processors keep bids firm.

Speculative positioning reflects this mixed setup. Funds trimmed shorts in corn and wheat, reducing
downside momentum, while soybeans saw outright long liquidation as Argentina’s tax holiday flooded the
market with cheap offers. The balance of positioning leaves markets sensitive: with fewer shorts to

squeeze, rallies will need true catalysts, disappointing yield reports, tighter stocks data, or fresh export
demand. Without such triggers, the path of least resistance remains sideways to slightly lower into early
October.

The backdrop going into the Oct 9 WASDE is balanced but fragile: trade consensus calls for corn yield at
184.5-185.0 bpa, soy 53.1-53.2 bpa, and only modest stock adjustments. Base case: December corn
consolidates at $4.22, November soybeans hover near $10.29, and December wheat trades around
$5.05. Carries remain moderate and storage returns positive, favoring elevators holding grain while end
users cover hand-to-mouth.

Bullish triggers: Any sustained Chinese soybean purchase, additional U.S. corn flash sales to Mexico,
or a shift in Russian export policy would prompt a stronger reaction given light liquidity. Improvement in
Mississippi River levels would also firm Gulf basis and narrow spreads, providing incremental board
support.

Bearish triggers: Ideal U.S. harvest weather and yields meeting USDA expectations could push prices
marginally lower. December corn risks testing $4.05, November soybeans $9.90–$9.95, and December
wheat could ease further if Russia continues to discount aggressively. A stronger dollar or a retreat in
crude oil would add weight to biofuel-linked demand.

Watchlist (Oct 9 – Oct 15):

USDA WASDE (Oct 9): Benchmark for new yield and stock guidance; assess whether the agency
confirms or diverges from trade expectations.

Harvest Pace: Monitor field progress into mid-month for logistical and basis implications.

River Logistics: Observe rainfall in the Ohio/Tennessee basins for potential draft relief and impact on
Gulf premiums.

Brazil Planting: Central Brazil rainfall consistency will determine whether early-season momentum is
sustained or delayed.

South American Policy & Black Sea Flows: Watch Argentina’s export rhythm post-tax window and
Russian FOB moves for any shift in global wheat pricing.

In summary: The grain complex enters WASDE week in a neutral-to-cautiously bearish posture. Supplies
are ample but manageable, spreads orderly, and cash flows differentiated by freight and domestic use.
Without a decisive catalyst, weather shock, policy disruption, or data surprise, price direction into mid-
October will likely remain rangebound, with corn and wheat favoring carry capture and soybeans defined
by South American competition and crush economics.

Ethanol for America Act

The major barrier to a higher Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) is the fuel versus food debate. Now is the
perfect time to move to E15. Corn prices are extremely low, and the latest USDA WASDE reported a record
crop and a record crop expansion.

USDA WASDE forecast corn production at 16.7 billion bushels, with the yield at 188.8 bushels per acre and
ending stocks at 2.1 billion. The season-average corn price dropped 30 cents to $3.90 a bushel. Most
importantly, 202526 crop year is expected to have 1.8 billion more bushels than 2024/25.

Executive Summary

Corn – Board Softens, Carry Incentivizes Storage
December corn eased to about $4.13/bu on Oct 15 (–2 1/4¢
w/w) as large yields and fast harvest kept pressure on the
board. The Dec/Mar carry widened to 16¢ (75 percent of full
carry), rewarding commercial ownership and confirming
ample supply. River basis stayed under stress from extreme
barge surcharges, while ethanol and feed bids in the interior
held comparatively firm. Weekly inspections (week ended
Oct 10) were 1.13 MMT, led by Mexico and Colombia;
export pace +65 percent y/y.

Soybeans – Weak Tone as Exports Lag

November soybeans slipped 15¢ to $10.07 (–1.5 percent), giving back last week’s modest gains. The
Nov/Jan spread reached 18¢ carry (100 percent of full carry) as harvest supplies swelled and Chinese
demand stayed light. Processors in the eastern Corn Belt kept crush margins positive, but river-exposed
bids weakened another 3–5¢ amid costly freight. Inspections (week ended Oct 10) were 0.994 MMT, still
roughly half last year’s pace. NOPA estimated September crush volume at 197.86 mbu exceeding
expectations, though soymeal basis stayed firm.

Wheat – Multi-Year Lows, Heavy Global Supply

Chicago SRW December fell 3¢ to $4.98/bu (–0.65 percent), touching contract low territory as Black Sea
exports and large EU stocks weighed. The Dec/Mar spread widened to 16 1/2¢ (75 percent of carry) and
open interest rose on fresh shorts. Export inspections (week ended Oct 10) 0.444 MMT, –19 percent w/w
but +17 percent y/y, led by Indonesia and Japan. Russia’s zero export tax and EU soft exports kept world
offers cheap.

visibility into ongoing flows.

Weather - Ideal Harvest Window, Brazil Dryness Emerges

Dry, warm conditions across the Midwest likely advanced corn and soy harvest from 30 percent and 50
percent (USDA, Sep 29) to an estimated 47 percent corn and 67 percent soy by Oct 13, amid the ongoing
USDA shutdown. Low river levels persisted in the Mississippi, exacerbating freight costs. Southern Plains
HRW saw limited moisture, Kansas establishment uneven. In South America, central Brazil turned dry
(Mato Grosso), stalling soy planting 11 percent complete nationally (CONAB, Oct 11), while Argentina
stayed moist, supporting wheat and early corn.

What’s Next (Oct 15 – Oct 22):

USDA Export Sales restart (Oct 19)): corn demand vs Brazil competition; soy sales to China watch

CFTC positions (Oct 20): gauge fund short extension.

River Logistics: Mississippi River levels and barge rates for basis relief or further weakness.

South America weather: central Brazil rains return vs delay scenario.

Ethanol: run rates and processor bids as harvest flows peak.

Russia/EU: export activity and tender results for wheat price direction.
