Corn Market Deep Dive

South America Outlook: South American production is the major wildcard for Q1. In Brazil, CONAB
projects 2025/26 corn output at 138.8 MMT, slightly below last year’s record (141 MMT), while we
estimate the crop closer to 136 MMT, reflecting a planted area of about 22.72 million hectares (+4 percent
YoY) and an expected yield just under 6.0 t/ha. Both agencies converge on the same acreage expansion,
but yield remains the key swing factor: CONAB assumes 6.11 t/ha, embedding a stronger La Niña risk
premium for the southern states, whereas our slightly lower yield expectation reflects a more cautious
view of early-season stress in Rio Grande do Sul and parts of Paraná even as conditions in the Center-
West remain supportive.

As of early December, northern and central Brazil (Mato Grosso, Goiás) are generally in good shape:
recent rains helped rebuild soil moisture and enabled excellent early development. By contrast, southern
Brazil (Paraná, Rio Grande do Sul) remains drier than ideal, and the planting window is closing rapidly.
Moisture deficits in RS remain a key watchpoint for first-crop yields and the timing of safrinha planting,
which begins in January and is particularly sensitive to delays. Meanwhile, Argentina’s corn outlook has
brightened significantly: the Buenos Aires Grain Exchange pegs the crop at 61 MMT, while private
forecasts stretch toward 58–62 MMT under trend-beating yield assumptions. Early planting benefited from
abundant spring rains, and field conditions are excellent, but January weather will be decisive.

If these production outlooks hold, combined Brazil + Argentina output would still deliver a sizable global
surplus, capping CBOT rallies through late Q1. But if southern Brazil’s dryness intensifies or Argentina
turns drier during pollination, the global supply narrative could quickly tighten.

Futures & Spreads: March corn traded essentially flat on the week, holding near $4.43/bu as strong
physical demand continued to offset the comfort of the broader supply backdrop. The nearby Dec–Mar
spread tightened to –11¢, representing roughly 48 percent of full carry and signaling firm nearby demand
from Gulf exporters and ethanol plants even as overall stocks remain ample. Volatility held low near 12
percent annualized, with no indication of stress or inversion in the curve. Futures remain locked in a mid-
$4 range, but the softening carry structure shows that users are still pulling hard on the front end.

Export Demand & Cash Basis: Weekly corn inspections totaled 1.421 MMT for the week ending Nov 27,
down from 1.696 MMT the prior week due to the Thanksgiving holiday but still 50% above the same week
last year. Season-to-date shipments reached 18.97 MMT, roughly 71% ahead of 2024/25, and well
aligned with an export program tracking above 2.9 bbu. Demand remains broad-based, led by Mexico,
Colombia, Japan, and South Korea. Cash markets continue to validate this strength: CIF Gulf bids firmed
another few cents and remain near multi-year winter highs, while ethanol plants in Iowa and Nebraska
continue aggressive bidding amid record-high U.S ethanol output of 1.201 mb/d, implying one of the
strongest weekly corn grinds ever. Together, basis, spreads, and inspections paint a picture of a physical
market far sturdier than the paper balance sheet suggests.

U.S Balance Sheet: The November WASDE held U.S ending stocks at 2.154 bbu, about 44 mbu above
the prior estimate, keeping the 2025/26 stocks-to-use ratio near 14 percent, comfortable enough to cap
flat-price rallies. But the physical pipeline remains tight: exports are outperforming early-season
expectations, ethanol grind is running at or near record pace, and basis levels have stayed historically
firm for late November. Until stronger farmer selling returns or export momentum slows, the board is
struggling to reflect the looseness implied by carryout.

So What? Corn continues to trade a split narrative: futures see comfortable stocks and the prospect of
massive South American production, while the cash market sees strong real-time demand and refuses to
loosen. Export pace, ethanol grind, and basis strength are anchoring the front end, narrowing spreads
and preventing breakdowns. At the same time, the shadow of a potential 195 MMT combined Brazil +
Argentina corn crop limits any sustained rally. Unless a demand shock (such as China returning as a
large buyer) or a weather disruption materializes, corn is likely to remain range-bound between $4.25 and
$4.50/bu, firm on breaks, capped on rallies, and increasingly sensitive to every South American forecast
update.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

South American Outlook: Brazil remains the dominant force in global soybean pricing. CONAB
estimates 2025/26 production at 177.6 MMT on 49.06 Mha planted, with yields near 3.62 t/ha. Our
updated forecast is higher at 179 MMT, assuming 49.25 Mha planted and a stronger yield profile near
3.66 t/ha. Expansion is centered in MATOPIBA and frontier regions where farmer margins remain
attractive. Central and northern areas (Mato Grosso, Goiás) recovered well after early-season dryness
thanks to late November rains, while Rio Grande do Sul and Paraná continue to experience below-
average moisture, a classic La Niña signature. If southern dryness persists through January, Brazil’s
soybean crop could slide toward 175–178 MMT, if rains normalize, 180 MMT remains the base case.

Argentina’s production outlook has improved dramatically versus last year. The Buenos Aires Grain
Exchange keeps its estimate near 50–52 MMT, but private models suggest potential for 55–56 MMT
under current moisture conditions. Planting progress is ahead of normal, soil moisture is excellent, and
early vegetative growth is strong. The swing factor is policy: talk of lowering or restructuring soybean
export taxes could shift planting behavior and marketing pace, adding another layer of uncertainty for Q1
global flows. Combined Brazil + Argentina production could exceed 235–238 MMT, easily surpassing last
year and increasing global ending stocks beyond USDA’s 121.99 MMT projection.

Futures & Spreads: January soybeans ended the week little changed, briefly pushing into the low
$11.40s before fading back toward $11.20/bu as the rally failed to build momentum. The market remains
split between strong near-term U.S demand and the gravitational pull of massive South American supply
expectations. The Jan/Mar spread tightened to –9¢ (41 percent of full carry), signaling firm nearby
demand from crushers and exporters even as the flat price struggles to break out. CIF NOLA barge bids
and Eastern Corn Belt processor basis stayed historically strong for early December, reflecting a pipeline
that is tighter than the balance sheet implies, processors and exporters are still competing for physical
beans.

Crush Margins & Domestic Demand: Domestic crush is the backbone of U.S soybean strength.
October NOPA crush hit a record 227.7 mbu, and industry chatter indicates that November crush stayed
extremely strong supported by favorable board margins and resilient soymeal demand. Soymeal remains
the star component: livestock and poultry sectors continue to pull aggressively, keeping interior processor
basis elevated. Soyoil softened alongside weaker diesel prices, but renewable diesel policy (45Z
anticipation, state LCFS incentives) continues to support crush margins. USDA left 2025/26 crush at 2.55
bbu, but the margin structure hints at upside risk if processors maintain current run rates.

Export Sales & Inspections: Weekly soybean export inspections were 0.92 MMT, bringing cumulative
shipments to 11.87 MMT, still about 30–35 percent behind last year but improving as recent Chinese
purchases begin to ship. Over the past two weeks, USDA confirmed roughly 1.6 MMT of U.S soybeans
sold to China, some likely destined for state reserves. These large flashes temporarily extended the U.S
export window amid Panama Canal congestion and Brazil’s slower early planting. Still, the sales book
remains fragile: USDA’s 1.635 bbu export target requires sustained Chinese buying into
January/February. Without continued follow-through, the export line will face downward pressure in the
January WASDE.

So What? Soybeans are trading between two powerful forces: a firm U.S physical pipeline in the short
run and the potential for overwhelming South American supply in the medium run. Tight Jan/Mar spreads,
strong crush, and improving exports keep the market supported for now, but the board cannot rally
meaningfully while Brazil and Argentina point toward record or near-record crops. If southern Brazil’s

dryness deepens or Argentina turns hot/dry during flowering, soybeans could quickly add a weather
premium. But if rains stabilize and Chinese buying fades, futures will struggle to hold the $11 range as Q1
approaches. In effect, the soybean market is pricing time, strength now, risk later, and the next 6–7
weeks of South American weather will determine which narrative wins.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: March SRW wheat traded in a narrow range this week, settling near $5.41/bu as the
market continued to digest the mid-November WASDE’s heavier supply outlook. Early-week weakness
gave way to a modest rebound driven by short-covering and another week of firm export execution. The
Mar/May spread held near –12¢ (50 percent of full commercial carry), slightly firmer than early November
but still consistent with a storage-rewarding structure rather than any sign of nearby tightness. Volatility
remains muted, and with funds still net short (but no longer adding aggressively), the curve is
broadcasting a classic carry market, one characterized by burdensome stocks offset by demand
steadiness that prevents further breakdown.

Global Supply & Trade Pressure: The November WASDE confirmed a heavy global backdrop: 2025/26
world wheat production at 828.9 MMT and ending stocks at 271.4 MMT, both above September and
above pre-report expectations. Russia remains the dominant bearish anchor, with production near 86.5
MMT, exports at 44 MMT, and FOB 12.5% protein offers still around $230/MT, comfortably undercutting
U.S and EU values. Black Sea export flow remains aggressive, though rising Russian internal prices and
steadily increasing export taxes could become mild friction points by Q1. For now, however, Russia
continues to set the global ceiling, and U.S wheat must price competitively to capture incremental
demand.

Cash & Basis: FOB U.S Gulf SRW wheat hovered near $230/MT ($6.85/bu equivalent), maintaining a
$20–25/MT premium to Russian offers into North Africa and Asia. This premium reflects quality and
freight, but underscores the structural disadvantage U.S wheat faces internationally. Domestic basis is
soft in most regions but shows pockets of firmness: HRW basis in the Southern Plains improved slightly
as feeders capitalized on cheap wheat relative to corn. Still, with carry near 50 percent of full and no
significant FOB tightening, the U.S cash market remains firmly in “storage mode,” not approaching any
scarcity threshold.

Trade Flows: U.S export performance remains modest by historical standards but continues to run well
ahead of last year. Weekly export inspections for the week ending Nov 27 came in at 384,881 MT
(correct), pushing cumulative 2025/26 shipments to 13.23 MMT, about 20 percent above the same period
last year (11.03 MMT). The steady outflow keeps USDA’s 900 mbu export projection possible, though still
requiring persistent execution through winter. Strength has come largely from Latin America (Mexico,
Brazil) and steady Asian demand (Philippines, Japan). A slightly weaker U.S dollar and stable freight
have improved competitiveness at the margin. Even so, the U.S remains a secondary supplier in most
global tenders, execution must remain strong to keep the export line on track.

So What? The wheat market continues walking the line between heavy global supply and incremental
demand resilience. U.S ending stocks stand at 901 mbu, world stocks above 271 MMT, and Black Sea
wheat continues to set the global floor. Yet futures have stabilized in the $5.20–$5.60/bu range,
supported by steady U.S shipments and perceptions that U.S SRW is already “cheap enough” to
discourage further fund selling. The market is not ignoring the surplus, it simply sees no urgency to push

prices dramatically lower. Chicago remains a classic carry market, biding time until a catalyst emerges:
Black Sea logistical disruption, Southern Hemisphere harvest shortfalls, or meaningful U.S winter wheat
stress. Until then, wheat is a carry trade, not a scarcity story.

US Cash Market & Basis

Corn: Cash corn basis remains historically firm for winter, with CIF Gulf bids quoted near +90¢ to +95¢
over March futures, levels rarely seen this time of year. Interior bids, particularly in the ethanol-heavy
Western Corn Belt, remain strong, with processors actively competing for spot bushels. Basis in Iowa and
Nebraska held firm to slightly higher on the week, supported by ethanol production that hit a record high
of 1.126 million barrels/day at the end of November. National basis sits around –34¢ under March,
roughly 5¢ firmer than the same time last year. The strength reflects a combination of robust domestic
demand, lean commercial ownership, and reluctant post-harvest farmer selling, many growers opted to
store rather than sell amid low flat prices and anticipation of better marketing opportunities ahead. While
the futures board continues to reflect a comfortable balance sheet, the basis structure tells a story of tight
nearby availability and strong pipeline pull.

Soybeans: Soybean basis is even tighter than corn. CIF Gulf barges for January are trading near +80¢
over Jan futures, down slightly from recent highs but still strong by historical standards. Interior processor
basis remains exceptionally firm, with spot bids in the Eastern Corn Belt (e.g. Decatur, Lafayette) at +60¢
to +75¢ over Jan, driven by record crush margins and steady soymeal demand. River elevators along the
Mississippi and Ohio have also firmed amid improving barge logistics and lingering export interest from
China. National basis averages near –26¢ under Jan, well above typical harvest-season levels. The
recent tightening of the Jan/Mar spread to –9¢ is consistent with this cash firmness. U.S exporters are
working through a burst of late-season Chinese sales, but forward basis values have started to soften
slightly as Brazil’s export season approaches. Cheaper South American offers for March forward slots are
already pressuring U.S FOB values, and exporters know they must stay competitive to defend market
share in early Q1.

Wheat: Wheat basis remains the weakest of the major row crops, but still stable given the heavier supply
backdrop. FOB Gulf SRW prices sit near $230/MT ($6.26/bu equivalent), a level that has attracted some
interest but still leaves U.S wheat $20–25/MT above Black Sea offers, particularly from Russia. Russian
12.5% protein wheat remains anchored near the low $230s/MT, and with freight advantages into North
Africa and Asia, continues to set the marginal price ceiling. In the interior U.S, HRW basis in the Southern
Plains showed minor strength this week in feed markets, as wheat remains competitive with expensive
corn in some rations. Elsewhere, basis was mostly steady to soft, in line with a comfortable carry market.
USDA’s 900 mbu export target remains achievable, but only if shipment pace continues and FOB
premiums remain defensible. For now, U.S wheat remains a storage market, not a basis-driven one.

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Brazil remains the global leader in grain export flows, even as seasonal slowdowns take hold.
November corn exports reached an estimated 5.5–6.0 MMT, slightly down from October’s record but still
robust thanks to Brazil’s massive safrinha corn crop. Soybean exports fell to 2–3 MMT as old-crop
supplies dwindled ahead of the new harvest cycle. FOB Santos soybean offers averaged $485–490/MT
($11.15–$11.25/bu), holding a $10–15/MT discount to U.S Gulf quotes for January loading. On corn,
Paranaguá FOB offers hovered near $205/MT ($5.20/bu), keeping Brazil firmly in control of Asian and
Middle Eastern destinations. Logistics through Santos and other corridors remain fluid, with no major
reports of congestion or freight delays. Central and northern soybean fields saw timely rains in late

November, improving early development, but lingering subsoil moisture deficits in parts of Goiás and the
MATOPIBA region may temper yield optimism slightly. Still, for now, Brazil remains the benchmark origin
for global corn and soybean trade into early 2026.

Argentina: Argentine export prices softened slightly in early December, weighed down by currency shifts
and political uncertainty. FOB corn (Rosario) offers were quoted near $180–185/MT, while FOB soybeans
dipped to $430–435/MT, both a touch weaker than November levels. Farmer selling has slowed again
after the expiration of the "soy dollar" FX incentive in October and in anticipation of the Dec 10
government changeover, which could include a formal peso devaluation and lower export taxes. With
informal exchange rates ballooning to ₱1,450–1460/USD in parallel markets, many growers are opting to
hold soybeans as a currency hedge, particularly ahead of expected policy clarity. Nonetheless, crush
plants around Rosario continue to operate steadily, drawing on stocks accumulated earlier in Q4. Planting
progress is strong: corn and soybean seeding both near 50 percent complete, supported by ample early
rainfall. Corn output is projected around 60–62 MMT, and soybeans at 50–55 MMT, a significant recovery
from last year’s drought-stricken campaign. Wheat harvest has begun in the north under mostly favorable
conditions, with 2025/26 production pegged around 16.5–17 MMT.

China: Chinese grain buying remains price-sensitive and cautious. U.S Gulf soybeans are offered at
+240¢/bu over Jan futures ($2.40/bu basis), which is 15¢/bu higher than Brazilian offers, keeping Brazil
as the favored origin for January/February deliveries. Chinese crushers booked additional Brazilian
cargoes in late November, while recent U.S sales are assumed to be for state reserves, not commercial
crushing. On corn, the Dec 1 removal of retaliatory tariffs on U.S grain has not yet triggered fresh
demand, Chinese buyers appear to be waiting for lower U.S prices or further policy clarity. Dalian Jan
corn futures (¥2,140/MT) remain well above world values ($6.40/bu equivalent), but internal buying
appetite is still tentative. For now, China is nibbling at U.S soy, avoiding corn, and watching the market
closely, not yet pivoting back to U.S origin in volume.

EU / Black Sea: The Black Sea continues to define world grain prices. Russian 12.5 percent protein
wheat FOB offers firmed slightly to $235–240/MT, lifted by ruble stabilization and a higher floating export
tax. But Russian shipments into North Africa and the Middle East remain strong, reinforcing their grip on
price-sensitive tenders. French wheat (FOB Rouen) near $230/MT remains at a discount to U.S Gulf
wheat, but still trails Russia in competitiveness. Ukrainian corn flows via Danube barges and rail continue
steadily into Europe, with offers around $205–210/MT, pressuring EU feed grain values. Internal EU
stocks are sufficient post-harvest, reducing short-term import demand. In protein meals, Black Sea
soymeal (Russia, Ukraine) is pricing below U.S origin and gaining share in southern Europe and the
Middle East, aided by cheaper freight and favorable FX terms.

Other Origins: No major changes from secondary exporters. Canada continues to ship spring wheat into
Asia and Mexico but remains a supplemental supplier. Australia’s wheat harvest is underway: Eastern
states report decent quality and protein, but Western Australia’s ongoing drought is dragging national
yield lower. Buyers expect mixed quality and smaller volumes than last year’s record crop. India remains
sidelined from export markets, with wheat and rice restrictions still active and no new policy guidance.
South Africa’s summer crop season is proceeding normally, and no significant disruptions have emerged
from other minor global suppliers.

So What? Global grain flows remain clearly bifurcated: Brazil and Russia dominate corn, soybeans, and
wheat, respectively, while U.S exporters play a secondary role, relying on regional advantages and niche
opportunities (e.g. corn to Mexico, soymeal to inland Asia, wheat to Latin America). The FOB spread

remains structurally wide, Brazilian corn/soy and Russian wheat continue to price below U.S Gulf
equivalents even with strong U.S basis and logistics. Unless weather, policy, or demand dynamics shift
materially, such as a South American crop shortfall or China returning as a consistent U.S buyer, the U.S
position in global flows will remain tactical rather than dominant.

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Nov 21 – Dec 4)

Government Data & Reporting: USDA data flow remained uninterrupted this week, with Export
Inspections and Sales reports released on time and no major scheduling delays reported. The market is
now turning its attention to the upcoming December WASDE (scheduled for Dec 9), which is not expected
to bring significant U.S balance sheet changes but may offer early guidance on South American crop
prospects or export line revisions. The return of CFTC Commitments of Traders reporting has restored
visibility into fund positioning, though speculative flows remain light overall.

Crop Progress: National harvest is now essentially complete. USDA did not publish a new Crop
Progress report during this period, as corn and soybean harvests are considered wrapped up for
statistical purposes. Private surveys and regional updates confirm that fieldwork has concluded across
most of the Corn Belt. In winter wheat, the market remains focused on condition ratings and drought
persistence in the central and southern Plains, particularly western Kansas and Oklahoma. Early-season
HRW ratings are mixed, and emergence is proceeding at a normal pace, though some key areas remain
moisture-deficient as dormancy sets in.

Export Inspections (USDA FGIS – week ending Nov 28): Corn inspections totaled 1.42 MMT, a
holiday-shortened volume but still well above last year’s 0.95 MMT for the same week. Season-to-date
corn loadings have reached 18.97 MMT, running 70 percent ahead of last year and staying comfortably
aligned with USDA’s upgraded 2.3 bbu export forecast. Soybean inspections came in at 0.92 MMT,
bringing cumulative shipments to 11.87 MMT, still sharply below last year’s front-loaded pace, but
improving modestly in recent weeks as Chinese purchases begin to ship. Wheat inspections were
384,881 MT, lifting cumulative exports to 13.23 MMT, roughly 20 percent above last year’s levels and
broadly consistent with USDA’s 900 mbu export projection. Despite seasonal slowing, physical movement
remains supportive across corn and wheat, while soybeans continue to rely on incremental Chinese
demand to narrow the year-over-year deficit.

Export Sales (USDA FAS – week ending October 30): Export sales data highlighted steady activity
across major commodities amid ongoing catch-up reporting due to funding delays. For corn, net sales
reached 2.36 MMT with exports at 1.54 MMT, led by consistent demand from markets like Mexico,
Colombia, and Japan, staying aligned with the pace needed to hit USDA’s approximately 2.975 bbu
forecast. Soybeans saw a solid performance with net sales of 1.33 MMT and exports at 1.03 MMT; recent
daily announcements include about 0.435 MMT in net Chinese purchases in late November (e.g.,
312,000 MT on November 28 and 123,000 MT on November 24), linked to a new U.S-China deal for 12
MMT in November-December, some potentially for state reserves. These flows are helping narrow the
year-on-year deficit, though total commitments remain behind the seasonal average. Wheat sales were
modest at 0.53 MMT net with exports at 0.30 MMT, unchanged versus recent weeks; a daily sale of about
133,000 MT of white wheat to China was reported on November 20, but overall, China has not yet
emerged as a significant buyer ahead of the December 1 tariff suspension. Traders are watching for
confirmation of additional business in the December 8 catch-up report. Overall, the sales tone improved,
but forward book growth will need to accelerate into January to justify USDA’s current export lines.

Ethanol Production & Stocks (EIA – week ending Nov 29): U.S ethanol production continued its strong
late-November run, with output rising to 1.126 million barrels/day in the week ending Nov 28, the highest
level of the month and up from 1.113 mb/d the prior week. The four-week trend has held between 1.07–
1.13 mb/d, confirming steady industrial demand and a consistently firm pull from Western Corn Belt
processors. At current yields, the latest print implies a weekly corn grind of roughly 100–102 million
bushels, supportive of nearby basis and spreads. Ethanol stocks ticked slightly higher, in line with normal
pre-year-end seasonal builds, while margins remain comfortably positive thanks to stable corn prices and
resilient DDGS values.

So What? Market sentiment this week was driven more by real-time signals than static supply numbers.
In corn, record ethanol output and strong inspections provided firm demand-side support even as carryout
remains heavy. Soybeans benefited from confirmed Chinese purchases and continued crush strength,
helping offset the lagging export book. Wheat remains the weakest on paper, but decent export execution
and limited fund pressure have helped it stabilize near mid-range levels. With no new WASDE revisions
yet and no South American crop cuts confirmed, traders continue to lean on physical indicators, basis,
inspections, processor bids, to define near-term direction. Futures are range-bound, but underlying
demand in corn and soy continues to validate board values even as global supply caps any sustained
rallies.

Weather & Crop Conditions

United States
Crop Progress & Logistics: U.S harvest has officially concluded, with both corn and soybean collection
finishing well ahead of the five-year average. Dry autumn conditions enabled rapid progress and minimal
quality issues. With row crops off the field, attention has shifted to winter wheat and infrastructure. Winter
wheat entered dormancy with a generally decent start, although key HRW areas in western Kansas and
the Texas Panhandle remain moisture deficient. Soil moisture is mostly adequate elsewhere, but spring
recharge will be essential in the drought-prone southern Plains. River levels, meanwhile, have rebounded
meaningfully from October’s historic lows: gauges at Memphis, St. Louis and Baton Rouge all showed
firm improvements, allowing barge drafts to normalize. Navigation on the Lower Mississippi and Ohio
Rivers is now operating under standard conditions, a positive shift for basis and export flow into year-end.

Temperatures & Energy: Mild early-winter weather across the U.S and Europe has helped hold natural
gas prices steady, with no polar vortex threats or significant frost events reported. For grain markets, this
reduces fertilizer cost pressure and keeps winterkill risks low. NOAA’s near-term outlook (6–10 day) shows
seasonal to above-normal temperatures in the Midwest and Plains, with limited precipitation expected for
the southwestern HRW belt.

Brazil
North–South Weather Divide Deepens: Brazil’s weather pattern remained sharply split between northern
and southern regions, a classic signal of the emerging La Niña. November’s second half delivered
consistent rains across Mato Grosso, Goiás and MATOPIBA, supporting strong soybean and first-crop corn
emergence. Planting is essentially complete in those zones, with agronomists noting “very good” early stand
ratings and topsoil moisture at or above normal. However, southern states like Rio Grande do Sul and
Santa Catarina stayed dry through late November and early December. Farmers in Paraná benefited from
earlier rains, allowing for good crop establishment, but later-planted fields in Rio Grande do Sul are now
entering reproductive stages under significant moisture stress.

Scattered early-December showers offered minor relief, but forecasts from INMET and NOAA signal subpar
rainfall across southern Brazil through at least mid-December. This is a critical window: first-crop corn is
nearing tasseling and early soybeans are moving into pod set. If dryness persists, yield loss in the far south

will become increasingly likely, potentially offsetting northern gains and trimming Brazil’s record production
potential. In MATOPIBA, improved rainfall since late October has firmed up yield prospects, especially in
irrigated zones of Bahia and Piauí. Port logistics and interior freight flows remain unimpeded by weather to
date.

Argentina
Planting Surge & Favorable Conditions: Argentina’s planting and early crop development continue to
progress under broadly favorable conditions. Soybean sowing accelerated meaningfully last week,
advancing 8.7 percentage points to cover roughly 44–45 percent of the projected 17.6 MHa for 2025/26.
Despite the strong weekly push, planting remains about 9 points behind last year and slightly below the
five-year average due to field-access issues in parts of central Buenos Aires, where excessive moisture
has slowed machinery entry. In contrast, first-crop soybean planting across both core regions is nearing
completion, and second-crop soybeans are now gaining momentum as winter grain harvest wraps up.

Corn planting reached about 44 percent of intended area after a solid 5-point weekly gain, with late-window
sowing opening up across the central and southern agricultural belt. Crop conditions are exceptionally
strong: 86 percent of planted corn is rated Good to Excellent, supported by widespread soil moisture
recharge. Nationally, 94 percent of the agricultural area sits within Adequate Optimal moisture ranges, one
of the best early-season profiles in recent years. While localized excess moisture persists in the Southern
Core and pockets of central Buenos Aires, these issues have not altered the overall narrative. Ample subsoil
reserves are ensuring uniform emergence and strong early vegetative development, placing Argentina on
a trajectory consistent with above-trend yield potential heading into the critical January weather window.

Global
Winter Wheat & Australian Harvest: The Northern Hemisphere’s winter crops entered dormancy under
mostly favorable conditions. Russia, Ukraine, France and Germany all reported sufficient pre-winter rainfall
and above-average temperatures, supporting good stand development and minimizing frost risk.
FranceAgriMer held French wheat ratings steady in the high-60s percent good-to-excellent. The Black Sea
region, particularly southern Russia, enjoyed mild weather that allowed late planting to finish without
interruption.

In Australia, harvest moved forward in New South Wales and Victoria with mixed yield outcomes. The
eastern belt received some late-season rainfall that improved quality, but Western Australia’s persistent
drought sharply curtailed output there. National wheat production will fall well short of last year’s record
but remains a meaningful contributor to global supply. Elsewhere, India’s rabi crop season progressed
normally, and South African summer grains are being planted under near-average early summer weather.

So What?
The global weather narrative remains heavily centered on South America. Brazil shows classic La Niña
divergence: the Central-West and MATOPIBA are in excellent shape after a rebound in November
rainfall, but southern states are deteriorating rapidly. Rio Grande do Sul in particular is approaching a
critical stage, and a continued dry bias into mid-December would introduce meaningful downside risk to
national yield potential. Argentina, by contrast, is operating under near-ideal conditions, with planting
ahead of schedule and moisture profiles rated excellent in most major zones.

In the U.S, the post-harvest lull means weather plays a secondary role, though improving river levels
have enhanced grain movement and preserved strong basis into year-end. The mild winter start globally
has further removed energy and fertilizer cost pressure. For now, the real volatility risk lies in southern
Brazil and, to a lesser extent, in Argentina’s January weather window. Markets will remain acutely
sensitive to rainfall updates from Rio Grande do Sul and crop model revisions over the next two weeks.

Synthesis & Outlook

Grain and oilseed markets head into December with a firm but uneasy, by resilient physical demand yet
constrained by towering global supply expectations. Futures remain rangebound across the board: March
corn holding near $4.40/bu, January soybeans fluctuating around $11.15–11.20, and SRW wheat
bouncing inside the $5.30–$5.60 range. In all three markets, spreads continue to tell a more supportive
story than flat price: the corn Mar/May narrowed under –11¢ (48 percent of full carry), soybean Jan/Mar
briefly reached –9¢, and wheat Mar/May trades steady near 41 percent of full carry, clear signals that
end-users are still bidding aggressively for nearby coverage even as longer-term outlooks lean heavy.

On the global front, South America is once again the market’s primary driver of potential change. Brazil’s
crop outlook is split: Northern and Central regions are recovering well with favorable rains, while the
South (especially Rio Grande do Sul) edges toward stress. Argentina, meanwhile, is off to its best start in
years, with near-perfect planting conditions and moisture reserves built for mid-season. This setup raises
the stakes for December weather. If La Niña-linked dryness worsens in southern Brazil, or Argentina’s
early-season luck turns, then the board may finally break out of its holding pattern. Until then, cash
market dynamics will continue to steer the ship, not macro sentiment or managed money.

Bullish triggers: Upside risks continue to cluster around strong U.S domestic demand: record ethanol
output, firm crush margins, and resilient basis all show that real use pull remains stronger than the
balance sheets imply. Weather is the second lever, any deterioration in southern Brazil or Argentina
during pollination would quickly challenge expectations for record South American crops. Additional
Chinese buying, whether in soybeans or a surprise corn tender after the Dec 1 tariff suspension, would
also tighten nearby spreads. Finally, if U.S export execution remains solid through December, it would
reinforce the physical foundation supporting the front end of the curve.

Bearish triggers: The key bearish catalyst remains confirmation of record-large South American crops
without meaningful yield losses, which would cement ample global supplies into Q1. Argentina delivering
above-trend yields would add further weight. A slowdown in Chinese buying after reserve needs are met,
paired with softer Gulf basis and re-widening spreads, would weaken the U.S outlook. And globally,
another move lower in Black Sea FOB wheat or continued aggressive Russian tendering would pressure
U.S exports and keep rallies capped.

Watchlist (Dec 7 – Dec 13):

Mid-month Brazilian rainfall forecasts - divergence between North and South remains critical

USDA export sales and inspections – are Chinese purchases converting to actual shipments?

U.S ethanol grind – does last week’s record output hold, or was it a one-off?

Argentine planting pace and early condition ratings from BCBA and private analysts

CIF basis and processor bids – are end-users still paying up for physical, or does demand start to
soften?

In summary: The grain market remains a tug-of-war between firm nearby usage and looming future
supply. U.S basis strength, ethanol and crush data, and export flow continue to validate current board
levels, even if the balance sheets suggest ample cushion. South America now holds the swing vote: if
Brazil’s southern belt or Argentina falter, the floor will rise; if both deliver big, the ceiling may fall. Until
clarity arrives, the board will likely continue to drift inside a narrow range, supported by strong physical
bids, but capped by the world’s surplus.

at 1.635 bbu, and crush unchanged at 2.55 bbu. Futures softened through Dec 10, with Jan trading below

notably firmer: national basis stayed elevated, interior processors continued bidding aggressively, and

Policy focus centered on China’s tariff rollback, now the primary wildcard for cross-commodity demand
into early 2026. While soybeans remain under MFN treatment, reduced tariffs on corn and wheat add
forward optionality for U.S exporters at a time when global supplies remain heavy and trade flows
sensitive to incremental shifts in relative pricing.

Weather – U.S Harvest Nears Completion as South American Patterns Reassert Market
Influence

With U.S corn and soybean harvests essentially wrapped up, weather’s influence shifted toward logistics
and export flow. Rainfall across central and northern Brazil improved soil moisture and helped planting
recover, while southern regions continued to face moisture stress that could shape early expectations for
soybeans and downstream safrinha corn. Argentina maintained a constructive pattern with adequate
moisture supporting early corn planting and wheat finishing. With WASDE’s South American production
assumptions already robust, any persistent dryness in southern Brazil, or a material deviation from normal
precipitation patterns, will become a more active driver of spreads and narrative into late December.

Corn Market Deep Dive

Post-WASDE Reaction & Balance Sheet: The December WASDE finally moved the corn balance sheet
in the direction the physical market had been trading for weeks, and this time the adjustment was large
enough to meaningfully shift market tone. USDA raised exports by 125 mbu to 3.2 bbu, the strongest
acknowledgement yet of the exceptional early-season shipment pace and pulled ending stocks down to
2.029 bbu from 2.154 bbu. That 125 mbu export jump is not cosmetic: it marks USDA’s recognition that
inspections running 60–70 percent above last year are not a fluke but a structural feature of the first
quarter.

Even so, the sheet remains comfortably supplied. A 2.0+ bbu carryout still places corn far from tight, and
stocks-to-use near 13.8 percent reinforces that domestic users will not face scarcity barring a South
American problem. The report tightened the narrative without flipping it, and that distinction matters:
WASDE confirmed that demand is materially stronger than earlier assumptions but also made clear that
the U.S remains well-supplied even after the adjustment.

Globally, USDA trimmed world stocks to 279 MMT, mostly on reduced Ukraine production. While this
nudges the global balance tighter, world stocks-to-use remains adequate and does not introduce scarcity
concerns. In short: WASDE validated the physical market’s message, corrected the export line
meaningfully, and narrowed the gap between paper and reality, yet kept the broader supply outlook
comfortably loose unless South American weather turns decisively negative.

Futures & Spreads: Futures traded that “tightening but not tight” message with a restrained bid rather
than a breakout. March 2026 corn spent most of the week gravitating in a narrow band around the mid-
$4.40s, ending modestly higher and near the top of the recent range as the post-WASDE bump added a
bit of optimism to an otherwise range-bound market. Volatility stayed low, firmly in the low teens on an
annualized basis, underscoring that the market is not pricing an imminent shock so much as a gentle
grind higher on better demand. The more telling move came in structure: the nearby Dec–Mar spread
tightened from –11¢ to roughly –7¢, only about one-third of full commercial carry. That is still a carry
market, but a relatively tight one for corn. It signals commercials are comfortable taking delivery or owning
corn nearby instead of demanding a full-carry discount to hold it, which lines up with how aggressively
exporters and ethanol plants are pulling on the pipeline. Further out, the curve still carries (Mar–May
around –11¢), so there is no sign of inversion or outright shortage, just a front end that feels much firmer
than a 2+ bbu carryout would normally suggest.

Export Demand & Cash Basis: Export inspections for the week ending Dec 4 reached 1.45 MMT,
keeping cumulative shipments well ahead of last year and broadly aligned with USDA’s decision to raise
exports to 3.2 bbu in December WASDE. The CIF Gulf remained well-supported, while interior processor
and ethanol bids held firm against limited farmer selling. Ethanol production for the week ending
December 5 averaged near 1.10 mbpd, in line with or slightly above typical early-December levels,
consistent with late-year seasonal strength and helping sustain firm interior basis. National basis near –
42¢ versus March futures reflect a market still pulling hard on nearby supply, even with carryout above
2.0 bbu. Until farmer movement increases or Brazil’s offers break the global feed-grain arbitrage, the cash
pipeline will continue to set the tone.

South America & Global Trade Context: South America remains the defining forward risk. Brazil’s crop
sits near 135 MMT, with strong early conditions in Mato Grosso and Goiás but persistent moisture
concerns in Paraná and Rio Grande do Sul that could affect first-crop yields and delay safrinha planting.
A late safrinha would push pollination deeper into the dry-risk window. Argentina, by contrast, is staging a
strong rebound toward 55 MMT, with upside if current weather holds. Policy shifts, particularly potential
devaluation or export-tax changes, remain a wildcard for flow timing. Brazilian FOB values near $5.20/bu
keep the country the cheapest major origin into global feed markets and reinforce the sense that a large
wave of supply could still arrive if weather cooperates.

So What? Corn enters mid-December balanced between a tight-feeling front end and a comfortable
forward supply outlook. WASDE finally acknowledged the demand pulse, but the combination of a still-
heavy U.S carryout and large South American potential caps rallies. At the same time, cash, spreads and
ethanol demand continue to impose a meaningful floor under the board, leaving futures in a stable, range-
bound structure biased firmer on dips. For end-users, that supports opportunistic nearby coverage; for
producers, it argues for incremental sales on rallies ahead of South America confirming, or disproving, the
surplus narrative.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

Post-WASDE Assessment: The December WASDE delivered a neutral-to-soft signal for soybeans,
keeping the U.S balance sheet ending stocks untouched at 290 mbu despite several weeks of sluggish
export performance. USDA left crush at a record 2.55 bbu and nudged global ending stocks higher to
around 122.4 MMT, driven mainly by larger South American potential and leaving the global stocks-to-use
ratio squarely in adequate, not tight territory even as nearby physical indicators remain firm. For a market
that came into the report with funds holding their largest net long since April, roughly 120k contracts,
expecting USDA to validate tightening through lower exports or a stronger domestic-use signal, the lack
of adjustment forced an immediate repricing. The result was classic long liquidation: not a collapse, but a
reset toward a world where today’s firm pipeline coexists with the prospect of a large South American
crop. In short, WASDE confirmed that nearby strength is real, but not yet strong enough for USDA to alter
its forward balance-sheet assumptions.

Futures & Spreads: Futures responded with a softer, choppy tone as January beans slipped into the
upper $10s after briefly testing the $11.40–$11.50 zone on optimism around Chinese buying and crush
margins. The neutral WASDE and improving South American moisture flow capped that move and
pushed futures back into the lower end of the recent range. The Jan–Mar spread eased from –7¢ to
around –11¢ carry, still only about half of full commercial carry, signaling that front-end tightness remains
but has relaxed slightly as late-November loadings and farmer movement worked through the system.
Further out, the curve returns to more traditional carry consistent with a market expecting comfortable
supplies once Brazilian harvest begins.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets continue to tell a tighter story than the board. CIF Gulf barges remain
elevated at +75–80¢ over January, and processor bids across major Midwest hubs hold near +60–75¢
over, aligning with historically strong crush margins. National basis remains firm for this point in the
season, underscoring that end-users still need coverage and are unwilling to relax bids even with a
comfortable forward balance sheet. The Jan–Mar spread, while slightly softer post-WASDE, remains only
half of full carry and matches the physical tightness observed across both export and crush corridors.

Funds & Positioning: Speculative positioning amplified volatility around the report. With no updated
CFTC data, precise figures remain unclear, but funds carried a sizeable net long into WASDE, making the
lack of a bullish adjustment especially impactful. The downward drift that followed fits a story of position
cleanup rather than bearish conviction. With futures stabilizing and spreads still relatively firm, speculative
influence has shifted from a tailwind to a neutral presence, leaving fundamentals, basis, spreads, and
weather, to guide direction.

Crush Margins & Domestic Demand: Crush remains the dominant source of nearby soybean support.
Record October NOPA crush at 227.7 mbu, and expectations for another near-record in November,
confirm processors are running hard into year-end. USDA held crush at 2.55 bbu in WASDE, a number
that many in the trade view as conservative given current margin structures. Soymeal continues to anchor
crush economics thanks to strong feed demand, while soybean oil lags on softer energy markets and
policy uncertainty, but still benefits from structural renewable diesel support. Every incremental rise in
crush carries direct balance-sheet implications, which keeps processors bidding aggressively for nearby
bushels even as futures soften.

Export Sales & Inspections: Weekly inspections beyond Dec 4 were not yet published, but the prior
report confirmed steady but seasonally modest volumes. USDA recorded 462,000 MT of soybean sales
to China on Dec 4 (4.9 million bushels), reflecting reserve-driven buying rather than improved crush
margins. Cumulative shipments remain sharply below last year, and Brazil continues to dominate forward
demand with more competitive FOB offers. With short-term volatility running in the high-teens and the
Jan/Mar spread easing toward –11¢, the export side remains a drag even as crush and basis stay
historically strong.

So What? Soybeans enter mid-December stuck between a firm nearby pipeline and a potentially heavy
forward supply picture. WASDE validated neither a tightening U.S sheet nor an export-driven bullish shift,
reinforcing a market that must balance record crush and historically strong basis against South America’s
large production potential and lagging U.S export pace. For now, crushers and cash strength keep the
board supported near $11, but rallies above the mid-$11s require either sustained Chinese commercial
buying or a meaningful deterioration in Brazil’s southern weather. Until one of those emerges, the market
is likely to continue trading a narrow, demand-supported but supply-capped range.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Post-WASDE Assessment: The December WASDE reaffirmed wheat as the heaviest balance sheet
among major row crops, but the weight remains overwhelmingly global rather than domestic. USDA left
U.S ending stocks unchanged at 901 mbu, already a six-year high, and made no adjustments to
production, use or exports. The bearish impulse came entirely from abroad: global ending stocks were
raised to 274.9 MMT, the largest in five years, driven by record crops in Canada (40 MMT) and Argentina
(24 MMT) along with incremental increases across the EU, Australia and Russia. The 7.5 MMT month-on-
month expansion pushed the world further from any tightness narrative and reinforced that the surplus
resides exactly where it matters most: export-oriented origins. For the U.S, the unchanged sheet
underscored the same message as November, wheat is heavy, but the new burden is global, not
domestic, and the market continues trading that distinction.

Futures & Spreads: Price action captured the WASDE tension: bearish global stocks met a U.S market
reluctant to break lower. March SRW briefly dipped toward $5.30/bu after the report before stabilizing as
buyers defended perceived value. The Dec–Mar SRW spread flattened to 0¢ carry, not because the front
end tightened, but due to delivery mechanics as the December contract rolled off. Structurally, wheat still
behaves like a classic carry market supported by abundant supply. The curve signals storage economics,
not scarcity, and nothing in WASDE altered that posture.

Cash & Basis: Cash wheat continues to behave better than the WASDE tables alone suggest. Gulf SRW
FOB values around $236.25/mt maintain moderate competitiveness, and steady demand from Latin
America and Asia persists despite Russian offers pricing lower. Weekly inspection data beyond Dec 4 is
not yet available, but cumulative shipments remain ahead of last year and consistent with USDA’s 900
mbu projection. Interior basis is steady to slightly soft but shows no signs of stress, confirming that
physical availability remains ample without weighing on spot bids.

Trade Flows: U.S wheat trade flows held steadier than the WASDE narrative would suggest. Weekly
export inspections came in at 393,341 MT, keeping cumulative shipments about 20 percent ahead of last
year’s pace and firmly on track with USDA’s 900 mbu projection. Despite facing deeply discounted Black
Sea competition, Russian 12.5 percent FOB wheat holding in the low-$230s/mt and continuing to anchor
global tender pricing, the U.S still secured consistent demand in Latin America, Africa, and quality-
sensitive Asian markets. The combination of stable execution, resilient FOB values near $236/mt at the
Gulf, and the absence of cancellations reinforced that U.S wheat is not being crowded out, but instead
carving out reliable, incremental business even in a surplus-heavy world. It is not a bullish export
program, but it is unquestionably stronger than the global stock backdrop implies, which helps explain the
board’s reluctance to break below the low-$5 range.

So What? Post-WASDE wheat remains a story of bearish paper vs. less-bearish physical reality. USDA
confirmed world supplies are the largest in five years and growing in the most competitive export regions,
cementing global surplus as the dominant narrative. Yet the U.S balance sheet did not worsen, basis

remains stable, exports continue to outperform expectations, and Gulf SRW still finds demand despite
cheaper Black Sea alternatives. The curve remains a classic carry structure, making wheat primarily a
hedge-selling and storage-capture market. Upside requires disruption, either Black Sea flow issues or
meaningful production losses in a major exporter. Absent that, sideways trade in the low-to-mid $5s
remains the baseline, with U.S execution preventing a breakdown and global surplus capping rallies.

US Cash Market & Basis

Corn: Corn cash markets continued to outperform the board, with basis strength and logistics
improvements reinforcing the same theme that has defined early December: the physical pipeline is
tighter than the futures curve suggests. Weekly export inspections printed 1.45 MMT, extending the
streak of strongly above-year-ago loadings and keeping cumulative shipments roughly 36 percent ahead
of last year’s pace. Gulf exporters remained active buyers as barge drafts on the Lower Mississippi
improved, and CIF Gulf corn held firm to slightly stronger, supported by a consistent pull from both export
channels and ethanol plants. Interior basis held steady across most processing and river corridors, with
plants still running hard enough to keep a reliable bid under nearby bushels despite softness in crude oil.
National basis remains described as “firm for early December,” reflecting ongoing restraint from farmers
who stored aggressively at harvest and limited new selling even as futures attempted to rebound.

Soybeans: Soybean cash signals remained the tightest of the three row crops. CIF barges held
historically strong for harvest, firming around expectations tied to record domestic crush demand and a
wave of Chinese buying that briefly lifted exporter urgency. Processor and river bids stayed firm, with
crushers continuing to anchor the market thanks to exceptional margins implied by record October NOPA
crush (227.65 mbu) and expectations for continued heavy throughput. Weekly inspections near 1.01 MMT
remain well below year-ago levels, yet basis strength reflects the broader theme of front-end demand
outstripping what the paper balance sheet implies. The narrowing of the Jan–Mar spread, from –14¢ to –
7¢, has been mirrored almost one-for-one in physical behavior: a market where crushers and exporters
will not relax their bids despite USDA’s export cut.

Wheat: Wheat basis was softer than corn and soybeans but still showed resilience given the global
surplus indicated by WASDE. Export inspections of 393.3k MT kept cumulative shipments in the high-
teens percent above last year, reinforcing the steady execution that has supported SRW and HRW basis
throughout Q4. Gulf and PNW FOB indications moved only modestly week-over-week even with Russian
12.5 percent wheat holding in the low-$230s/mt, a sign that U.S exporters are still finding demand in
regional markets despite heavy Black Sea competition. Interior basis across the Southern Plains milling
markets remains defensive but not collapsing, consistent with a curve that remains in carry but where
exporters see no need to aggressively discount to clear supply.

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Brazil remained the dominant global supplier of both soybeans and corn, with export pace and
FOB pricing continuing to shape U.S competitiveness. For soybeans, Gulf-to-China spreads remained
pressured by strong Brazilian FOB offers, which stayed competitive into Asia and undercut U.S values
despite firm U.S basis. Corn also remained firmly in Brazil’s hands, with its FOB pricing into Southeast
Asia still the cheapest origin and supported by ample internal supply and efficient freight. Central and
northern soybean-planting regions progressed normally thanks to scattered rainfall, while parts of Rio
Grande do Sul and Paraná continued to face moisture deficits that could introduce early-season risk
premium. Export corridors at Santos and Paranaguá were reported as running smoothly, with no major
congestion.

Argentina: Up-River FOB prices were steady to slightly lower, with corn near $205/MT and soymeal
around $305/MT, both broadly in line with recent weeks. Local liquidity remained cautious as farmers
slowed sales following the end of Argentina’s export incentive window. Early corn and soybean
establishment benefited from improved soil moisture, and wheat harvest conditions were largely normal.
Argentina’s broader weather backdrop remains more favorable than Brazil’s southern regions, but
currency pressure in parallel markets keeps farmer selling patterns uneven and export pricing slightly
more volatile.

China: China remained firmly Brazil-centric in its import activity. While the U.S scored notable soybean
business earlier in the period, approximately 800,000 tonnes linked to COFCO plus 792,000 tonnes
confirmed in USDA daily sales, there were no additional flash sales reported during this week’s window.
U.S offers into China remained at a premium to Brazilian equivalents, limiting incremental demand.
China’s tariff rollback on U.S wheat and corn (soybeans unchanged under MFN) has not yet translated
into visible buying shifts, though it remains a medium-term wildcard. Dalian markets reflected a cautious
domestic tone: soymeal eased 1.7 percent, while corn held firm, still sitting well above import parity and
offering limited incentive for replacement buying.

EU / Black Sea: Russian wheat continues to anchor global pricing, with 12.5 percent protein FOB values
in the low-$230s/mt, cheap enough to cap global wheat upside and limit U.S competitiveness in major
tenders. EU wheat moved only modestly, with Euronext Dec near €197.5/mt, keeping EU origin
competitive but not aggressive enough to displace Russia in North African and Middle Eastern tenders.
Black Sea competitiveness remains the structural headwind for U.S exporters, even as U.S shipments
continue outperforming year-ago levels.

So What? The U.S cash markets continue to deliver a tighter message than the futures curve, especially
in corn and soybeans where basis and export execution remain far stronger than the paper ending-stocks
figures imply. Internationally, Brazil and Russia maintain pricing leadership, Brazil on corn and soybeans,
Russia on wheat, limiting the U.S ability to gain traction in major import corridors. China’s buying remains
the swing variable in soybeans, while improving South American weather tempers frontline risk. Until FOB
spreads narrow or Chinese buying meaningfully reaccelerates, U.S strength will remain anchored in
domestic demand (crush, ethanol, river flows) rather than export arbitrage.

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Dec 4 – Dec 10)

Government Data & Reporting: USDA releases ran normally this week, giving the market a clean read
on inspections and the December WASDE. Corn saw a sharp export increase to 3.2 bbu, soybeans were
unchanged with a 290 mbu carryout and record crush, and wheat moved heavier globally with the largest
world stocks in five years. Reporting clarity helped firm price interpretation, especially in soybeans where
recent Chinese activity needed official confirmation. With no CFTC updates, traders again relied on
spreads, basis and flow rather than speculative positioning. Crop Progress is effectively finished for corn
and soybeans, shifting market focus fully to logistics and execution.

Crop Progress: Harvest is no longer driving price discovery. With corn and soybeans essentially
wrapped up, the market now watches whether river systems, processors and export channels can
continue absorbing supply at the pace suggested by strong basis behavior. In South America, early-
season conditions remain the key input: central and northern Brazil improved on moisture, while southern

states stayed patchy enough to preserve an early risk premium. Argentina maintained broadly favorable
conditions, supporting global supply stability.

Export Inspections (USDA FGIS – week ending Dec 4): Export inspections for the week ending Dec 4
showed another week of solid corn movement at 1.45 MMT, keeping cumulative shipments well above
last year and aligned with USDA’s upward export revision in the December WASDE. Soybean inspections
printed about 1.01 MMT, essentially steady week-over-week but still far behind last year’s pace, reflecting
continued dependence on intermittent Chinese reserve buying rather than broad-based commercial
demand. Wheat inspections came in at roughly 393k MT, keeping cumulative shipments in the high-teens
percent above last year and reinforcing the view that U.S wheat continues to execute respectably despite
globally heavy stocks.

Export Sales: Chinese demand was quieter this week. Earlier COFCO purchases (≈800k tonnes) and
USDA daily flashes totaling 792,000 tonnes had lifted sentiment earlier in the period, but no new sales
were reported during the Dec 4–10 window. China continued favoring cheaper Brazilian coverage,
keeping U.S exports reliant on sporadic reserve-driven buying rather than commercial crusher demand.
Corn and wheat likewise showed no meaningful booking response to China’s tariff rollback, which
remains a medium-term rather than immediate catalyst for U.S demand.

Ethanol Production & Industrial Demand: Ethanol production held steady through the period, with
weekly output near 1.10 mbpd, consistent with typical early-December strength and helping sustain firm
interior bids. Softer crude narrowed blending margins somewhat, but plants continued to pull hard on
nearby bushels, reinforcing the tighter Dec–Mar spread and contributing to the front-end firmness visible
across basis markets. Industrial use is not expanding, but it remains reliably strong enough to keep
processors competitive for supply.

NOPA Crush & Soy Products: Crush remains a defining pillar of soybean support. October NOPA crush
set a record at 227.65 mbu, and margins remain historically wide despite softer soybean oil. USDA held
its full-year crush at 2.55 bbu, already conservative, which continues to validate strong processor bids
and a front end tighter than the 290 mbu carryout implies. Soymeal remains the margin driver; oil remains
weaker but still structurally supported by renewable diesel.

So What? With WASDE absorbed, the market traded physical signals over paper theory. Corn
fundamentals firmed again on strong inspections and resilient basis, supporting a front end much tighter
than the carryout implies. Soybeans balanced weak exports against record crush and recent Chinese
buying, keeping nearby strength intact but forward risk capped by South America. Wheat continues to
contend with heavy world stocks, yet steady U.S exports and stable FOB values prevent a breakdown.
With no CFTC clarity and South American weather now critical, the next move will be driven by logistical
performance and export cadence, not by the static balance sheets.

International Reports
Brazil: Brazil remained the anchor of global grain flows, with FOB Santos soybean offers still holding a
competitive edge over the U.S Gulf and corn maintaining strong pricing into Asia. Planting progress
continued to diverge, central and northern regions moved at a normal pace with supportive rainfall, while
Rio Grande do Sul and Paraná faced intermittent dryness and patchy emergence, preserving early-
season risk premium. Export corridors at Santos and Paranaguá operated smoothly with no congestion,
and although no new CONAB updates were released, private analysts maintained a cautious tone toward
southern yield potential. Brazil’s combination of pricing strength and smooth logistics kept it firmly in
control of export competitiveness.

Argentina: Argentina’s balance remained steady as improved soil moisture supported early corn and
soybean establishment and wheat filling progressed normally. Up-River FOB values were stable (corn
near $205/MT, soymeal around $305/MT) and crushers continued drawing from inventories accumulated
under earlier incentive programs. Farmer selling stayed cautious amid ongoing macro uncertainty and a
weakening parallel peso, but export flows and crush operations remained consistent. Overall, Argentina
stayed competitive but macro-sensitive, contributing steady volume without shifting global trade direction.

China: China’s buying cooled sharply after the mid-month surge that included roughly 800,000 tonnes via
COFCO and 792,000 tonnes in USDA daily flashes, with no new U.S purchases reported in this period.
Importers continued favoring cheaper Brazilian offers, while domestic soymeal futures fell 1.7 percent on
soft feed demand and weak crush margins. The earlier tariff adjustments on U.S corn and wheat did not
spur immediate buying shifts, and cumulative U.S soybean inspections remained 42 percent below last
year, reinforcing that recent activity was reserve-driven, not commercial. China remained a supportive but
inconsistent buyer rather than a structural demand engine.

EU / Black Sea: Russian wheat maintained its role as the global price anchor, with 12.5% FOB offers
steady in the low-$230s/MT, securing most regional tenders and keeping upside capped for U.S and EU
wheat. Euronext futures saw only modest week-to-week movement as European internal supply
remained comfortable and unpressured by import needs. Ukrainian corn and wheat continued flowing via
Danube and Black Sea routes at competitive prices, adding to global availability. With logistics functioning
smoothly, the Black Sea continued to dictate global pricing and maintain downward pressure on
alternative origins.

Global: No major multilateral revisions were released, leaving markets to trade the ample global supply
picture reaffirmed in the WASDE, particularly in wheat. Freight conditions, container availability, and
shipping lanes remained stable, and the key forward risks centered on southern Brazil’s rainfall pattern
and China’s willingness to extend soybean purchases beyond reserve-driven buying. Broadly,
international trade continued to reflect abundant supply rather than scarcity.

So What?

Global grain markets remain defined by Brazil’s dominance, China’s selective and reserve-driven
soybean buying, and Russia’s competitive wheat pricing, all of which continue to limit U.S export
momentum despite firm domestic basis and crush-driven strength. Argentina adds stability but remains
exposed to macro pressures, while South American weather, particularly in southern Brazil, has emerged
as the next catalyst for directional risk. With logistics fully functional and no major multilateral
adjustments, the international landscape continues to price abundant supply rather than scarcity. Until
China demonstrates sustained forward demand or Brazil’s weather profile materially deteriorates, U.S
spreads and basis will remain driven overwhelmingly by domestic demand rather than export arbitrage.

Weather & Crop Conditions

United States
U.S harvest was already 90 percent + complete entering the Dec 4–10 window, leaving weather
secondary to logistics as the primary near-term driver. Early-week rainfall across the Ohio Valley and Mid-
South improved barge drafts along the Lower Mississippi, helping normalize movement after recent low-
water constraints and reinforcing the firm CIF tone in both corn and soybeans. Winter wheat
establishment progressed unevenly across the Plains, scattered showers aided surface moisture in parts
of Kansas and Oklahoma, but persistent dryness kept early HRW gains limited. Mild temperatures

allowed fieldwork to finish smoothly and minimized early-season stress. Near-term forecasts remain warm
with incremental rainfall expected for the lower Mississippi basin, a constructive backdrop for barge
logistics heading deeper into December.

Brazil
Weather remained split between north–central improvement and southern stress. Regular rainfall across
Mato Grosso, Goiás and Matopiba supported soybean planting and early establishment, bringing
progress closer to normal. In contrast, Paraná and Rio Grande do Sul continued to face intermittent
dryness and uneven emergence, preserving a modest early-season risk premium for soybeans and
downstream safrinha corn. The longer this southern dryness persists, the more the market will begin to
reassess USDA’s large-crop assumptions for both soybeans and second-crop corn, though for now the
trade remains in monitoring mode rather than repricing. Logistically, Santos and Paranaguá continued to
operate smoothly, allowing Brazil to maintain export leadership even as internal weather risk builds at the
margin.

Argentina
Argentina extended its favorable early-season pattern. Improved soil moisture supported corn and soybean
emergence, while wheat filled under mostly normal conditions. Periodic thunderstorms and moderate
temperatures kept the moisture profile stable, keeping Argentina aligned with USDA’s large-crop
assumptions and acting as a stabilizing counterweight to Brazil’s more uneven distribution.

Global
Northern Hemisphere winter wheat conditions remained broadly supportive, with Russia and Ukraine
benefiting from adequate moisture and mild temperatures that aided emergence and early tillering.
Europe also maintained a steady setup, with consistent precipitation across major producers and no early
stress signals from France, Germany or Poland. Globally, weather continues to reinforce the looser wheat
balance highlighted in WASDE.

So What?
With U.S harvest nearly complete, weather now influences markets mainly through logistics rather than
field conditions, and improved river performance has materially supported basis and export flow.
International focus centers on Brazil’s rainfall divide, improving in the north but still uneven in southern
states, while Argentina’s favorable pattern steadies overall South American supply expectations. This
week’s weather narrative ultimately echoes the broader WASDE message: domestic fundamentals are
being driven by physical flow, and forward risk hinges on whether southern Brazil’s dryness persists into
mid-December.

Synthesis & Outlook

The market spent the Dec 4–10 window trading a very different reality from what the December WASDE
implied. USDA raised corn exports by 125 mbu to 3.2 bbu, cutting ending stocks to 2.029 bbu, left
soybeans unchanged at 290 mbu, and confirmed that wheat sits on one of the heaviest global balance
sheets in five years at 274.9 MMT. Yet across all three markets, futures reacted quietly while the physical
pipeline continued to do most of the heavy lifting. Corn futures held a narrow band in the mid-$4.30s to
mid-$4.40s (Dec ’25 settlement: $4.40), with the Dec–Mar spread tightening to roughly –7¢, about one-
third of full commercial carry, supported by firm basis and improving river logistics. Soybeans softened
into the high-$10s as South American weather improved and USDA declined to adjust exports, but
nearby structure remained steadier than the board would imply thanks to persistent processor strength.
Wheat stabilized in the low-$5.30s despite record-large global stocks, supported by steady export
execution and SRW Gulf values near $236/mt, which kept U.S wheat relevant in regional demand
channels even as Black Sea competition remained aggressive.

Across all three markets, physical indicators outperformed the WASDE narrative. Corn inspections
reached 1.45 MMT, maintaining a shipment pace roughly 70 percent above last year’s levels and
reinforcing a front end far firmer than the balance sheet alone implies. Soybean inspections of about 1.01
MMT highlighted the still-sluggish export program, though strong crush and firm basis remained
supportive nearby. Wheat inspections of 393k mt kept cumulative shipments comfortably ahead of last
year, preventing the heavier global supply backdrop from translating into deeper domestic weakness.

Internationally, South America and China continued to shape the forward tone. Brazil’s rainfall pattern
stayed uneven, improving across central and northern regions while southern states remained drier,
preserving a modest weather premium in soybeans and keeping downstream implications alive for
safrinha corn. Argentina maintained its constructive early-season trajectory, reinforcing USDA’s large-
crop assumptions and acting as a counterweight to Brazil’s regional variability. China’s tariff rollback
reshaped sentiment in wheat and corn but has yet to translate into materially stronger U.S bookings,
while soybean demand remains dominated by state-reserve activity rather than crusher-driven imports. In
short, international signals offered support at the margin but stopped short of providing the sustained
demand uplift needed to fundamentally shift the U.S balance sheets.

Bullish triggers: bullish triggers remain concentrated in the physical market. In corn, export strength, firm
ethanol demand, and historically strong CIF basis continue to act as a floor under the board even as
carryout remains comfortable. Soybeans maintain the cleanest near-term upside skew: record crush,
strong basis, and a more supportive Chinese policy backdrop leave room for firmer trade if southern
Brazil’s dryness persists or if Chinese buying expands beyond reserve programs. Wheat retains a
narrower bullish lane, most notably if Russian logistics falter or FOB offers rise further, but steady U.S
export execution should continue to prevent a break below recent lows.

Bearish triggers: Bearish risks hinge on the global supply outlook and the degree to which South
America fulfills its production potential. Any normalization of rainfall in southern Brazil would erode the
mild weather premium now embedded in oilseeds, while a 178–180 MMT Brazilian soybean crop
combined with Argentina’s rebound would leave global stocks substantially heavier by late Q1. For
soybeans, the largest vulnerability remains China: if reserve buying slows and commercial crushers
continue favoring Brazilian offers, USDA’s 290 mbu ending stocks could prove conservative. Wheat faces
continued pressure from Russia’s dominant export posture and record global inventories, limiting the
durability of any recovery rallies.

Watchlist (Dec 11 – Dec 17):

Follow-through on China’s tariff rollback and early booking behavior

Gulf basis performance as river logistics continue to normalize

Southern Brazil rainfall distribution and implications for soy/safrinha

Ethanol production trajectory as crude trades below $60/bbl

Russian FOB offers and competitiveness across Black Sea tenders

In summary: the week underscored the split between comfortable balance sheets and a physical pipeline
that continues to run firmer than the board. Corn’s front end held strong on export and ethanol pull,
soybeans stayed supported nearby despite weaker futures, and wheat avoided further downside thanks
to steady U.S execution. With South American weather now the main driver and Chinese demand still
uneven, the next move hinges on logistics and rainfall rather than anything left in the WASDE tables.

Executive Summary

Corn – Nearby Demand Anchors Spreads as Export
Flow and Ethanol Grind Stay Strong
March corn futures held steady near $4.36/bu this week (–
2¢ w/w), as firm spot demand from exporters and
processors continued to support the front end despite
nominally ample stocks. Nearby structure stayed tight even
after the Dec roll, with the Mar/May spread narrowing to 10¢
(46 percent of full carry), reinforcing the nearby strength.
Weekly export inspections came in at 1.58 MMT, pushing
season-to-date totals to 69 percent ahead of last year and
keeping pace with a projected 3.2 bbu program. Interior bids
improved incrementally as seasonal winter frictions and

tighter spot barge availability kept river logistics more sensitive for this time of year. Gulf CIF remained
historically firm in the low-70s over March (around +72¢), reflecting slower barge movement and
continued competition for nearby ownership. Tight spreads and persistent processor pull continue to
anchor the futures curve, despite nominally comfortable paper stocks.

Wheat – Heavy Global Balance Sheet Caps Board, but US Exports Hold the Line

Chicago March wheat eased to the low $5.20s, retracing some recent strength as cheap Russian FOB
offers and increasing Argentine availability pressured sentiment. Still, the Mar/May spread held firm near
–12¢ (55 percent of carry), and cumulative US export inspections are running 22 percent ahead of last
year. Soft white wheat to Asia and HRW to Latin America remain the key drivers of performance. While
Argentina’s Rosario Exchange raised its wheat production forecast to a record 27.7 MMT, local corn
estimates are now projected between 48 and 55 MMT, depending on the source, following better-than-
expected yields through the latter half of harvest. Gulf SRW basis remains steady, and PNW demand
continues to clear. Global supply remains heavy, but resilient US logistics and improved export execution
have provided some cushion.

Soybeans – Futures Break Lower on Brazil Rains, Even as Nearby Crush Keeps Basis
Elevated
January soybeans fell 29¢ to $10.66/bu as improved rainfall across central Brazil and soft US shipment
data kept pressure on the board and encouraged position cleanup. The Jan/Mar spread widened slightly
to –11¢ (52 percent of carry), still well inside seasonal averages and consistent with continued
commercial interest. CIF Gulf soybean basis held firm in the low-80s over January (around +82¢), and
processor bids in the Eastern Corn Belt stayed supportive following NOPA’s record November crush print
of 216.0 mbu. Export inspections totaled 0.796 MMT, down 24 percent from the prior week and well

Macro / Policy – Dollar Slips, Argentina Deregulates, China Remains Cautious

The US Dollar Index settled near 98.3–98.4 on Dec 17, up modestly on the day but slightly lower on the
week. Crude oil steadied near $60/barrel, offering a mixed backdrop for input and freight costs. The
Brazilian real held near R$5.50/USD. In Argentina, the policy focus this week was on fresh export-duty
reductions announced Dec 9: soybeans to 24 percent (from 26 percent), corn to 8.5 percent (from 9.5
percent), and wheat to 7.5 percent (from 9.5 percent), framed as permanent cuts to improve
competitiveness and accelerate FX inflows into Q1 2026.

In China, tariff suspensions for US corn and wheat technically remain in place, but commercial
engagement has been minimal. Recent soybean purchases are widely believed to be for state reserve
use rather than commercial restocking. Meanwhile, US biofuel policy remains unresolved, as the EPA’s
final 2026 RFS mandate has been postponed to early 2026, extending the window of regulatory ambiguity
for corn ethanol and soybean oil demand.

Weather – Brazil’s North-South Divide Persists as Argentina Holds Steady

Brazil’s north–south split remains the clearest weather signal in the market. Central and northern areas
continued to benefit from timely rains, supporting early soybean and full-season corn development in
Mato Grosso and Goiás. Meanwhile, southern states, particularly Rio Grande do Sul and western Paraná,
remain short of moisture, and crop scouts warn that without meaningful rain in the next 10–14 days, yield
risk rises quickly as later-planted soybeans enter reproductive stages. Argentina remains on firmer footing
with generally solid moisture supporting early corn and soybean development, though forecasts lean drier
for Córdoba and southern Santa Fe and bear watching into January. In the US, winter wheat is settling
into dormancy under mostly stable conditions, with lingering soil-moisture concerns across parts of the
HRW belt but no widespread winterkill threats on the radar. Overall, the market’s near-term weather
sensitivity is increasingly tied to whether southern Brazil can stabilize conditions before January yield
potential starts to firm up.

What’s Next (Dec 17 – Dec 24):

Export Sales (Dec 18): Follow-through expected after recent Chinese soybean flashes; corn bookings to
Japan and Mexico also in focus.

South American Weather: Key 7-day outlook for southern Brazil and Argentina—crop stress likely to
build if rainfall underperforms again.

River Logistics: Monitor barge and rail premiums for signs of freight bottlenecks heading into holiday
slowdown.

NOPA Crush Follow-Through: Track processor bids to see whether record crush volumes lead to
further interior basis strength.

Argentine Export Activity: Watch Up-River FOBs and lineups to assess pace of post-policy-shift
marketing.
