Corn Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: March corn futures closed at $4.36/bu, down 2¢ w/w, extending a multi-week
consolidation as paper markets reflect comfort while physical flows stay firm. The Mar–May spread
narrowed to 10¢, or roughly 46 percent of full carry, pointing to steady front-end pull from processors and
exporters. Implied volatility held near 12 percent, consistent with a market lacking directional urgency.
Open interest rose modestly, signaling that commercials continue to layer in Q1 hedges without

prompting broader fund activity.

Cash & Basis: CIF Gulf basis held in the low-70s over March (around +72¢), supported by winter
logistics frictions (tow delays/ice risk/holiday scheduling) and tighter spot barge availability, even as river
levels have improved from the fall lows. Interior basis was firmer in pockets, with Western Corn Belt
processors generally ranging from a few cents under to the teens under March. National average basis
sits near 40¢ under March, roughly 20¢ firmer than normal for mid-December and consistent with ongoing
nearby demand.

Funds & Positioning: Positioning turned modestly more supportive in the latest Disaggregated COT
snapshot. Managed money was still slightly net long (+23k) in CBOT corn, and the weekly shift reflected
meaningful short-covering alongside a small add in longs, leaving funds more net-long than the prior
week. Producer/merchant hedging increased on the other side, consistent with steady commercial selling
into carry. Net, flows were supportive, but the market still appears primarily driven by cash signals, basis,
spreads, and demand execution.

Export Sales & Inspections: Export sales data remain the latest available through Nov 20, with corn net
sales at 1.936 MMT. More current flow signals stayed strong, while inspections for the week ending
December reached 1.583 MMT, down from last week but still strong, keeping YTD volumes approximately
69 percent ahead of last season. Mexico, Japan, and Colombia continue to lead, with steady PNW
loadings to South Korea and Taiwan underpinning late-Q4 execution. Despite Brazil’s competitive FOB
offers, the US program into Latin America remains resilient.

So What? Corn sits in a steady stalemate: futures pricing reflects abundant stocks and South American
optimism, while cash markets continue to tell a different story. Strong Gulf basis, active ethanol grind, and
firm export inspections all point to tighter-than-assumed front-end supply. Commercials are gradually
building coverage, while speculative pressure remains muted. With logistics under strain and Argentine
offers still slow to materialize, dips are well-bid and rallies still capped. Until new data emerges, the
market appears anchored in the $4.25–$4.50 range, with spreads remaining the clearest signal of nearby
tightness.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: January soybean futures fell 29¢ this week to settle at $10.66/bu, breaking lower
after two weeks of range-bound trade. The Jan–Mar spread widened to –11¢, or roughly 52 percent of full
carry, showing some softening in front-end tightness while still reflecting firm commercial interest. The
pullback followed improved rainfall across central Brazil and underwhelming US export data, prompting
speculative longs to exit. Even so, the forward curve remains compressed by historical standards for
December, supported by persistent domestic crush demand and slow farmer movement.

Speculators are beginning to unwind long positions built up during recent US–China trade optimism,
particularly after Trump-era rhetoric suggested large Chinese demand that has not materialized.
Improved rainfall in Brazil and CFTC data revealing net longs near decade highs have prompted position
cleanup, reinforcing the complex’s downside bias.

Cash & Basis: CIF Gulf soybean basis was in the low-80s over January (around +82¢), supported by
firm nearby demand and river logistics. Processor bids remained supportive but mixed, stronger in key
Eastern Corn Belt locations (examples near flat to small premiums), while many interior markets still
posted discounts. National average soybean basis was roughly 25–30¢ under January, still firm for mid-
December. Cash is helping stabilize the front end even as export execution lags.

Funds & Positioning: Managed money remains heavily skewed to the long side in soybeans, sitting
roughly +215k net long contracts, little changed on the week. That matters because it keeps the board
liquidation-prone on favorable Brazil weather or soft US export execution, there’s still length in the system
that can be reduced. At the same time, the lack of a big unwind this week suggests the break lower was
more fundamentals-led than flow-driven. Downside pressure can persist if exports stay sluggish and
Brazil improves, while any durable recovery likely needs a fresh catalyst, weather deterioration in South
America or a clearer demand re-acceleration, especially from China

Crush Margins & Domestic Demand: Soymeal continues to do the heavy lifting for crush economics.
NOPA’s November crush printed 216.0 mbu, a new record, consistent with steady soymeal offtake and
strong processor run rates into year-end. Meal demand has kept interior bids supported, while soybean
oil has remained a weaker leg of the complex, limiting the contribution from oil to the board crush. Even
so, crush margins have stayed attractive enough to keep plants pulling hard for nearby coverage, which
continues to underpin soybean basis despite soft export execution.

Export Sales & Inspections: Export sales data remain the latest available through Nov 20, with soybean
net sales at 2.455 MMT, including 1.707 MMT to China (2025/26). Still, total commitments remain 35
percent behind last year’s pace, with new demand heavily concentrated in Mexico and smaller Asian
markets. Inspections for the week ending Dec 11 fell to 0.796 MMT, down 24 percent from the prior week
and 46 percent below the same time last year. China's recent activity appears limited to strategic reserve
purchases, with no evidence yet of broad-based commercial buying. Forward visibility remains murky.

So What? Soybeans are stuck between strong domestic crush dynamics and persistent export drag.
Commercials remain active buyers in the cash market, and crushers are still bidding aggressively. But
without a clear signal of sustained Chinese demand, or meaningful weather-driven supply risk out of
Brazil, futures are likely to stay under pressure. Basis strength and firm spreads continue to anchor the
front end, but for the board to move meaningfully higher, the market will need either a deterioration in
South American yield potential or a broader demand recovery out of China.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: Chicago March SRW futures softened 7¢ on the week to close at $5.23/bu,
retracing part of last week’s modest recovery. Kansas City HRW held steady around $5.07, while
Minneapolis HRS edged marginally higher to $5.63. The Mar–May SRW spread remained stable at –12¢,
or about 55 percent of full carry, indicative of a storage-led market with little urgency on either side. US
futures remain pressured by heavy global supplies and unrelenting Black Sea competition, though recent
signs of improved US execution have helped prevent further breakdown.

Cash & Basis: Wheat basis held steady in mid-December, consistent with a carry-driven market and
limited nearby urgency. Gulf SRW FOB values were in the low-$6s/bu range (roughly $220–$235/MT
equivalent), still carrying a premium to key Black Sea offers and limiting US competitiveness in tenders.
Southern Plains HRW basis firmed slightly on localized feed demand, while PNW soft white bids stayed
supported by steady Southeast Asian interest. National basis averages remain near –60¢ to –72¢ under
March for SRW and –74¢ under KC March for HRW, typical of a surplus environment where movement
stays tactical rather than structural.

Export Sales & Inspections: Export sales data remain the latest available through Nov 20, with all-
wheat net sales at 381,100 MT. Weekly inspections rose to 488,000 MT for the period ending Dec 11, up
23 percent week-over-week and running ahead of the same week last year. Season-to-date inspections
now sit at 14.125 MMT, keeping shipments on a 22 percent year ago advantage. Soft white wheat from

the Pacific Northwest remains the bright spot into Southeast Asia, while HRW movement from the Gulf is
steady. Even so, US FOB offers remain priced above key competitors, keeping the export book tactical
rather than transformational.

Funds & Positioning: Managed money in Chicago SRW wheat remains net short about –44k contracts,
but the week showed a mild de-risking as funds added length and trimmed the bearish edge by roughly
10k. Positioning is still negative, so rallies remain fundamentally capped by global surplus, but the market
is less “one-way” than it would be if shorts were actively building, leaving more room for stabilization and
occasional short-covering pops on export or logistics surprises.

So What? Wheat markets continue to operate under the weight of global surplus. Russian and Argentine
export programs are defining the price ceiling, leaving US wheat to fill niche demand at a relative
premium. While US execution has quietly improved, the lack of sustained momentum and structural
pricing disadvantage remain headwinds. However, the scale of speculative short interest leaves the door
open to short-covering rallies on any shift in global logistics, weather, or currency. Until then, futures are
likely to stay anchored near recent lows, with commercial activity focused on breaks rather than
breakouts.

US Cash Market & Basis

Corn: Corn basis remains resilient for December, with CIF Gulf bids quoted in the low-70s over March
(around +72¢), still historically firm for the season. Ice buildup and winter logistics frictions have slowed
Gulf arrivals at times, lending support to spot premiums. Interior bids remain strongest in the Western
Corn Belt, where ethanol grind continues at near-record levels. Iowa and Nebraska processors were
generally near flat to modestly under the board for spot delivery, as plants compete for limited available
bushels. National basis now averages around –41¢ under March, roughly 20¢ stronger than the five-year
average for this date. Farmer sales remain minimal, particularly in areas with firm local basis and low flat-
price motivation. End-user competition for immediate ownership is keeping the front end tight, even with a
nominal 2.1 bbu carryout on paper.

Soybeans: Soybean basis continues to reflect tight nearby supply, underpinned by record domestic
crush and a reluctant farm seller. CIF Gulf barges for January shipment held steady in the low-80s over
Jan futures (around +82¢), with limited give despite recent board weakness. Processor bids across key
Eastern Corn Belt locations (Decatur, Lafayette, Morristown) were quoted between +65¢ and +75¢ over
Jan for prompt delivery, supported by firm soymeal pull. River basis improved modestly as barge traffic
stabilized, but freight remains a volatile input. National average basis sits near –26¢ under Jan, roughly a
dime firmer than the seasonal norm. While export demand remains soft, crushers are still bidding
aggressively, and the Jan/Mar spread continues to suggest commercial willingness to carry inventory.
Brazilian forward offers remain cheaper into March, keeping a cap on Gulf premiums heading into Q1.

Wheat: Wheat basis remains stable but directionless. Gulf SRW FOB values were in the low-$6s/bu
range (roughly $220–$235/MT equivalent), still carrying a premium to key Black Sea offers and limiting
US competitiveness in tenders. Russian 12.5 percent protein wheat remains anchored near $230/MT,
keeping global benchmarks subdued. HRW basis in the Southern Plains saw marginal strength as feed
users sought alternatives to expensive corn, but broader movement remains muted. In the Pacific
Northwest, soft white bids held firm on continued interest from Southeast Asia. Overall, the US cash
wheat market continues to reflect a carry-driven dynamic: flat prices are too low to incentivize sales, but
basis lacks the momentum to flip the narrative. The USDA’s 900 mbu export forecast remains feasible,
but only if FOB spreads stay defensible through late Q1.

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Grain exports from Brazil remain seasonally active but are beginning to slow as the old-crop cycle
winds down. ANEC now pegs December soybean exports at 3.57 MMT, roughly 200,000 MT above last
week’s estimate, while corn shipments were nudged up to 6.35 MMT (vs. 6.30 MMT previously), still
elevated relative to historical norms given the size of the safrinha crop. Soymeal loadings were also
raised to 2.0 MMT for December, reinforcing Brazil’s strong protein export program into year-end. FOB
Santos soybean offers were still hovering near $10.05–10.10/bu for January loading, keeping Brazil the
preferred origin for Jan/Feb shipments, while US Gulf values held a $12–15/MT premium. Corn FOB at
Paranaguá traded near $204/MT, preserving a pricing advantage into Southeast Asia and the Middle
East. Logistical flows through southern ports remain fluid, with no significant congestion reported. Recent
rains improved soil profiles in Mato Grosso and Goiás, supporting early soybean development, while
conditions in the south remain mixed, Rio Grande do Sul continues to battle dryness, though safrinha
timing has yet to be compromised. For now, Brazil retains the competitive edge across corn, soybeans,
and soymeal heading into Q1.

Argentina: Argentina's post-election policy overhaul is beginning to reshape its export dynamics. A sharp
peso devaluation and lower export taxes have reset FOB pricing: corn offers fell to $178–182/MT,
soybeans to $428–432/MT. However, volumes remain thin as growers await further currency stabilization.
Farmers are reportedly cautious amid ongoing regulatory recalibration and uncertainty around new fiscal
policy. Domestic crush plants around Rosario continue to draw on pre-election inventories, while planting
progress is solid, soybeans and corn at 59 percent, helped by decent moisture, though recent forecasts
show emerging dryness in Córdoba and central production areas. The wheat harvest is over 60 percent
complete, with local analysts lifting the production estimate toward 27.7 MMT. If logistical and policy
conditions stabilize, Argentina is well positioned to become a more aggressive exporter in early 2026.

China: China remains deliberate and price-sensitive in its grain purchasing, with crushers still favoring
South American origin for early-2026 arrivals given the premium in US Gulf offers versus Brazil. The
latest confirmed US export sales report (still only through Nov 20) included a highlight showing 1.707
MMT of soybeans to China for 2025/26 activity the trade continues to interpret as largely state-directed
rather than broad-based commercial restocking. On corn and wheat, the tariff suspension has not
translated into material new buying, and commercial participation remains minimal. Domestic Dalian corn
values remain elevated, but no sustained arbitrage window has opened. Soymeal futures stayed firm near
¥3,570/MT on livestock feed demand, but until commercial margins improve and buying broadens beyond
tactical coverage, US exporters are unlikely to see sustained Chinese engagement across the grain
complex.

EU / Black Sea: Russian FOB wheat offers held firm near $232–237/MT this week, supported by ruble
stabilization and renewed regional demand. Ukraine's grain corridor continues to function, with Danube
and rail flows moving steadily into the EU. Ukrainian corn offers around $205/MT remain a key pressure
point for EU feed markets. While French wheat (FOB Rouen) held near $229/MT, EU exporters continue
to trail Black Sea pricing in key North African and Middle Eastern tenders. Russian and Ukrainian
soymeal has also made inroads into Mediterranean feed markets, thanks to advantageous freight rates
and softer currency terms.

Other Regions: Australia’s wheat harvest progressed across eastern states, with yields holding steady,
though drought in Western Australia has trimmed national output potential. Total production is expected
below 25 MMT, down sharply from the 2022 record but still a contributor to global supply. Canadian
spring wheat exports continue into Asia and Latin America on a routine basis. India’s grain export
restrictions remain unchanged, and no easing is expected in the near term. South Africa’s summer crop
season is on track, and no significant disruptions have been reported from other minor origins.

So What? Global flows continue to be led by Brazil and Russia, whose aggressive pricing and logistics
networks define the world’s marginal grain supply. Argentina is poised to regain competitiveness, but
farmer behavior and logistics will dictate pace. US exporters remain essential to traditional partners but
lack pricing power in global tenders. Recent Chinese buying does little to change this equation. Without a
major weather or policy catalyst, US export market share will remain opportunistic, not directional. For
now, global FOB spreads continue to anchor world price direction outside the US

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Dec 10 – Dec 17)

Crop Progress: With US harvest fully complete, weekly updates have paused for the season. Winter
wheat condition ratings remain the focus, last reported at 48 percent good/excellent. Dryness persists in
key HRW zones across western Kansas and central Oklahoma. With crops now entering dormancy, the
spotlight shifts to subsoil recharge potential ahead of spring.

Export Inspections (USDA FGIS – week ending Dec 11): Corn inspections held firm at 1.583 MMT,
sustaining a pace well above last year and the five-year average. Cumulative corn exports now exceed
22.5 MMT, tracking comfortably toward USDA’s 3.2 bbu projection. Soybean inspections declined to
0.796 MMT, the lowest in four weeks, reinforcing broader concerns around export slack, even with recent
Chinese flash purchases. Cumulative soybean loadings remain approximately 46 percent behind last
year’s pace. Wheat inspections rose modestly to 488,000 MT, lifting the season-to-date total to 14.124
MMT, or 22 percent ahead of last year, keeping the 900 mbu annual target within reach.

Export Sales (USDA FAS – latest report available through week ending Nov 20): Weekly export
sales reporting remains delayed, so the most recent confirmed figures are still for Nov 20. Corn net sales
were 1.936 MMT, reflecting steady demand led by Mexico, Japan, and “unknown” destinations. Soybean
net sales totaled 2.455 MMT, and while reporting detail has been uneven, the export “highlights” table
flagged 1.707 MMT of soybeans to China for 2025/26, volume the market is still treating cautiously as
potentially tactical/state-directed until the backlog and buyer mix normalize. All-wheat net sales were
381,100 MT, consistent with routine business skewed toward HRW/soft wheat programs.

Ethanol Production & Stocks (EIA – week ending Dec 12): Ethanol production stayed elevated at
1.131 mbpd, reflecting a strong early-December grind. That implies weekly corn use of roughly 100–102
mbu on the high end of seasonal norms. Stocks rose slightly in line with holiday-season builds, while
margins remained positive, underpinned by firm corn basis and steady DDGS values. Processor bids in
Iowa and Nebraska continue to reflect aggressive commercial pull.

CFTC Positioning (latest available Disaggregated COT snapshot): Managed money positioning
remains split across the grain complex. In corn, funds are still slightly net long (about +23k CBOT
contracts), with the latest weekly shift reflecting meaningful short-covering alongside a small add in
longs—supportive flow, but not the primary driver versus cash signals. In soybeans, managed money
remains heavily net long (roughly +215k), which keeps the board liquidation-prone on favorable Brazil
weather or continued soft US export execution; the fact that length did not unwind sharply this week
suggests the break lower was more fundamentals-led than purely flow-driven. In Chicago SRW wheat,
funds remain net short (around –44k), though the week showed mild de-risking as shorts were trimmed
by roughly 10k, leaving positioning less “one-way” and keeping the door open to short-covering pops on
export, logistics, or headline surprises even as the global surplus still caps sustained rallies.

NOPA Crush (November – released Dec 16): November soybean crush reached 216.0 million bushels
a new monthly record and toward the upper end of trade expectations. Soymeal continues to lead
demand, with export shipments holding steady and domestic livestock use remaining robust. Soybean oil

yield and ending stocks were slightly above forecasts, but SBO remains a secondary driver relative to
meal. The strong print reinforces firm processor bids and supports continued strength in front-end
spreads.

So What? Markets continue to lean on real-time commercial signals, with WASDE now in the rearview
and positioning data offering only a partial snapshot of risk appetite. Corn demand remains the standout:
ethanol production and inspections are validating current board levels despite a nominally comfortable
carryout. Soybeans are posting historic crush demand but remain constrained by export
underperformance outside of tactical Chinese reserve buying. Wheat’s shipment pace has been quietly
constructive, helping stabilize the board even as global surplus keeps rallies capped. Until broader clarity
emerges, via South American yield signals and clearer speculative conviction, basis, inspections, and
spreads will remain the market’s most reliable directional guideposts

International Reports

Brazil: Brazil remains the focal point of global grain pricing as the country navigates contrasting weather
patterns and maintains smooth logistics. Soybean and corn FOB offers at Santos and Paranaguá remain
competitive into Asia, with corn quoted near $206–208/MT and soybeans holding a $10.05–10.10/bu
equivalent. Favorable rainfall in central and northern regions has kept early planted soy and corn in solid
shape, but southern states, especially Rio Grande do Sul, continue to show signs of mounting dryness.
CONAB revised its soybean production to 177.1 MMT, noting localized replanting and lower stand counts
in the south. Despite this, export flows are running without disruption, with no significant port congestion
reported. With field progress nearing completion, the market’s next focus is the weather in January as
early reproductive stages begin.

Argentina: The Argentine market is responding quickly to the government’s post-election economic reset.
A steep peso devaluation and reduced export taxes have boosted FOB competitiveness and encouraged
farmer selling. Soybeans are offered around $428–432/MT and corn near $178–182/MT, though volume
remains uneven as producers assess inflation and policy uncertainty. Soybean and corn planting stands
at 59 percent, both tracking slightly ahead of last year. Most of the growing belt still enjoys above-average
moisture, but short-term forecasts have shifted drier for Córdoba and central zones. Domestic crushers
continue operating steadily on pre-election inventories, and Argentina remains a reliable supplier of
soymeal, supported by strong export margins and structural processing capacity.

China: After a wave of US soybean purchases earlier in the month, primarily attributed to state reserves,
commercial interest has cooled again. Flash sales in December totaled over 1.5 MMT, but recent buying
appears sporadic and tactical rather than part of a broader restocking effort. US Gulf soybeans still hold a
premium to Brazilian equivalents, and Chinese crushers are cautious amid thin margins and weak
demand for feed. Soymeal futures have softened in response to government stock releases and rising
inventory. Despite the tariff suspension on US corn and wheat, there has been no meaningful pickup in
commercial activity. For now, China remains active on a case-by-case basis, but not a dependable
growth engine for US exports.

EU / Black Sea: Russia continues to set the tone in global wheat pricing, with steady FOB offers near
$230–232/MT. Ukrainian grain movement faces renewed friction after damage to key infrastructure earlier
in December, pushing more volume through Danube ports and rail corridors. Ukrainian corn is offered
near $218–220/MT, adding pressure to EU feed grain markets. EU internal demand remains well-
supplied, and wheat exports, especially from France, are trailing last year. The region is not lacking in
volume but remains secondary in global trade flows as Black Sea origins retain cost advantage and
logistical access. Unless currency dynamics shift or weather introduces disruptions, the EU’s export share
is likely to stay capped.

Global: With few surprises from recent government or private estimates, the global supply picture
remains ample. Freight rates have eased, Baltic Dry Index down nearly 20 percent in December,
improving netback margins for many origins. Argentina and Brazil remain on track for major export
programs, though Brazil’s southern dryness bears watching. Australia’s wheat harvest is progressing
without major logistical issues, and no supply shock is currently visible across secondary origins. Barring
a major turn in South American weather or a sustained return of Chinese grain buying the international
trade balance remains neutral to heavy.

So What? Global grain pricing continues to revolve around Brazil’s smooth flows and Russia’s aggressive
wheat offers. Argentina is re-entering with policy-driven competitiveness but still faces uncertainty.
China’s return has been noticeable but not consistent, and buyers remain price sensitive. The US
remains a key supplier to traditional customers but isn’t leading the global trade narrative. Unless January
weather in South America triggers a production cut or China steps up with forward purchases, export
arbitrage will continue to favor lower-cost origins, keeping US competitiveness in check.

Weather & Crop Conditions

United States
With harvest now complete, weather’s role has shifted toward supporting winter wheat establishment and
maintaining logistical fluidity. Crop progress updates have paused for the season, but soil moisture
remains a concern in key HRW areas. Kansas and western Oklahoma continue to report abnormally dry
to moderate drought readings, with patchy emergence in some fields. Adequate recharge between now
and February will be essential to avoid early-season stand degradation.

On the logistics front, Mississippi River levels have continued to improve after October’s lows. Gauges at
Cairo and Memphis ticked higher this week, and most draft restrictions have been lifted. Barge
movements are operating near standard winter capacity, a notable relief for export flow. The 10-day
forecast shows seasonal to slightly above-average temperatures across the Midwest and Plains, with
limited precipitation expected, reducing immediate threats, but also offering little help in rebuilding soil
moisture. Natural gas and diesel markets remain steady, with no energy bottlenecks or polar events
currently threatening fertilizer distribution or crop safety.

Brazil
Weather in Brazil continues to show a pronounced north-south divide. Central and northern zones,
including Mato Grosso, Goiás, and western Bahia, received consistent rainfall last week, further
stabilizing early soy and full-season corn. Stand counts and emergence remain strong, and vegetative
growth is advancing rapidly. The story is very different in the south. Rio Grande do Sul and western
Paraná saw only isolated showers, insufficient to offset deepening moisture deficits. Later-planted
soybeans in these zones are now entering reproductive stages under mounting stress. Crop scouts warn
that without meaningful rainfall in the next ten days, irreversible yield losses could begin. Current
forecasts from INMET and private models maintain a below-normal precipitation outlook across southern
Brazil through late December. Nationwide planting is now nearly complete, shifting market attention fully
to reproductive-stage weather and early yield signals in January–February.

Argentina
Argentina’s crop year continues to perform above expectations. Soybean and corn planting are around 59
percent, both slightly ahead of last year’s pace despite some delays from excess rainfall in Buenos Aires
province. Conditions remain exceptional across the primary growing belt: over 90 percent of the
agricultural area is rated as having adequate to optimal moisture, and early planted corn shows strong
emergence, uniform growth, and minimal pest pressure.

Global
Winter wheat in the Northern Hemisphere entered dormancy under broadly favorable conditions. Russia,
Ukraine, and much of Europe wrapped up fall planting with sufficient moisture and no frost exposure.
Stand establishment across these zones is mostly complete and stable. In Australia, harvest is
concluding in New South Wales and Victoria with average to above-average yields, while Western
Australia continues to struggle with drought-driven yield cuts. National output will fall short of last year’s
record but remains a significant contributor to global balance sheets. India’s rabi crop season is
proceeding on schedule, with no major disruptions reported across other minor exporters such as South
Africa.

So What?
Weather risk is becoming more concentrated and nuanced. Brazil’s Center-West looks increasingly
stable, but southern regions are flirting with active yield stress as dryness deepens. With reproductive
stages underway in key soy zones, the next two weeks will carry heavy directional weight. Argentina
offers a bullish offset, ideal moisture and crop health are still holding, but any drying trend into January
will quickly raise flags. In the US, logistical bottlenecks have eased, and winterkill risk remains low,
supporting basis and interior movement. Global conditions remain benign overall, but South America
holds the cards now, how January weather plays out across southern Brazil and central Argentina will
likely determine the first major inflection point of 2026.

Synthesis & Outlook

Grain and oilseed markets remain rangebound but increasingly shaped by real-time fundamentals rather
than macro signals or speculative flows. Corn futures continue to consolidate around $4.35–$4.40,
soybeans have broken lower into the $10.60s amid Brazilian rainfall and export headwinds, and wheat
has drifted back toward $5.20 despite steady US shipments. The consistent thread is a divergence
between weak futures sentiment and firm cash market behavior. Basis strength, resilient end-user bids,
and historically tight nearby spreads all signal that commercial players are still competing for physical
ownership, even as global supply expectations hover near record levels.

The structure of the futures curve reinforces this tone. Corn’s Mar/May spread narrowed to –10¢ (46
percent of full carry), soybeans held Jan/Mar near –11.25¢ (52 percent of full), and wheat’s Mar/May
remains steady near –12.25¢ (55 percent of carry), all pointing to ongoing spot-market firmness. Export
inspections for corn and wheat remain ahead of seasonal pace, ethanol production continues to post
record or near-record weekly prints, and crush margins are still strong enough to keep soybean processor
bids well-supported into year-end. These cash signals are validating board values, even as the paper
narrative remains one of ample stocks and ideal South American potential.

The central axis for volatility now lies firmly in South America. Brazil’s outlook is split: the Center-West is
performing well, but southern states continue to face yield-threatening dryness just as soybeans
approach key reproductive stages. Argentina, by contrast, is still tracking toward trend or better yields,
with moisture conditions among the best seen in years. Over the next two to three weeks, rainfall, or its
absence, in southern Brazil and parts of Argentina will begin to define market direction into Q1. If
meaningful production losses materialize, especially in southern Brazil’s soy and corn areas, the board
will need to reprice risk. If those risks fade, the weight of supply could begin to assert more pressure on
spreads and basis.

Bullish triggers: Upside risks remain clustered around firm US physical demand: ethanol output remains
near record levels, while crush margins continue to support processor bids. Soymeal strength and slow
farmer selling are sustaining interior basis. If weather in southern Brazil worsens, or Argentina’s current
moisture surplus begins to fade, yield potential may face meaningful cuts. Another wave of Chinese
soybean purchases, or a surprise corn tender post-tariff suspension, would likely pull nearby spreads

tighter and support the front end of the board.

Bearish triggers: The downside setup hinges on confirmation that Brazil and Argentina deliver full
season record crops without material weather losses. If production risk fades, global supply pressure will
reassert control and weigh on US export competitiveness. A seasonal drop in ethanol output, pullback in
Chinese demand, or easing Gulf CIF values could loosen basis and compress spreads. Continued
undercutting from Black Sea wheat and growing soymeal flows from Russia and Ukraine would further
cap US recovery potential.

Watchlist (Dec 18 – Dec 24):

Brazil rainfall maps: focus remains on Rio Grande do Sul, western Paraná

Export inspections: especially soybean shipment conversion from recent sales

Ethanol data: do processors maintain +1.10 mbpd grind into holiday slowdown

Argentina’s mid-season moisture profile: any deterioration from current highs

CIF and processor basis: signal shifts in nearby commercial appetite?

In summary: Markets are being pulled in two directions: cash fundamentals remain resilient, while futures
reflect caution and macro heaviness. South America holds the key to resolving this split. If Brazilian and
Argentine weather cooperate, the weight of supply will reassert control. But if conditions worsen,
especially in Brazil’s south, the board will need to adjust upward to reflect diminished availability. Until
then, spreads and basis will continue to anchor price discovery in the absence of fresh supply shocks.

Ethanol for America Act

The major barrier to a higher Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) is the fuel versus food debate. Now is the
perfect time to move to E15. Corn prices are extremely low, and the latest USDA WASDE reported a record
crop and a record crop expansion.

USDA WASDE forecast corn production at 16.7 billion bushels, with the yield at 188.8 bushels per acre and
ending stocks at 2.1 billion. The season-average corn price dropped 30 cents to $3.90 a bushel. Most
importantly, 202526 crop year is expected to have 1.8 billion more bushels than 2024/25.

With current ethanol production consuming 5.6 billion bushels, a 10 percent increase in consumption would
consume an additional 560 million bushels. The reality is that year around E15 would add approximately
50 million bushels and regulatory streamlining would add another 50 million bushels. At some point over
the next ten years, the additional corn consumption could be 2.8 billion bushels minus lower fuel
consumption resulting from electric vehicles. The ethanol corn consumption increase is likely to be more
of a S curve as new compacity comes online.

With Brazil and the US corn and soybean production increasing, 100 million bushels of ethanol corn
consumption will barely move the needle. The ethanol production capacity expansion that would be three
to four years from now is when the corn consumption impact to the corn market would be felt.

Executive Summary

Corn – 2025 Ends With the Physical Market Still
Calling the Shots
March corn finished the year at $4.50/bu (+14¢ vs Dec 17),
and the front of the curve never really “gave up” to storage
economics. Mar/May near –5¢ (33 percent of carry) kept
signaling that end users still care about nearby ownership
even as the balance sheet looks comfortable on paper.
Holiday execution slowed, but it didn’t break, inspections
printed 1.747 MMT (Dec 18) and 1.301 MMT (Dec 25), while
CIF Gulf stayed in the mid-70s over March (+74¢) with
winter logistics and spot barge tightness keeping
replacement values elevated. Same closing lesson as most

of 2025: futures can drift, but the cash market keeps setting the guardrails.

Wheat – Plenty of Exportable Supply, Yet U.S. Movement Still Matters

Chicago March wheat ended at $5.19/bu (–4¢ vs Dec 17) with the ceiling still defined by Black Sea
competition and Argentina’s improving availability. Even so, the market didn’t completely “let go” on the
front end: Mar/May around –12¢ (75 percent of carry) stayed supportive, and U.S. inspections remain 22
percent ahead y/y into year-end. The pattern has been consistent: global surplus limits follow-through, but
steady U.S. shipments keep dips from turning into free-falls when competitors don’t fully undercut.

Soybeans – Crush Keeps Nearby Supported, While Brazil/Exports Control the Tone
January soybeans closed at $10.52/bu (–14¢ vs Dec 17), with improving Brazil moisture and a softer U.S.
shipment backdrop weighing on sentiment into the turn. Still, nearby structure held together: Jan/Mar near
–6¢ (27 percent of carry) and CIF Gulf in the low-90s over January (+93¢) reflect that domestic demand
continues to absorb bushels. That domestic “engine” remains the anchor after NOPA’s record 216.0 mbu
November crush, but the upside stays harder to sustain until exports show clearer acceleration.

(Carry % calculated assuming 7% annual interest and \$0.05/bu per month storage/insurance cost over the spread interval.)

Macro / Policy – Freight Softens, Argentina Sweetens Terms, China Remains Measured

Macro inputs were mostly quiet into year-end. DXY was around 98.3–98.4 on Dec 30 (slightly softer on
the week), crude hovered near $60/bbl, and BRL stayed close to R$5.50/USD. Freight also leaned easier,
BDI slid roughly 20% over December, improving netbacks for key exporters. Argentina added another
competitiveness lever by cutting export duties (soy 24 percent, corn 8.5 percent, wheat 7.5 percent),
aiming to pull forward selling and FX inflows into early 2026.

China continues to act like a selective buyer rather than a broad restocker. Even with suspensions still

Weather – Year-End Risk Stays Localized, With South America’s Rain Map the Key
Variable

Weather closes 2025 as a localized risk story rather than a broad yield threat. In the US, row-crop
weather has faded, and the market is watching two practical levers: winter wheat establishment
(dormancy setting in, with Plains moisture pockets still relevant ahead of spring) and the reliability of river
logistics when cold snaps and short-term level drops tighten barge flow. In South America, totals matter
less than placement. Brazil’s Center-West has kept enough rainfall rhythm to support early stands, while
the South remains the swing zone where interruptions can still translate into premium as the crop
advances. Argentina remains generally supported on moisture, but timing is now the risk: any sustained
drying in the core belt would start to matter quickly as crops move deeper into their critical development
window.

What’s Next (Jan 01 – Jan 08):

Export Inspections: First clean post-holiday read on execution, corn needs to stay firm to keep the cash-
led narrative intact; soybeans need any rebound to slow the y/y deficit story.

Export Sales: Watch whether soy demand shows follow-through beyond tactical China coverage; corn
bookings to Mexico/Japan remain the consistency check.

EIA Ethanol: Confirm whether the late-December dip was holiday noise or a real easing trend, production
near 1.10 mbpd and stocks behavior will set the tone for corn’s domestic demand floor.

South America Weather: Brazil South vs Center-West remains the key divide. Argentina heat/dryness in
the core belt would reprice soy risk quickly, while “good enough” rains keep rallies capped.

River Logistics / Freight: Spot barge tightness and replacement values will show up first in basis and
nearby spreads as normal business resumes.

Argentina Follow Through: Duty cuts are only bullish/bearish if they turn into volume, watch Up-River
offers, lineups, and farmer selling behavior.

Corn Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: Corn spent 2025 rotating between two realities: board-level comfort and cash-level
insistence. The year’s tone was set early when March futures pushed into the high $4.60s/low $4.70s
(mid-January) on risk premium and fund participation, but the market couldn’t sustain it as weather fear
faded and supply confidence rebuilt, by late June, the trade was probing the low-$4.20s ($4.18) again.
The back half of the year repeated the same lesson in smaller steps: futures struggled to trend, but
whenever the board tried to lean too bearish, the physical market tightened the conversation through
spreads, basis, and shipment follow-through.

Into the finish, March corn closed at $4.50 and Mar/May ended near –5¢ (33 percent of carry),

underscoring how rarely full carry took control in 2025. Even with the holiday slowdown, inspections (1.74
MMT on Dec 18; 1.30 MMT on Dec 25) stayed strong enough to keep the export program “real” while Gulf
replacement values remained historically firm for late December as winter logistics and spot barge
tightness elevated nearby coverage costs.

Price Trajectory and Volatility Patterns: The year’s price path ultimately behaved like a mean-reverting
market more than a trending one, with weather scares and macro bursts creating short-lived premium that
faded once supply confidence returned. Options pricing reflected that tone: implied volatility hovered near
12 percent into the close, low by historical standards, and signaled limited speculative urgency. In
practice, corn spent most of 2025 trading “in pockets,” where the board could drift but the front-end
structure and cash replacement values repeatedly defined where the market found traction.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets delivered the steadiest signals all year, and the close of 2025 captured that
resilience clearly. By late December, CIF Gulf bids lingered in the mid-70s over March (around +74¢),
buoyed by winter frictions and spot barge constraints that limited downside. Interior spots shone where
processors pulled hardest, with Western Corn Belt bids ranging from flat to a few cents under March.
National average basis ended around –30¢ under March, about 20¢ stronger than typical for the season,
mirroring how basis repeatedly propped up the front during 2025’s softer board moments.

Funds & Positioning: Speculative flows influenced 2025 but seldom overrode cash and spread cues.
The early-year bullish turn in funds sparked short-covering flurries on logistics or weather pops. By year-
end, managed money had swung to a modest net short (around –53k contracts, as of Dec 16), with
recent moves more about trimming longs than bold bets, balanced by rising producer/merchant hedges
that maintained the market’s equilibrium.

Export Sales & Inspections: Demand came down to execution over hype in 2025. Year-end inspections
provided a solid gauge: corn ran 1.74 MMT (Dec 18) and 1.30 MMT (Dec 25), lifting cumulative exports
past 25 MMT, on track for USDA’s 3.2 bbu outlook and up 66 percent y/y. Sales data, though lagged,
showed net sales around 1.2 MMT (week ending Dec 11), with Mexico, Japan, and Colombia as steady
takers, plus reliable PNW flows to Asia.

So What? Corn is stuck in a familiar stalemate: the board keeps leaning on “ample stocks” and South
America optimism, but the cash market still refuses to fully agree. Gulf basis continues to hold up, ethanol
grind stays active, and inspections have not rolled over in a way that matches a truly comfortable front
end, spreads are still doing most of the talking. Commercials look like they’re quietly extending coverage
rather than waiting for a deeper break, while specs remain relatively muted, keeping selling pressure
more controlled than it could be.

With logistics still prone to winter friction and Argentine export offers slow to show up in size, breaks keep
finding buyers even as rallies struggle to extend. Until something forces a new narrative, the market looks
anchored in that $4.25–$4.50 pocket, and the curve, especially nearby spreads, remains the cleanest
read on how tight (or not) the front end really is.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: Soybeans spent 2025 stuck in a recurring loop: rallies needed export proof, while
breaks kept finding a domestic floor. Early-year strength had January futures near the upper-$10.80s/low-
$10.90s ($10.94) on weather risk and headline optimism, but mid-year trade pressure pulled values
toward the low-$10.00s ($10.20 late June) as supply confidence rebuilt and Brazil regained control of the
forward export window. By year-end, the complex was still living inside that same tug-of-war, export
uncertainty overhead, but meal-led crush and cash strength keeping the front end from fully loosening.

January closed at $10.52 (–14¢ vs Dec 17) with Jan/Mar –6¢ (27 percent of carry) and Gulf CIF steady in
the low-90s over Jan (+93¢), consistent with a year where commercials stayed involved even when
futures lacked a demand catalyst. The clearest “why it mattered” signal in 2025 was the domestic engine:
NOPA’s record 216.0 mbu November crush captured how aggressively the system ran, while exports
remained the limiter with inspections still running 46 percent behind y/y on the season.

Price Trajectory and Volatility Patterns: Soybeans carried a higher risk premium than corn through
2025 because the market repeatedly had to price South American weather and demand uncertainty at the
same time. Implied volatility ended the year near 18 percent, elevated versus corn but still contained
compared with prior spikes, reflecting a market that stayed sensitive to headline turns yet struggled to
hold follow-through. The board repeatedly responded to the same triggers, Brazil rain placement,
shipment pace, and meal-led crush signals, creating sharp swings that often reverted once the catalyst
passed. Spec flows fueled ups and downs in 2025. Headline optimism, like US-China talks, piled on
length prone to unwinds on Brazil improvements. Year-end echoed that: rains and soft data left the setup
ripe for more liquidation, biasing the board down absent fresh sparks like South American hiccups or
demand revs.

Cash & Basis: Cash acted as the steady hand through 2025, evident again at close. CIF Gulf basis clung
to low-90s over January (around +93¢), propped by nearby needs and river tweaks. Processor bids mixed
but solid, Eastern Corn Belt spots near flat to premium in primes, interiors with discounts. National
average basis around –20¢ under January, firm for late December and true to the year’s motif: cash
resisted the board’s bear vibes often. Processor hunger stabilized the front amid export lulls.

Funds & Positioning: Funds drove much of soy’s narrative in 2025, with the complex holding “built-in
length” quick to shed on weather turns or export misses. Latest read: managed money heavily net long at
155k contracts (as of Dec 16), steady w/w. Less a weekly mover, more a closing state: it primes the board
for further unwinds on Brazil gains or US export softness. No sharp exit this time hints the dip was
fundamentals-first. Downside lingers if exports drag and South America cooperates; upside wants
catalysts like weather woes or China shifts.

Crush Margins & Domestic Demand: Crush anchored the complex in 2025, meal the powerhouse.
NOPA’s November hit 216.0 mbu, a record underscoring aggressive runs and meal uptake into year-end.
That echoed throughout: crushers bid through futures pressure. Oil lagged margins often, capping its
crush role, but meal strength kept plants humming. Overall economics held plants chasing coverage,
bolstering basis despite export weights.

Export Sales & Inspections: Exports capped rallies most of 2025, year-end data in line. Sales confirmed
to late November at 2.4 MMT, with 1.7 MMT to China (2025/26), but commitments remain materially
behind last year, focused on Mexico, smaller Asia over broad China buys. Flow stayed soft: inspections
0.75 MMT week ending late December, down w/w and 46 percent y/y cumulative at 15.4 MMT vs 28.7
MMT prior. China’s buys seemed reserve-tactical, clouding ahead and keeping the board touchy on
execution slips.

So What? Soybeans are still caught in the same tug-of-war: domestic crush is doing real work and the
cash market keeps proving it, but exports continue to be the cap on futures. Commercials remain steady
buyers and crushers are still bidding aggressively to secure nearby ownership, which is why basis and
spreads have stayed firm even when the board tries to leak lower.

The problem is the market still doesn’t have a clean catalyst on the demand side. Without a clearer signal
of sustained Chinese buying, or a weather-driven shift that meaningfully dents Brazil’s yield potential
futures remain vulnerable to pressure and liquidation on rallies. For the board to move higher in a durable
way, it likely takes either South America losing some production potential, or China demand improving
beyond “hand-to-mouth” coverage. Until then, the front end stays supported by crush/basis, while the
upside stays capped by export drag.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: Wheat’s 2025 was a story of ceilings, not floors. Early-year pricing near the upper-
$5s ($5.70 mid-Jan) had room for weather-led pops, but the market repeatedly ran into the same
constraint: abundant exportable supply and a competitor complex (especially the Black Sea) willing to
defend market share. By late June, futures were back near the low-$5.30s, and the year’s final stretch
kept expressing the same pattern, short-lived rallies, limited follow-through, and a steady reliance on
niche demand lanes rather than broad tender dominance. Chicago March ended at $5.19 (–4¢ vs Dec 17)
with Mar/May –12¢ (75 percent of carry), while US shipment execution remained a stabilizer with
cumulative inspections 22 percent ahead y/y.

Price Trajectory and Volatility Patterns: Wheat’s volatility stayed relatively muted into year-end (implied
vol near 13 percent), consistent with a market dominated by global supply competition rather than
domestic scarcity. Most 2025 moves were less about sustained US fundamentals and more about
whether Black Sea offers, freight, and FX shifts temporarily opened (or closed) competitiveness windows.
That kept the board reactive and range-bound, with rallies struggling to extend unless a clear disruption
forced repricing.

Cash & Basis: Wheat cash in 2025 mostly cleared on dips, not frantic owns, with late December
mirroring that calm. Basis stayed stable, aligning with a carry-heavy board and subdued nearby push.
Gulf SRW FOB in the mid-$6s/bu ($220–$235/MT), premium to Black Sea and curbing US tender wins.
Southern Plains HRW firmed a bit on feed swaps, while PNW soft white stayed supported by consistent
Southeast Asia pulls, a standout US Lane all year. National basis remained typical of excess: –60¢ to –
72¢ under March for SRW, –74¢ under KC March for HRW, with movement opportunistic over systemic.

Export Sales & Inspections: Exports let the US edge in niches in 2025, seldom leading the world book.
Latest weekly net sales were 450k MT (week ending Dec 11), steady if not breakout. Flow was brighter:
weekly inspections 302k MT ending late December, season-to-date 15.06 MMT (+22 percent y/y). PNW
soft white to Southeast Asia shone, Gulf HRW held steady, decent runs, yet priced above
Russia/Argentina, keeping the US program tactical rather than market-making.

Funds & Positioning: Specs capped wheat’s upside in 2025, amplifying supply bears. Managed money
in Chicago SRW remained net short at roughly –49k contracts (as of Dec 16), leaving room for short-
covering rallies on any catalyst even as the broader surplus keeps follow-through limited. The setup is still
bearish by structure, but the short base means wheat doesn’t need a full bull story to pop, just a trigger
that forces covering.

So What? Wheat closed 2025 under the weight of a global surplus, with Russia and Argentina still setting
the ceiling and keeping US wheat boxed into premium, niche demand rather than market-making export
flows. US execution improved enough to provide a cushion at times, but the structural headwinds have
remained the same, wide price gaps versus competitors and plenty of exportable supply that makes it
hard for rallies to extend. That’s why the year’s better tells were often structure and basis, not the flat
price: we started in the upper $5s ($5.70 mid-Jan), bled into the low $5s ($5.30 late-Jun), and finished
near the mid-$5s ($5.19 late-Dec).

The market is still operating in surplus mode, and until Russia/Argentina offers lose their grip, through
logistics disruption, weather risk, or a meaningful currency shift, futures are likely to stay anchored near
recent lows. The one consistent upside risk is positioning: specs are short enough that wheat doesn’t
need a full bull story to rally, it just needs a catalyst that forces short covering. Until that happens,
commercials are more likely to buy breaks than chase breakouts, and the curve/basis will remain the
cleanest read on where US demand is absorbing wheat despite the global overhang.

US Cash Market & Basis

Corn: Corn basis demonstrated notable resilience throughout 2025, often outpacing board expectations,
and wrapped the year maintaining that cash-driven firmness. CIF Gulf bids closed in the mid-70s over
March (around +74¢), historically robust for December, bolstered by persistent winter logistics challenges
and constrained spot barge supply that intermittently hampered Gulf inflows and upheld premiums.
Interior markets were most robust where processor demand dominated, with Western Corn Belt ethanol
needs solidifying local spots. Iowa and Nebraska bids typically ranged flat to slightly under the board for
immediate delivery, as facilities vied for bushels amid minimal farmer sales in regions with strong basis
and uninspiring flat prices. National average basis concluded around –30¢ under March, roughly 20¢
above the five-year norm, encapsulating 2025's overarching dynamic: despite paper carryout signaling
comfort, end-user rivalry for prompt ownership consistently tightened the front and curbed any loose
tendencies.

Soybeans: Soybean basis mirrored the complex's year-long balancing act, export shortfalls frequently
weighed in, yet domestic forces reliably steadied the front. CIF Gulf barges for January held in the low-
90s over futures (around +93¢) with scant retreat amid board softness, underscoring blended support
from nearby pull, river dynamics, and hesitant sellers. Processor bids in prime Eastern Corn Belt areas
remained among the firmest, with spot premiums echoing vigorous soymeal demand and urgent crush
requirements. River basis saw slight gains as barge flows normalized, though freight volatility lingered as
a pivotal element into Q4 close. National average basis settled near –20¢ under January, about a dime
stronger than usual, and the setup signaled ongoing commercial eagerness to hold nearby stocks despite
sluggish exports. Brazilian forwards stayed cheaper heading into Q1, tempering Gulf upsides, but 2025's
key takeaway endured: crushers consistently bid to prevent front-end erosion, even as futures remained
exposed.

Wheat: Wheat cash markets held steady yet aimless for much of 2025, in line with a carry-oriented
landscape where worldwide rivalry set ceilings and US wheat targeted selective channels. Gulf SRW FOB
values lingered in the low-$6s/bu ($220–$235/MT equiv.), sustaining premiums over Black Sea rivals and
restricting US tender participation. Russian 12.5 percent protein anchored globally near $230/MT,
subduing benchmarks and affirming surplus vibes. Southern Plains HRW basis edged firmer in spots via

feed substitutions when corn stayed pricey, but overall flow was subdued. Pacific Northwest soft white
bids remained resilient on reliable Southeast Asian uptake, one of US wheat's steadier avenues yearly.
Broadly, the US cash wheat scene echoed 2025's pattern: flat prices seldom spurred heavy sales, but
basis missed the spark for reversal, directing commercials toward opportunistic clears over tight shifts.

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Even late in December, Brazil is still the reference point for nearby coverage. ANEC currently
points to December loadings near 2.81 MMT soybeans and 1.62 MMT corn, with soymeal 1.5 MMT
keeping protein flows steadier than whole beans into the turn. On price, Brazil remains the cheaper
nearby origin: Santos January beans around $10.05–10.10/bu leave the U.S. Gulf carrying a clear
premium, and Paranaguá corn near $204/MT keeps Brazil competitive into parts of Asia/MENA.
Operationally, nothing suggests major port gridlock. Agronomically, the market is still trading geography:
Center-West rainfall has been “good enough” for early development, while southern consistency is the
piece that can still inject risk if it turns choppy at the wrong time.

Argentina: The story is no longer the decree, it’s whether it converts into farmer selling. The duty cuts
and currency reset mechanically improve offer values (corn $178–182/MT; soybeans $428–432/MT), but
volumes will tell the truth as the new framework settles. Planting progress remains constructive (soy/corn
59 percent), supported by workable moisture, though the watch item is any meaningful drying trend
developing in Córdoba and nearby areas as crops move deeper into the critical window. Wheat is the
near-term lever: with harvest at 60 percent complete and production ideas near 27.7 MMT, Argentina has
the supply to show up, participation and logistics decide the pace.

China: Demand still looks selective rather than rebuild-mode. Crushers continue to prefer South
American arrivals for Q1 on pricing, and recent U.S. soybean business (1.707 MMT for 2025/26 through
the Dec 11 reporting week) still reads more strategic than broad commercial restocking. Corn and wheat
remain the louder absence, tariff suspensions may still be on the books, but follow-through buying has
been limited. Domestic pricing is firm, yet not consistently strong enough to force a durable import
arbitrage that pulls the U.S. into the center of the story.

EU / Black Sea: Wheat stays capped by the Black Sea’s ability to defend share. Russian FOB remains
the benchmark in the upper-$220s to mid-$230s/MT, while Ukraine continues to move grain through
Danube/rail channels despite periodic infrastructure risk. Ukraine corn $205/MT keeps pressure on EU
feed economics, and France around $229/MT leaves Europe competing for demand rather than setting it.
Net effect: the global hierarchy still favors the cheapest, most consistent origin, and that keeps rallies
hard to extend without a disruption.

Other Regions: Australia is wrapping harvest without major logistical drama, though output expectations
below 25 MMT reflect WA dryness even as eastern areas performed better. Canada continues routine
spring wheat movement, and India remains a non-factor on exports given its restrictive stance. No
secondary-origin shock is emerging that would meaningfully tighten the global balance into early Q1.

So What? Into year-end, the marginal price signals still come from the same places: Brazil for oilseeds
(nearby coverage) and the Black Sea for wheat (the ceiling). Argentina has improved competitiveness on
paper, but the timing depends on farmer selling and export execution. China remains present, but
uneven, enough to influence day-to-day tone, not enough to flip the balance.

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Dec 17 – Dec 30)

Crop Progress (USDA): With harvest complete, Crop Progress remained on hiatus through the holiday
window, keeping the US weather conversation centered on winter wheat dormancy/recharge and logistics
rather than row-crop yield updates. No new national winter wheat ratings were issued during the period.

Export Inspections (USDA FGIS): Export pace dipped during the holiday stretch, but the overall
marketing year’s story remained divided by crop. For the week ending Dec 18, corn inspections reached
1.74 MMT, soybeans 0.93 MMT, and wheat 0.64 MMT. The week ending Dec 25 saw drops to 1.30 MMT
for corn, 0.75 MMT for soybeans, and 0.30 MMT for wheat. Marketing-year-to-date totals through Dec 25
stood at 25.6 MMT for corn (up 66 percent from last year), 15.4 MMT for soybeans (down 46 percent),
and 15.1 MMT for wheat (up 22 percent).

Export Sales (USDA FAS): The latest full weekly report in the window covered the week ending Dec 11
(released Dec 23) and broadly echoed what inspections have been showing. Net sales came in at 1.2
MMT for corn, 1.5 MMT for soybeans, and 0.45 MMT for all wheat, with shipments of 1.4 MMT corn, 0.72
MMT soybeans, and 0.49 MMT wheat. Daily flashes added a bit of headline support without changing the
core trend: Dec 17 featured 198,000 MT soybeans to China and 177,000 MT corn to Mexico, both for
2025/26, positive on paper, but still consistent with soy demand looking more tactical than sustained while
corn continues to grind out reliable execution.

Ethanol Production & Stocks (EIA): Biofuel metrics stayed constructive but cooled slightly into the
holiday window, reinforcing a “steady, not accelerating” demand backdrop. For the week ending Dec 19,
ethanol production slipped to 1.095 mbpd from 1.131 mbpd the prior week, while stocks edged higher to
22.5 million barrels versus 22.4 million. The pull remains supportive in the bigger picture, but the late-
December tone suggests less urgency to chase near-term grind than earlier in the month, keeping
spreads/basis as the cleaner real-time demand read.

CFTC Positioning (latest available Disaggregated COT snapshot): The most recent snapshot (as of
Dec 16) fit the year-end structure: specs were not positioned in a way that forces a strong directional
move, but the bias differs by market. Corn showed managed money 234k long vs 288k short (net –53k),
consistent with muted speculative conviction versus the steadier cash signals. Soybeans remained
heavily supported by length at 196k long vs 41k short (net +155k), leaving the complex more vulnerable
to liquidation if South American weather stays friendly or exports fail to re-accelerate. In wheat, managed
money stayed net short across classes (HRW: 62k long vs 89k short, net –27k; HRS: 10k long vs 30k
short, net –20k), which continues to frame wheat’s upside risk as more “short-covering on catalysts” than
a clean fundamental bull trend.

NOPA Crush: No fresh NOPA report landed within Dec 17–30, but the prior print still mattered into year-
end because it anchored the “domestic engine” narrative for soybeans. November’s record 216.0 mbu
crush remained the most recent signal of how aggressively the system has been running, and it continues
to explain why the front end has held together even with soybean export performance lagging, cash bids
and spreads have stayed firmer than the board alone would suggest.

So What? Late-December fundamentals leaned heavily on execution metrics, and holiday slowdowns
added nuance without flipping trends: corn’s shipment pace stayed validating even with ethanol easing,
soybeans held crush-led floors but remained capped by export underperformance, and wheat’s steady
movement provided quiet support in a surplus-driven global backdrop. Until South American yield
outcomes clarify or demand reaccelerates in a sustained way, inspections/sales plus spreads and basis
remain the most actionable guideposts into early January.

International Reports

Brazil: Late-December flow indicators remained robust on estimates. ANEC's lineup projected December
soybean exports at around 2.81 MMT, corn at 1.62 MMT, and soymeal near 1.5 MMT. The group's full-
year 2025 tallies hit records, with soybeans at 110 MMT and corn exceeding 50 MMT (soymeal around
21 MMT). For the new crop, CONAB's December survey held Brazil's soybean estimate large at 177.6
MMT for 2025/26, positioning output near all-time highs despite regional weather variances.

Argentina: Argentina ramped up its profile on policy tweaks and wheat surplus. The government locked
in export duty cuts via decree, soybeans to 24 percent (from 26 percent), corn to 8.5 percent (from 9.5
percent), wheat to 7.5 percent (from 9.5 percent), aimed at spurring Q1 2026 sales and FX boosts.
Meanwhile, the Rosario Grains Exchange lifted its wheat forecast to a record 27.7 MMT, signaling
substantial volumes entering export streams in harvest's latter phase.

China: Buying signals leaned cautious over bold replenishment. Reporting highlighted ample near-term
stocks and muted downstream pull: port soybean inventories around 10.3 MMT mid-November, with
November imports at 8.11 MMT (up 13.4 percent y/y per customs). This setup points to sufficient
coverage, with crushers prioritizing margins, aligning with patchy, tactical purchases rather than sweeping
forward commitments.

EU / Black Sea: Russia anchored wheat pricing. IKAR/Reuters quotes placed Russian 12.5 percent
wheat FOB at $228/MT (late January/early February delivery), holding global floors in the low-$220s to
low-$230s. Ukraine posed ongoing logistics headlines: Reuters noted strikes on Odesa facilities, with
marketing year-to-date grain exports down 13 percent y/y, underscoring why flows carry embedded risk
premiums amid plentiful overall supply.

So What? Late-December's international snapshot stayed "abundant supply / fluid movement," with
Brazil as prime price setter (hefty December lineups + premium holds), Argentina gaining traction via
duties and wheat volumes, China stocked to pick selectively, and Black Sea wheat ceilings intact while
Ukraine's infrastructure kept mild risk layers. Trade flows didn't pivot in the window, but tilted to cost-
efficient suppliers, underscoring US competitiveness as niche over leading.

Weather & Crop Conditions

United States
With U.S. harvest finished, weather is no longer a yield headline, it’s a winter setup and logistics story.
The market’s two practical watch points are how winter wheat goes into dormancy and whether Plains
moisture pockets recharge ahead of spring, and whether cold snaps and short-term river level swings
create friction in barge flow as normal business resumes. South America remains the bigger pricing
variable, but even there the emphasis is shifting from “total rainfall” to where the rain lands, especially the
South vs Center-West split in Brazil and any meaningful drying trend in Argentina’s core belt as crops
advance into their more sensitive stages.

Brazil
Brazil’s weather signal into year-end has been less about “nationwide threat” and more about regional
dispersion, the market keeps weighting rainfall consistency in the Center-West and how quickly southern
areas can stabilize as reproductive stages expand. USDA’s Weekly Weather and Crop Bulletin (covering
the week ending Dec 21) noted beneficial heavy rain across central and southern Brazil, a constructive
backdrop for early crop development and stand establishment in key production zones. With planting
essentially wrapped up (DATAGRO indicated Brazil soybean planting near completion by late December),
attention naturally shifts toward the first concrete field reads that start to show up in January, especially
where rainfall distribution has been uneven.

Argentina
Argentina has generally kept a sturdier moisture profile than the market feared earlier in the cycle, but the
week-to-week monitoring remains important because the crop calendar is now deep into the period where
rainfall timing matters more than totals. USDA’s Weekly Weather and Crop Bulletin (week ending Dec 21)
highlighted that rainfall increased moisture for summer crops in Argentina, while also noting that dryness
was still present in some areas, meaning conditions are supportive overall, but not uniformly “bulletproof”
across the belt. Planting progress has continued moving forward with corn and soybeans advancing
meaningfully through late December (as referenced in the same USDA bulletin), keeping the crop on
track as the calendar flips.

Global
Outside the Americas, the late-December global weather backdrop has stayed relatively benign in the
places that matter most for near-term trade psychology. Northern Hemisphere winter wheat is largely in
its dormancy window, and the bigger “watch items” have been logistical/operational rather than weather-
driven supply shocks. In Australia, USDA’s Weekly Weather and Crop Bulletin noted harvest progress
supported by favorable conditions in key areas, keeping export execution steady into the seasonal
transition.

So What?
The year ends with weather risk concentrated rather than broad-based. The US has moved into a
dormancy-and-logistics phase: winter wheat dryness pockets still matter, but the larger swing factor for
nearby cash has been that the Mississippi system is operating without the same intensity of disruption
that defined the worst of the 2025 low-water stretch. In South America, the market’s early-2026 sensitivity
stays tied to whether Brazil’s rainfall distribution stays consistent as the crop pushes further into
reproductive stages, while Argentina’s profile remains generally supportive but still monitored for any
meaningful drying trend.

Synthesis & Outlook

Grain and oilseed markets closed out 2025 much like the latter half unfolded: futures in tight ranges, with
cash flows and basis offering the sharpest insights. Corn stood out as the steadiest on demand delivery,
soybeans leaned on crush amid export drags, and wheat navigated surplus pressures while US
shipments provided quiet backing. Holiday thinness amplified some moves, but spreads, basis, and
verified flows drove the core narrative over broader macros.

Recent weekly reads into late December highlight the divides. Export inspections for the week ending
Dec 25 came in at 1.30 MMT for corn, 0.75 MMT for soybeans, and 0.30 MMT for wheat. Marketing-year-
to-date, corn flows lead last year (25.6 MMT vs 15.4 MMT for corn last year), wheat edges ahead (15.1
MMT vs 12.4 MMT), and soybeans trail sharply (15.4 MMT vs 28.7 MMT). Ethanol held constructive but
eased: output at 1.095 mbpd (down from 1.131 prior), stocks steady near 22.5 million barrels. In short,
corn pull persists, but 2026 opens with less urgency to chase processor volumes than early December
suggested.

Weather remains the prime swing factor into the new year, though signals grew subtler lately. USDA's
bulletin flagged helpful Dec 21 rains in Brazil's central and southern zones through Dec 21, drier
northeast, and solid Argentina core moisture with isolated hotter/drier spots. This pivots early-Q1 focus to
rain placement, southern Brazil vs Center-West, and Argentina's hold on current levels, over blanket
bull/bear calls

Bullish triggers: US corn shipments picking up post-holidays (weekly inspections above winter norms),
ethanol stabilizing near early-Dec highs. For soybeans, either export bookings converting faster or
weather dents shifting South American yields. Tighter nearby spreads or Gulf/processor basis lifts would

confirm commercials vying for front-end control.

Bearish triggers: South American weather staying mostly cooperative into reproductive starts, southern
Brazil dodging big stress, could expose soybeans further and erode nearby premiums. Corn faces
looseness from ethanol slowdowns or export fades. Wheat sees clean Black Sea bids and Argentine
pace capping US ups, keeping gains opportunistic.

Watchlist (Year-End / Early Jan):

Export inspections: Track corn/soy through holiday logistics (execution over flashes key).

EIA ethanol: Production near 1.10 mbpd hold, stocks contained?

South America: Confirm rains (Brazil north-south; Argentina cores), watch anomaly shifts.

Spreads + basis: Tightening/firming as top real-time gauge for demand/ownership.

In summary: Markets leave 2025 with corn validating front via demand, soybeans crush-backed but open
to export/South American hits, wheat surplus-capped despite US flow holds. If South America weather
aligns, US cash must overmatch paper into early 2026.

Ethanol for America Act

The major barrier to a higher Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) is the fuel versus food debate. Now is the
perfect time to move to E15. Corn prices are extremely low, and the latest USDA WASDE reported a record
crop and a record crop expansion.

USDA WASDE forecast corn production at 16.7 billion bushels, with the yield at 188.8 bushels per acre and
ending stocks at 2.1 billion. The season-average corn price dropped 30 cents to $3.90 a bushel. Most
importantly, 202526 crop year is expected to have 1.8 billion more bushels than 2024/25.

With current ethanol production consuming 5.6 billion bushels, a 10 percent increase in consumption would
consume an additional 560 million bushels. The reality is that year around E15 would add approximately
50 million bushels and regulatory streamlining would add another 50 million bushels. At some point over
the next ten years, the additional corn consumption could be 2.8 billion bushels minus lower fuel
consumption resulting from electric vehicles. The ethanol corn consumption increase is likely to be more
of a S curve as new compacity comes online.

With Brazil and the US corn and soybean production increasing, 100 million bushels of ethanol corn
consumption will barely move the needle. The ethanol production capacity expansion that would be three
to four years from now is when the corn consumption impact to the corn market would be felt.
