Corn Market Deep Dive

Pre-WASDE Positioning: Trade talk continues to center on whether final Crop Production trims USDA’s
current 2025 yield (186 bpa) and whether strong export execution gives USDA room to keep the balance
sheet tighter via higher exports. The market’s bias has leaned toward “modest tightening” (yield risk +
export-friendly math), but without a verified Reuters poll table in hand, the clean anchor remains
execution data, inspections, Gulf values, and whether the next weekly Export Sales report (week ended
Jan 1) shows meaningful catch-up post-holidays.

Futures & Spreads: March corn settled at $4.45/bu (+5¢ w/w) and continues to trade like a market that
isn’t short nearby ownership, even without a headline catalyst. Calendar structure is still carrying, but not

“max carry”: the Mar/May spread is 7¢ carry (about 50 percent of full carry), keeping the curve’s message
closer to steady demand underneath than burdensome supply. Technically, the market is hovering
around the 200-day moving average near $4.45, which traders have treated as an important “line in the
sand” going into Monday’s reports.

Funds & Positioning: Managed money remains net short -53,192 contracts in CBOT corn futures-only
as of Dec 30, 2025 (Long 309,183 vs Short 362,375). That keeps positioning from being outright bullish,
but it matters into Jan 12 because any surprise tightening in final yield or stocks can still force incremental
short covering, especially if spreads/basis refuse to break.

Cash & Basis: Gulf basis remains the anchor for the front end. In your cash set, CIF Gulf sits near +82¢
over March and FOB Gulf near +106¢ over March, a structure that still reads as export replacement
values holding together even as futures churn. Interior tone remains steady rather than defensive, which
fits the message from the board: carry is present, but it hasn’t been able to fully take control of nearby.

Export Sales & Inspections: The clean, verifiable signal this week is inspections. USDA’s export
inspections show corn inspections at 1.21 MMT for the week ended Jan 1, versus 877,219 MT the same
week last year. On the sales side, the market is also watching whether the next weekly report confirms
continued strength: USDA reported net corn sales of 756,400 MT for the week ended Dec 25, and
2025/26 commitments (sales + exports) at 1.99 bbu, up 30 percent y/y, important context for why the
curve has stayed supported even without a weather scare.

International Trade / Competition: Global price competition hasn’t disappeared, but near-term US
export execution is doing enough to keep the market from slipping into a purely storage-driven structure.
The other key international variable for January is less about “new” export business and more about what
South America weather implies for late-Q1 and Q2 supply, especially Argentina corn during critical
development stages. If South America stays broadly favorable, the market will likely need Monday’s US
reports to be the bullish catalyst; if Argentina turns meaningfully drier/hotter, that becomes a second path
to tightening spreads and keeping funds from pressing shorts.

So What? Corn is acting like a market with quiet demand gravity: futures are stable-to-firmer, spreads are
only paying partial carry, and inspections are still strong enough to keep Gulf values from cracking. The
Jan 12 reports are the hinge, if final yield or Dec 1 stocks tighten the implied balance sheet, the market
has room to react because managed money is still net short (futures-only) and the curve isn’t “fully
carried.” If the reports lean neutral-to-bearish, the path of least resistance is not necessarily a collapse,
it’s more likely a drift lower with spreads doing the real signaling day-to-day.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

Pre-WASDE Positioning: The soybean story into Jan 12 remains split between soft shipment execution
and renewed China headline demand. The base-case trade view is that USDA won’t need to reinvent the
US balance sheet unless it chooses to re-tilt demand between exports and crush in response to the
slower export trajectory versus last year and the steadier processor pull. What changed this week is the
tone around China: USDA daily flashes confirmed multiple soybean sales to China (including 336,000 MT
on Jan 2), and market chatter has focused on whether state buying (Sinograin) is re-entering in size for
spring shipment. The key pre-WASDE question remains the same, does USDA continue to defend
exports, or lean more heavily on crush to keep demand intact as the marketing-year pace becomes
harder to ignore?

Futures & Spreads: March ’26 soybeans settled at $10.67/bu, up +5¢ w/w, but the path was choppy,
more “headline-driven pop” than a clean trend. Structure is still doing most of the talking, the Mar/May

carry sits at +11¢, about 50 percent of full carry, which reads as adequate nearby coverage rather than
any front-end shortage. Farther out, the curve is sending a different signal: Jul ’26 vs Nov ’26 remains
inverted by 12¢, keeping a weather-premium feel embedded in summer ownership even as the nearby
stays commercially supplied

Products & Crush: Soybean products provided steady underlying support, with both meal and oil firming
modestly on the week. The latest available NOPA crush data (November) printed 216.0 million
bushels, exceeding last year’s pace and reinforcing the view that domestic processing demand remains
resilient despite slower export shipments. Crush margins remain positive and continue to incentivize run
rates near capacity, keeping processor bids engaged across the interior. Into the January WASDE, this
keeps crush as the most defensible demand line item, raising the question of whether USDA offsets any
export caution by leaning more heavily on domestic processing rather than reducing total use.

Cash & Basis: Gulf signals were steady-to-softer but not weak: CIF NOLA is around +100¢ over Jan,
while FOB Gulf is near +102¢ over Jan, consistent with a cash market that’s being supported by nearby
logistics/friction and steady processor demand, but still lacking the kind of relentless export pull that would
force a sharper basis surge. Brazil remains the reference competitor: Paranaguá Feb FOB indications
(12¢/bu over March equivalent) keep the export program price-sensitive, especially if buyers can wait for
South America.

Funds & Positioning: Managed money positioning remains a swing factor, but it’s not screaming
“crowded long.” On a futures-only basis, managed money is net long +121,811 as of Dec 30, 2025 (long
203,843 vs short 82,032), which leaves room for additional buying if China buying persists and/or South
American weather risk re-prices.

Export Sales & Inspections: Execution remains the constraint. US soybean export inspections totaled
0.98 MMT (36 mbu) for the latest week, bringing cumulative shipments to 16.40 MMT (603 mbu), still 45
percent below last year’s pace. Export sales have improved at the margin, net sales of 504k MT in the
most recent report, but commitments remain insufficient to materially close the shipment gap. That’s why
the Sinograin headline matters: it doesn’t fix execution overnight, but it reduces the “no-China” tail risk
and helps explain why futures can firm even as the export tape remains heavy.

Policy / China Demand Context: This week’s soybean support came less from broad macro and more
from a very specific demand narrative: state buying + a push to clear domestic inventory space (Sinograin
auctions) to accommodate incoming US cargoes. If that state-led buying continues, it’s the cleanest path
to a pre-WASDE repricing, because it attacks the market’s biggest doubt: whether US export demand can
stabilize at all this season.

So What? The soybean board is still being supported more by crush and curve structure than by clean
export execution. Nearby spreads only pay partial carry and the back end remains inverted, which keeps
ownership from getting too comfortable even as shipments lag. The Sinograin headline matters because
it reduces the “no-China” tail risk, but it does not repair the export math overnight, inspections remain well
behind last year on a cumulative basis, and sales need sustained follow-through to change that. Into Jan
12, the market is effectively asking whether USDA defends exports or leans harder on crush to keep the
balance sheet stable. Without repeatable China business or a weather premium, soybeans likely stay
range-bound, with structure doing most of the signaling.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Pre-WASDE Positioning: Ahead of Jan 12, the trade expects only marginal adjustments to the US wheat
balance sheet, with attention centered on the “January bundle” reports (Grain Stocks + Winter Wheat
Seedings) more than routine WASDE line edits. Execution has been respectable (shipments running
ahead y/y), which keeps “exports could be revised up” on the list, but global competition remains the
limiting factor. With funds still meaningfully short in CBOT wheat (futures-only), the market is more
vulnerable to sharp rallies if seedings print lower or stocks come in tighter than expected, though any
bullish reaction still faces a ceiling from ample Black Sea and Southern Hemisphere supply.

Futures & Spreads: CBOT March SRW wheat settled at $5.20/bu, up roughly 14¢ w/w, remaining range-
bound despite recent short-covering attempts. The Mar/May SRW spread holds near +11¢ carry, roughly
40 percent of full commercial carry, signaling comfortable nearby availability without forcing full storage
economics. KC HRW March closed near $5.28/bu, maintaining an 18¢ premium to SRW, while
Minneapolis HRS March finished near $5.56/bu. Volatility remains muted, and open interest changes
suggest the price action continues to be positioning-driven rather than fundamentally led. The curve
structure still rewards storage and offers little indication of front-end tightness.

Cash & Basis: US wheat cash markets remain weak relative to global competition. SRW FOB Gulf
values near $6.23/bu and HRW FOB Gulf near $6.56/bu keep US origin priced $15–25/MT above Black
Sea offers, limiting competitiveness in major tenders. Interior basis has been largely unchanged, with
HRW bids in Kansas and Oklahoma around 20–40¢ under March, and SRW river bids holding near 15–
20¢ under. Protein premiums remain intact, but overall cash movement is slow as mills remain covered
and export demand favors cheaper origins.

Export Sales & Inspections: Weekly US wheat export inspections totaled 183,000 MT (6.7 mbu), down
w/w but still leaving marketing-year shipments near 15.263 MMT, roughly six percent ahead of last year’s
pace. While execution remains solid, new sales activity has slowed materially, and the US continues to
miss major North African and Middle Eastern tenders dominated by Russian and EU wheat. Mexico and
select Latin American destinations remain the most consistent buyers, but volumes are insufficient to
materially shift the global balance. The market continues to distinguish between decent execution and
weak forward demand.

Global Supply & Competition: Russia remains the dominant force in global wheat trade, with FOB
offers near $229–233/MT, supported by a weak ruble and aggressive export pace. Australia’s harvest has
added additional exportable supply, while Argentina’s record wheat crop (27–28 MMT) is flowing
aggressively into Brazil and Asia. EU exports remain steady but unremarkable. Despite dryness concerns
in parts of the US Plains, global supply remains ample, and no meaningful exporter is signaling restraint
at this stage.

Funds & Positioning: Managed money remains heavily net short -70K contracts, with only modest short-
covering observed recently. The size of the short leaves wheat vulnerable to brief rallies on headline risk,
but without a structural tightening signal, those rallies continue to fade. Commercials remain opportunistic
buyers at low price levels, but not aggressive enough to alter the broader market tone.

So What? Wheat remains a market supported by positioning rather than fundamentals. Spreads continue
to encourage storage, cash markets show no tightening signal, and global competition remains intense.
While US export execution has improved year-over-year, it has not translated into stronger forward
demand or improved competitiveness. Unless winter wheat acreage surprises lower or Black Sea flows
are disrupted, Chicago wheat is likely to remain range-bound, with rallies capped by global supply and
weak export pricing power. The market is firming at the margins, but it is not tightening.

US Cash Market & Basis

Corn: River basis improved modestly this week amid stable water levels on the Lower Mississippi, though
colder weather introduced some logistical caution. Illinois River bids firmed to –18¢ under March, up 2¢
w/w, while the Lower Miss held near –40¢ to –43¢ under with steady drafts and traffic. Spot freight from
Cairo to Memphis eased to $19.00/ton, down slightly on quieter post-holiday movement. CIF Gulf basis
strengthened to +82¢ over March, up 1¢, bolstered by robust export inspections and Mexican buying.
FOB Gulf offers remained near +106¢ over March, reflecting solid replacement values. Processor bids in
Iowa and Nebraska stayed firm at +12¢ to +18¢ over, supported by steady ethanol economics. National
average corn basis was near –35¢ under, firmer by 3¢ on the week.

Soybeans: Processor bids in the Eastern Corn Belt held firm, aided by supportive crush margins and
consistent soymeal pull. River basis was mostly steady where barge logistics improved on the Illinois and
Lower Mississippi, but export demand from China stayed uneven despite recent flashes. CIF Gulf
soybean basis slipped to +100¢ over January, down 2¢, amid better freight availability but softer new
sales. FOB Gulf offers were near +102¢ over January, down 6¢ w/w. National average soybean basis
hovered near –72¢ under the March futures equivalent, slightly firmer from last week.

Wheat: HRW and SRW FOB Gulf values stayed flat near $6.56/bu and $6.23/bu, respectively, with export
basis unchanged amid quiet global tenders. Interior bids in Kansas and Oklahoma remained soft at –45¢
to –50¢ under March, influenced by storage incentives over spot consumption. Basis levels in the
Southern Plains milling market were steady as January coverage held firm. Domestic demand from flour
buyers was consistent but lacked fresh spot urgency, keeping interior values range-bound.

So What? Logistics remained stable with river levels supportive, allowing Gulf basis to hold firm in corn
while soy and wheat faced global competitive pressure. Export flow anchored corn cash strength,
processors provided the soy floor, and wheat stayed defensive without new demand catalysts. Basis tone
in corn and soy indicates demand is absorbing nearby supply without excess pressure. Absent stronger
China export confirmation or weather risks, domestic users will keep setting the nearby cash pace

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Brazil continues to lead global soybean and corn exports, with December loadings showing
strength despite the onset of early harvest pressures. ANEC reported December soybean exports near
3.02 MMT, while corn paced around 6.35 MMT, both solid but reflecting a seasonal slowdown from peak
months. FOB Santos soybean offers held near $422/MT ($11.49/bu), maintaining a competitive edge over
US Gulf equivalents into China. Corn FOB values stayed firm around $222/MT ($5.64/bu), positioning
Brazil as the preferred origin for Southeast Asia. Soybean harvest progressed to early stages in Mato
Grosso, with estimates around 5-10 percent complete amid generally favorable but locally wet conditions
that could delay logistics. Export corridors at Paranaguá and Santos remained efficient, with minimal
congestion reported.

Argentina: Up-River FOB prices were steady: corn offered around $218/MT, while soymeal traded near
$345/MT (47 percent protein basis), aligning with recent export trends. Farmer sales moderated post-
election stability, but dryness in southern regions raised concerns for corn and soybean development
during key growth phases. The Rosario Exchange noted corn crops in good condition overall, though
moisture deficits persist in parts of Buenos Aires and La Pampa. The peso weakened further in parallel
markets, with the unofficial rate near ARS 1,470/USD, adding to export incentives amid macro
adjustments. Wheat harvest advanced to nearly 93 percent complete, with production expectations hitting
a record 27.8 MMT under mostly dry conditions. Crushers maintained steady operations, drawing on

accumulated stocks.

China: Import focus shifted toward US soybeans amid state-led buying, with recent purchases pushing
totals near 10 MMT for the 2025/26 marketing year. US Gulf offers have remained generally less
competitive than Brazilian nearby export values, but the recent USDA flashes signaled improving US
traction for spring coverage. Crushers secured Q1 coverage via mixed origins, with confirmed US sales
including 336,000 MT reported early January. Dalian Jan corn futures settled around ¥2,400/MT
($6.80/bu equivalent), above import parity but reflecting domestic supply pressures. Market discussions
on long-term commitments (12 MMT in 2026 and beyond) continued, treated as directional amid tariff
stability.

EU / Black Sea: Russian FOB wheat offers for 12.5 percent protein firmed to $228–233/MT, supported
by reset export taxes and steady tender wins in Egypt and MENA. French wheat near $228/MT (Rouen)
stayed on the sidelines, with recent tenders favoring Black Sea origins. Ukraine sustained corn exports
via Danube and rail, with offers around $173–175/MT into Spain and Italy, up slightly on demand. EU
grain stocks improved post-harvest, curbing import needs. Russian and Ukrainian soymeal undercut US
offers into southern Europe, aided by freight and currency advantages.

Other Regions: Australia's harvest progressed strongly, with CBH receiving 23.5 MMT total (mostly
wheat), setting receivals records amid improved yields and protein. Canada maintained steady spring
wheat flows to Mexico and Asia. India stayed sidelined in global trade, with no policy changes. South
Africa reported no significant shifts.

So What? US exporters face ongoing challenges into Asia and MENA as Brazil and Russia hold price
advantages. China's pivot to US soybeans offers Gulf support, but execution lags. Argentina's dryness
adds risk premium potential, though not yet disrupting flows. Until FOB differentials narrow or demand
reallocates, US cash resilience will hinge on domestic pull and basis rather than global arbitrage.

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Dec 17 – Dec 30)

Crop Progress (USDA): No formal Crop Progress report is issued during winter, but state-level updates
and private assessments pegged national winter wheat conditions near 52 percent good-to-excellent, up
slightly from late December readings but still reflecting patchy dryness in the southern Plains. Emergence
was effectively complete, with Kansas reporting 60 percent good-to-excellent (vs 47 percent last year)
and Texas near 45 percent (improved w/w on scattered rains). Dryness in western Oklahoma and eastern
Colorado kept some stands stressed, but overall ratings held steady without widespread winterkill risks in
the forecast.

Export Inspections (USDA FGIS): Corn inspections hit 1.21 MMT (+8 percent w/w), outpacing last
year’s pace by 69 percent and pushing cumulative 2025/26 shipments to 885.5 mbu. Soybean
inspections slipped to 0.98 MMT (–12 percent w/w), the softest in three weeks, underscoring slower
China pull versus Brazil’s ongoing flow. Wheat inspections totaled 183k MT (–27 percent w/w), focused
on the Gulf but lagging seasonal averages. Overall, the data reinforces corn’s export strength, soy’s
shipment lag, and wheat’s mixed competitiveness.

Export Sales (USDA FAS): The next weekly Export Sales report (covering the week ended Jan 1) is due
Jan 8, with the market watching whether holiday-delayed bookings surface. Daily sales flashes kept
demand headlines active, including 336,000 MT of soybeans to China (Jan 2) and a 150,000 MT corn
sale to Mexico (Jan 6). Outside of the China business, there have been no confirmed large soybean
bookings, keeping attention on whether the upcoming sales report shows enough follow-through to
influence USDA’s export assumptions into the January WASDE.

Ethanol Production & Stocks (EIA): Ethanol output eased to 1.098 mbpd (–22,000 bpd w/w), reflecting
post-holiday adjustments and steady blending rates. Stocks built to 23.652 million barrels (+708,000 w/w),
consistent with seasonal patterns and no major disruptions. Implied corn grind hovered near 98 mbu,
supported by stable margins and firm processor pull in the Western Corn Belt.

CFTC Positioning (latest available Disaggregated COT snapshot): Commitments of Traders (as of
Dec 30, published Jan 2): Managed money held net short in corn (–53,192 contracts, little changed w/w)
and wheat (–70,991 contracts, minor covering), while soybeans stayed net long (+121,811 contracts)
after light additions. Open interest dipped modestly across the complex, signaling positioning was more
about Jan 12 prep than aggressive bets. Without official surprises, the data keeps funds as a potential
volatility amplifier if reports lean bullish, but not the primary driver.

NOPA Crush: No fresh data released in the window; the next monthly report (December) is due Jan 15.
Private estimates for December point toward another solid print above 195 mbu, backed by strong crush
economics and soymeal demand. Processor bids stayed active, confirming throughput remains a key
offset to softer soy exports.

So What? Data this week was mostly confirmatory rather than game-changing: corn exports and ethanol
use provide the supportive undercurrent, soybeans lean on flashes and crush to counter soft inspections,
and wheat’s execution stays decent but uninspiring. With no Crop Progress and the big USDA event
looming, physical signals (Gulf basis, inspections) are doing the heavy lifting. If Jan 12 validates export
upgrades or yield trims, funds have room to react; otherwise, the tone drifts neutral with South America
weather as the wildcard.

International Reports

Brazil: ANEC's early-January lineup data pegged soybean exports tracking around 2.8 MMT for the
month so far and corn near 5.2 MMT, in line with seasonal wind-down for old-crop soy but still reflecting
solid safrinha movement. FOB Santos soybeans were quoted near $422/MT ($11.49/bu), holding a
competitive $10/MT edge over US Gulf into Asian markets, while corn offers around $222/MT ($5.64/bu)
kept Brazil leading feed grain flows. Mato Grosso soybean harvest pushed to about 8 percent complete
by Jan 5, helped by generally supportive rains but with pockets of excess moisture slowing logistics in
northern regions. CONAB held off on a fresh bulletin this week, though trade sources anticipate a slight
bump to 2025/26 soybean output in the upcoming release. Port operations at Santos and Paranaguá
stayed efficient, without notable backups despite early wet-harvest chatter.

Argentina: The Buenos Aires Grain Exchange noted wheat harvest nearing 93 percent done as of Dec
30, lifting its production outlook to 27.7 MMT amid favorable late-season conditions in key zones.
Soybean planting advanced to 82 percent complete, with crops mostly in good shape but dryness building
in southern areas, while corn development held steady without major revisions. MAGyP's latest weekly
confirmed planting stability but flagged emerging moisture deficits in Buenos Aires and La Pampa. Up-
River FOB corn indications sat near $218/MT, soymeal around $345/MT, both unchanged w/w. The peso
slipped to about 1,470 per USD in informal channels, bolstering export edges amid ongoing macro
tweaks. Farmer forward sales picked up modestly post-holidays, with crushers tapping into earlier
stockpiles from incentive programs.

China: Amid renewed state-led US soybean purchases, CNGOIC's early-January grain update
highlighted steady feed consumption but emphasized plans to boost domestic soybean capacity, with
total grain feed/residual use seen near 287 MMT for 2025/26. No fresh tariff shifts were announced, but
crushers leaned into US origins for Q1–Q2 coverage, with bookings approaching 10 MMT ytd. Dalian Jan

corn futures closed around ¥2,400/MT ($6.80/bu eq), soybeans near ¥4,850/MT, and soymeal
¥3,200/MT, all firmer on the week amid import momentum. MARA and Customs issued no new reserve or
import directives in the period, though market buzz around long-term commitments (up to 25 MMT+
through 2028) kept demand sentiment afloat without firm confirmations.

EU / Black Sea: Russian 12.5 percent wheat FOB offers edged to $228–233/MT (+1 w/w) following a
duty cut to 97.3 RUB/ton from Jan 12, with further zeroing eyed mid-month, aiding tender wins in MENA
and beyond. Ukrainian corn offers via Danube held near $173–175/MT, finding takers in EU southern
ports. FranceAgriMer trimmed its 2025/26 soft wheat export forecast outside the EU to 7.6 MMT but noted
stable winter cereal conditions, with French wheat ratings around 68 percent good-to-excellent.

So What? Worldwide flows are still led by Brazil's corn/soy strength and Russia's wheat edge, with
Argentina's dryness injecting some yield uncertainty but not yet derailing competitiveness via currency
plays. China's US bean pick-up offers a demand lifeline without fully closing FOB gaps. Absent new
global revisions or logistics snags, international prices key off exporter rivalry more than tightness. Next
movers likely tie to Argentina's mid-Jan rain (or lack thereof) and China's follow-on buying, which could
either underpin US basis firmness or let seasonal pressure creep in ahead of WASDE.

Weather & Crop Conditions

United States
With no formal Crop Progress reports in winter, private and state assessments indicate winter wheat
conditions broadly steady, with national ratings near 40 percent good-to-excellent. Kansas remains
relatively strong near 60 percent G/E, while Texas sits closer to 45 percent after scattered showers.
Dryness persists in western Kansas and Oklahoma, where recent rainfall remains 15–30 mm below
normal, and warmer-than-seasonal temperatures have limited soil recharge despite low winterkill risk.

The Mississippi River system stabilized post-holidays, with modest gauge improvements at Memphis and
Baton Rouge supporting more normal barge drafts. Freight rates on the Cairo–Memphis stretch eased
toward $19/ton, though levels remain below seasonal averages and logistics margins elevated. Looking
ahead, NOAA’s 6–10 day outlook favors above-normal temperatures and below-normal precipitation
across much of the Plains and Midwest, suggesting continued river support but ongoing dryness risk in
HRW areas.

Brazil
Rains picked up in the Center-West over the week, boosting early harvest and easing logistics in core
zones. IMEA estimates show Mato Grosso harvest around eight percent complete as of Jan 5, with
scattered showers of 20–50 mm providing relief but creating wet spots in northern areas that could slow
trucking. Forecast models from INMET and NOAA point to more precipitation through mid-January, with
40–70 mm expected in central Brazil, sufficient to maintain crop momentum if consistent. Southern states
(Paraná, Rio Grande do Sul) remained mostly favorable after earlier wetness, supporting vegetative
stages without major stress.

Argentina
Dryness intensified in southern provinces, with BCBA flagging moisture shortfalls in Buenos Aires and La
Pampa that could start impacting soybean and corn yields during pod-set. Wheat harvest pushed to
nearly 93 percent complete under mostly dry skies, locking in strong output near 27 MMT. Forecasts
indicate limited thunderstorms in central and northern zones, with 15–30 mm possible through mid-month,
but southern dryness may persist. No widespread crop deterioration was reported yet, but risks are
building.

Global
In the Northern Hemisphere, winter wheat establishment advanced without major issues. Russia and
Ukraine noted typical emergence under mild fall temps, with stable soils. Europe saw steady progress, as
FranceAgriMer held French wheat ratings near 68 percent good-to-excellent, and Germany/Poland
benefited from adequate moisture for stands. Australia's harvest wrapped up mixed, with persistent
dryness in Western Australia capping yields, while New South Wales and Queensland got timely rains
improving quality but not totals. No notable disruptions hit India, South Africa, or Canada.

So What?
US winter wheat is in decent shape with low winterkill odds, but dryness in the Plains keeps recharge in
focus. Stabilized rivers have eased export flow without slashing freight, though costs linger high, limiting
basis upside. Brazil's rain recovery is the core global driver: harvest is underway, but steady moisture is
key to firming yield outlooks. Argentina's emerging dryness adds a risk layer, while Russia, the EU, and
Australia stay supportive overall, making South America's mid-Jan weather the main swing factor for
oilseed and grain pricing.

Synthesis & Outlook

The first week of January brought the grain complex into a classic pre-WASDE holding pattern, with
USDA's "January bundle" looming and physical signals doing the interim work amid light holiday trading.
After months of leaning on inspections, basis, and flashes for direction, the market now awaits official
tweaks that could endorse or challenge the export-led tone in corn and the crush/export split in soy.
Futures chopped in tight ranges through Friday, March corn near $4.45/bu, March soybeans at
$10.67/bu, and March Chicago wheat around $5.20/bu, as positioning stayed cautious ahead of the data
dump. Spreads held supported but not tight, with corn Mar/May at about 50% of full carry, soybeans
Mar/May near 50%, and wheat Mar/May close to 40%. Gulf basis firmed in corn, processors kept soy bids
engaged, and volatility stayed low.

The vibe was one of quiet anticipation, with traders prepping for potential balance-sheet shifts without
committing big. Speculative activity was subdued, as managed money held net short in corn (around -53k
contracts) and wheat (near –71k), while adding lightly to soy longs (roughly +122k). CME open interest
ticked lower but reflected a commercially driven market focused on rolls and hedging over outright bets.
The resumption of full data flow sharpens visibility, but it also amps up risk: after drawing on inferred
demand from Gulf values, ethanol, and China headlines, the complex will recalibrate to quantifiable
numbers. If WASDE backs export upgrades or yield trims, the recent firmness could evolve into
conviction; if it underscores global supply, the stability may reveal itself as fragile.

Globally, Brazil held export dominance in soybeans and corn, with Russia steering wheat trade. Santos
soybeans quoted near $422/MT ($11.49/bu), about $10 under US Gulf, and corn FOB around $222/MT.
Early Mato Grosso harvest hit 8 percent, with rains aiding but subsoils still thin. Argentina stayed
competitive via currency weakness, with wheat output near record 27 MMT. Russian 12.5 percent wheat
offers firmed to $228–233/MT without slowing tenders, and China's state buying pushed US soy
purchases toward 10 MMT. The world sheet thus remains ample, but with Argentina dryness brewing and
eyes on US reports, the tone moved from post-harvest drift to watchful prep.

Bullish triggers: The upside hinges on WASDE affirming US demand strength. Robust inspections,
steady Gulf basis, and ethanol output above 1.1 mbpd could support corn export hikes, slimming carryout
modestly. For soy, crush upgrades plus persistent China flashes (near 10 MMT bought) could offset soft
shipments, especially if Brazil/Argentina weather slips, lifting spreads and pushing March futures toward
the mid-$10.60s. Wheat could extend if seedings surprise low or Russian duties constrain flow, fueling
short-covering. With funds short in corn/wheat and vol muted, even mild bullish leans might spark sharp

moves.

Bearish triggers: Downside looms if WASDE highlights abundance and static demand. Holding corn
exports flat, sticking with big South American crops, or bumping world stocks could widen carries. In soy,
fading China momentum amid Brazil's harvest pressure might refocus on global oversupply and soften
Gulf values. Wheat stays exposed if Russia keeps undercutting tenders, sidelining US offers. That path
could drag futures to range bottoms, with corn near $4.35, soy around $10.45, and wheat back to the
$5.00s. Watchlist (Jan 8 – Jan 14): USDA January reports (Jan 12): WASDE tweaks, final 2025 yields,
Dec 1 stocks, winter wheat seedings Export sales catch-up (Jan 8) and any new flashes to China or
Mexico Argentina dryness updates in Buenos Aires/La Pampa and mid-Jan rain verification Gulf
basis/logistics flow and barge freight follow-through Russia/Black Sea tender pace, EU competitiveness,
and BRL/USD shifts

In summary: With the big USDA event front and center, the grain market is pausing after a demand-
stabilized close to 2025, ready for data to either confirm or upend the narrative. Corn holds the steadiest
footing via exports and ethanol, soy balances crush against shipment lags, and wheat's firmness leans
more positional than fundamental. The next days will test if those underpinnings endure or shift under
fresh intel. For the moment, the complex sits poised but patient, eyeing validation of recent hints.

Ethanol for America Act

The major barrier to a higher Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) is the fuel versus food debate. Now is the
perfect time to move to E15. Corn prices are extremely low, and the latest USDA WASDE reported a record
crop and a record crop expansion.

USDA WASDE forecast corn production at 16.7 billion bushels, with the yield at 188.8 bushels per acre and
ending stocks at 2.1 billion. The season-average corn price dropped 30 cents to $3.90 a bushel. Most
importantly, 202526 crop year is expected to have 1.8 billion more bushels than 2024/25.

With current ethanol production consuming 5.6 billion bushels, a 10 percent increase in consumption would
consume an additional 560 million bushels. The reality is that year around E15 would add approximately
50 million bushels and regulatory streamlining would add another 50 million bushels. At some point over
the next ten years, the additional corn consumption could be 2.8 billion bushels minus lower fuel
consumption resulting from electric vehicles. The ethanol corn consumption increase is likely to be more
of a S curve as new compacity comes online.

With Brazil and the US corn and soybean production increasing, 100 million bushels of ethanol corn
consumption will barely move the needle. The ethanol production capacity expansion that would be three
to four years from now is when the corn consumption impact to the corn market would be felt.

Executive Summary

Corn – Supply Reset Pressures Futures, but Export
Flow Continues to Anchor the Front End
March corn settled at $4.22/bu on January 13, down nearly
25¢ on Monday, as the January USDA reports finalized a
record 2025 crop and lifted it expectation for new-crop US
ending stocks to 2.227 bbu. The scale of the production
revision (+269 mbu) forced futures sharply lower, but nearby
structure softened only modestly. The Mar/May spread held
near an eight-cent carry (about 40 percent of full carry),
signaling that commercial interest in nearby ownership
remains intact despite a looser balance sheet. Export
execution continues to validate that signal, with inspections

confirming strong early-season movement and cumulative shipments running well ahead of last year.
January data effectively removed the pre-report tightening narrative, yet steady export flow and firm
replacement values continue to limit downside follow-through.

Wheat – Global Supply Overhang Dominates, While US Movement Remains Orderly

March SRW wheat closed at $5.13/bu, down six cents w/w, with structure reflecting a storage-driven
market rather than nearby stress. The Mar/May spread held near a 10¢ carry (roughly 35 percent of full
carry), consistent with ample supply and limited urgency for immediate ownership. USDA’s January
WASDE lifted US ending stocks to 926 mbu and raised global ending stocks to 278.3 mmt, driven
primarily by larger crops in Argentina and Russia. Despite the heavier balance sheet, export execution
remains supportive at the margin, with weekly inspections at 0.32 mmt and cumulative shipments running
about eight percent ahead of last year. Wheat continues to trade the contrast between burdensome
global availability and a physical market that has not materially weakened.

Soybeans – Export Downgrades Shift the Burden to Domestic Crush as Brazil Advances

March soybeans settled at $10.43/bu on January 13, down 13¢ on the week, as January WASDE
reduced US exports to 1.575 bbu and raised ending stocks to 350 mbu. At the same time, domestic crush
was increased to 2.57 bbu, partially offsetting weaker export demand. Structure reflects that balance, with
the Mar/May spread holding near a 10¢ carry (about 45 percent of full carry), signaling adequate nearby
supply without forced liquidation. While weekly inspections showed episodic strength, cumulative
shipments remain roughly 40 percent behind last year, reinforcing that domestic crush, not exports, now
carries the balance sheet as Brazil’s record 178 mmt crop advances.

Corn Market Deep Dive

Post-WASDE Balance Sheet: The January USDA data delivered a decisive supply reset for corn,
anchored by USDA’s final production estimate for the 2025 crop confirming a record 17.021 bbu crop on
a 186.5 bpa yield across 91.3 million harvested acres. USDA’s December 1 Grain Stocks report
reinforced that outcome, with total inventories reported at 13.28 bbu, up 10 percent year over year,
pointing to larger-than-expected availability entering the first quarter. USDA’s January WASDE
predictions translated those findings directly into the 2025/26 balance sheet, lifting beginning stocks to
1.551 bbu and raising production by 269 mbu from December. On the demand side, stronger September–

November disappearance inferred from stocks prompted USDA to increase feed and residual use by 100
mbu to 6.200 bbu, while exports were left unchanged at 3.200 bbu.

Even with the feed adjustment, supply growth overwhelmed use, pushing US ending stocks up 198 mbu
to 2.227 bbu and lifting stocks-to-use to 13.6 percent. That shift effectively erased the tightening narrative
that had been building late last year, re-anchoring the balance sheet in surplus territory. The outcome is a
structure that rewards carry rather than scarcity, with downside risk now defined more by how quickly
demand can absorb the record crop than by further supply surprises. Absent a meaningful acceleration in
exports or a weather-driven shock in South America, the January data firmly re-establish corn as a
supply-led market.

Futures & Spreads: Futures adjusted quickly to the revised balance sheet, with March corn settling at
$4.22/bu on January 13, down 25¢ on the week, primarily due to the drop on Monday. Forward structure
softened in a controlled manner rather than collapsing. The Mar/May spread widened to an eight-cent
carry, roughly 40 percent of full carry, reflecting improved nearby availability without forcing full storage
economics. Structure suggests urgency to own nearby corn has eased, but the market is not discounting
supply aggressively enough to signal distress.

Funds & Positioning: Managed money positioning in corn shifted modestly following the January data
release. On a futures-only basis, funds held a small net short of roughly 13,000 CBOT contracts as of
January 6, reflecting a reduction in long exposure alongside only limited short-covering. While positioning
has improved from late December, it is not yet consistent with aggressive bearish conviction nor with
meaningful short-covering pressure. As a result, corn remains less sensitive to fund-driven volatility,
leaving spreads, basis, and export replacement values as the primary near-term drivers.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets reflected the same balance between increased supply and steady demand.
Gulf basis firmed modestly, with CIF corn trading near +84¢ over March and FOB values around +110¢,
signaling continued exporter interest despite lower futures. Interior bids were generally steady to slightly
weaker following the Grain Stocks report, consistent with a market that is better supplied but not
burdensome. Logistics remained orderly, with stable river conditions and freight holding near recent
levels, allowing basis to cushion the futures decline rather than amplify it.

Export Sales & Inspections: Export execution remains the key stabilizing factor. Corn inspections
totaled 1.49 mmt for the week ending January 8, lifting cumulative shipments to roughly 24.1 mmt,
approximately 60 percent ahead of last year’s pace. That performance supports USDA’s decision to leave
exports unchanged in January despite the supply revisions. Daily sales activity during the period,
including a 310,000 mt sale to unknown destinations and an additional 204,000 mt to South Korea,
reinforced the pattern that demand re-emerges on price breaks even as weekly sales volumes moderate
seasonally.

Global Context: On the global side, January WASDE added further supply weight, raising world corn
production to 1,296.0 mmt, up 13.1 mmt from December, with notable increases in the United States and
China. World ending stocks climbed to 290.9 mmt, reinforcing the perception of ample global availability
and limiting the scope for balance-sheet-driven rallies. With global supply comfortable, marginal price
discovery increasingly depends on execution and weather rather than structural shortages.

So What? The January data marked a definitive shift in the corn narrative from tightening risk to supply
management. Futures repriced lower, but spreads, exports, and basis behavior suggest the downside
remains disciplined rather than disorderly. Record production and higher stocks cap upside potential, yet
strong export execution and firm replacement values continue to establish a floor. Corn is now trading a

looser balance sheet, not a broken one, with physical demand still defining the guardrails for price
discovery.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

Post-WASDE Balance Sheet: January USDA data clarified the soybean balance sheet by decisively
shifting the demand burden away from exports and toward domestic processing. USDA’s final 2025 crop
production estimate confirmed US soybean output at 4.262 bbu on a 53.0 bpa yield across 80.4 million
harvested acres, USDA modestly refined its acreage estimate higher from its December estimate.
USDA’s assessment of December 1 grain stocks reinforced a looser starting point, with total stocks
reported at 3.290 bbu, above last year and slightly above trade expectations. USDA’s January WASDE
incorporated those findings while cutting its prediction of new-crop exports by 60 mbu to 1.575 bbu,
reflecting a sluggish shipment pace and intensifying South American competition, while raising its
2025/26 US crush prediction by 15 mbu to 2.570 bbu on resilient processor demand.

Despite the anticipated increase in US new-crop crush, total use declined as the export cut dominated,
lifting USDA’s estimate of new-crop US ending stocks by 60 mbu to 350 mbu and pushing stocks-to-use
up to 8.2 percent. That adjustment marked a clear loosening from December and removed much of the
residual tightening narrative that had been tied to export assumptions. The balance sheet is now firmly re-
centered on domestic demand strength rather than export recovery, leaving price direction increasingly
dependent on sustained crush performance and South American weather risk rather than a rebound in
US shipment pace.

Futures & Spreads: Futures adjusted modestly relative to corn, with March soybeans settling at
$10.43/bu on January 14, down 13¢ week over week. However, prices remain in the upper end of the
extended trading range established between $10.20 and $10.90 per bushel that the market traded within
for the majority of 2025. Structure reflected adequate nearby supply without distress, as the Mar/May
spread held near an 10¢ carry, roughly 45 percent of full carry. The curve continues to balance softer
nearby export demand against resilient domestic crush, signaling that concerns about demand
outstripping supply have eased decreasing the urgency for ownership that drove prices up to almost
$11.75 in mid-November has eased. However, the market is not pricing excess supply aggressively,
leaving prices likely rangebound until something changes in the outlook for supply. As a result, the
soybean market structure remains functional rather than punitive following the January revisions.

Products & Crush: Soybean products provided steady underlying support, with both meal and oil firming
modestly on the week. The latest available NOPA crush data (November) printed 216.0 million bushels,
exceeding last year’s pace and reinforcing the view that domestic processing demand remains resilient
despite slower export shipments. Crush margins remain positive and continue to incentivize run rates
near capacity, keeping processor bids engaged across the interior. USDA’s changes to its predictions in
the January WASDE highlight USDA’s crush projection as the most defensible demand line item, raising
the question of whether USDA offsets any export caution by leaning more heavily on domestic processing
rather than reducing total use.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets softened modestly alongside futures, particularly in export channels. CIF
NOLA soybean bids eased to roughly +95¢ over January, while FOB Gulf values slipped to near +100¢,
reflecting reduced urgency from exporters as Brazil advances toward peak availability. Interior basis was
steadier in processing regions, supported by firm crush margins and consistent plant demand. Basis
behavior continues to highlight the divergence between export weakness and domestic demand
resilience.

Funds & Positioning: In soybeans, managed money continues to hold a net long, but positioning has
moderated meaningfully. As of January 6, funds were net long approximately 66,000 CBOT futures-only
contracts, after a sizable reduction in gross length over the past week. That adjustment aligns with
weaker export signals and advancing Brazilian harvest pressure. While positioning is no longer crowded,
it remains vulnerable to additional long liquidation if demand does not improve, keeping fund flows
reactive rather than supportive.

Export Sales & Inspections: Export execution remains the weakest leg of the US soybean balance
sheet. Weekly inspections totaled 1.53 mmt for the week ending January 8, but cumulative shipments
reached only about 19.1 mmt, roughly 40 percent behind last year’s pace. The lag justified the January
export downgrade and reinforced the shift in USDA’s demand assumptions. Last Thursday, USDA
reported that weekly export sales for the period totaled 877,900 mt, while cumulative commitments
remained near 32.7 mmt, approximately 30 percent below last year. While prior Chinese purchases
continue to provide episodic support, shipment pace remains insufficient to offset the growing influence of
South American supply.

Global Context: Globally, January WASDE reinforced the supply-heavy backdrop. World soybean
production was raised to 425.7 mmt, up 3.1 mmt from December, driven primarily by Brazil, where
production was increased to a record 178.0 mmt. World ending stocks rose to 124.4 mmt, adding weight
to the forward outlook and increasing competitive pressure on US exports. As Brazil’s harvest
accelerates, global availability becomes a dominant factor in shaping nearby trade flows and limiting
upside for US prices absent a demand shock.

So What? January data repositioned soybeans as a market supported by domestic crush rather than
export strength. Higher ending stocks and slower shipment pace cap rallies, while structure and
processor demand continue to provide a floor. With Brazil’s record crop looming and global stocks rising,
soybeans remain range-bound with a defensive tone, requiring either a material shift in export flow or a
weather-driven disruption to change the sentiment of the market. Until then, price discovery is likely to
remain anchored between resilient domestic demand and expanding global supply.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Post-WASDE Balance Sheet: January USDA data delivered only marginal numerical changes to the US
wheat balance sheet, but reinforced an already heavy supply backdrop. USDA held its assessment of the
2025 US wheat crop steady at 1.985 bbu on a 53.3 bpa yield across 37.2 million harvested acres,
confirming that production was not the source of adjustment this month. Instead the changes were driven
by USDA’s quarterly Grain Stocks report. USDA’s December 1 inventory assessment pointed to weaker-
than-expected disappearance early in the marketing year, prompting its analysts to cut estimates of
2025/26 feed and residual use by 20 mbu to 100 mbu in the January WASDE. With exports and food use
left unchanged, that demand-side revision pushed US ending stocks up to 926 mbu.

The resulting stocks-to-use ratio climbed to 45.6 percent, underscoring how little balance-sheet support
prices have absent an external shock. While the domestic changes were modest, they validated the
broader narrative that supply continues to outrun demand. Globally, that tone was reinforced by higher
production in key exporters, with world output raised to 842.2 mmt and ending stocks lifted to 278.3 mmt,
led by Argentina and Russia. Taken together, January data left wheat firmly anchored in a surplus-driven
environment, where rallies remain dependent on positioning or headline risk rather than fundamentals
tightening.

Futures & Spreads: Futures reflected a steady but heavy tone. March SRW wheat settled at $5.13/bu on

January 13, down six cents week over week. Structure remained firmly in carry, with the Mar/May spread
holding close to a 10¢ carry (roughly 35 percent of full carry). The curve continues to reward storage
rather than nearby ownership, consistent with ample supply and limited urgency from end users.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets remained defensive, reflecting global competition and comfortable supply.
FOB Gulf values were largely unchanged, while interior basis across SRW and HRW regions remained
soft as mills stayed well covered. Basis levels continue to reflect limited urgency from domestic buyers
and steady competition from offshore origins, reinforcing the storage-oriented signal already embedded in
futures structure.

Export Sales & Inspections: Export execution remains constructive at the margin but insufficient to alter
the broader supply picture. Weekly wheat inspections totaled 0.32 mmt for the week ending January 8,
bringing cumulative shipments to approximately 16 mmt, about eight percent ahead of last year. Weekly
export sales for the period reached 118,700 mt, modestly improved but still below historical averages. US
wheat continues to clear into traditional destinations, yet global competition limits the ability for exports to
drive a material reassessment of demand.

Global context: Globally, January WASDE added further weight to the wheat complex. World wheat
production was raised to 842.2 mmt, up 4.4 mmt from December, driven primarily by Argentina, where
production was increased to a record 27.5 mmt, and Russia, which was raised to 89.5 mmt. World ending
stocks climbed to 278.3 mmt, underscoring the abundance of exportable supply. With major exporters
well supplied, US wheat remains price-taker rather than price-setter in global trade.

Funds & Positioning: Wheat positioning remains the most asymmetric across the grain complex.
Managed money was net short roughly 109k CBOT SRW contracts as of January 6, with the short
expanding over the past week. That level of speculative exposure leaves wheat structurally vulnerable to
short-covering rallies on headline or weather risk, even as the underlying global balance sheet remains
heavy. In the absence of a fundamental tightening catalyst, however, rallies driven by positioning alone
are likely to remain corrective rather than trend changing.

So What? Wheat remains the heaviest balance sheet in the grain complex. Modest domestic adjustments
did little to change the broader narrative, as rising global production and stocks continue to cap rallies.
Structure encourages storage, export demand is steady but unremarkable, and cash markets show little
urgency. Absent a disruption to global supply or a sharp shift in demand, wheat is likely to remain range-
bound, trading positioning and spreads rather than fundamentals.

US Cash Market & Basis

Corn: Corn basis remained firm relative to the futures selloff following the January USDA reports,
reflecting steady export replacement demand. CIF Gulf corn bids were quoted near +84¢ over March,
with FOB Gulf values around +110¢ over March as of January 14, signaling continued interest from
exporters despite looser balance sheets. Interior bids were generally steady to slightly weaker after the
December 1 Grain Stocks report, consistent with improved availability but not a burdensome supply
environment. Logistics remained orderly, allowing basis to absorb futures weakness rather than amplify it.
The cash market continues to suggest that nearby demand remains engaged even as the board adjusts
to higher production and stocks.

Soybeans: Soybean basis softened modestly in export channels while remaining supported in
processing regions. CIF NOLA soybean bids eased to roughly +95¢ over January, with FOB Gulf values
near +100¢, reflecting reduced urgency from exporters as Brazilian harvest approaches. Interior basis
was steadier where processor demand remains firm, supported by resilient crush margins despite weaker

export flow. The divergence between export softness and domestic demand continues to define the cash
market, with crushers providing a floor while global supply pressure caps Gulf premiums.

Wheat: Wheat basis remained largely unchanged and directionless, consistent with a carry-driven
market. FOB Gulf wheat values were broadly steady, reflecting ample global competition and limited
urgency from buyers. Interior basis across SRW and HRW regions stayed soft as mills remained well
covered, while export channels continued to face pressure from lower-priced Black Sea and Argentine
supplies. Overall, the US wheat cash market continues to reflect comfortable supply conditions, with basis
lacking the momentum to challenge the storage-oriented signal embedded in futures structure.

So What? Cash markets continue to do the work of absorbing the post-WASDE adjustment, but the tone
has shifted from resilience to selectivity. Corn basis remains the strongest signal, with export replacement
values still providing support even as futures reset lower on higher stocks. In soybeans, the split between
softer export channels and firm processor demand is becoming more pronounced, reinforcing crush, not
exports, as the primary near-term anchor. Wheat remains the weakest leg, with basis offering little
resistance in the face of ample global supply and storage-driven structure. With logistics running smoothly
and no immediate weather or demand shock, nearby cash strength is now more a function of end-user
coverage than scarcity, suggesting basis can hold, but may struggle to strengthen further without a new
demand catalyst.

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Brazil remains the dominant supplier in global grain trade as harvest advances. ANEC estimates
January soybean exports near 3.7 mmt, while corn shipments are projected around 3.27 mmt, reflecting
continued strength from the prior safrinha cycle. FOB Santos soybean values were quoted near $420/mt,
while corn FOB traded around $220/mt, preserving Brazil’s pricing advantage into Asia and the Middle
East. Harvest progress reached roughly 8 percent in Mato Grosso, with logistics reported as fluid and no
major congestion at key ports. Adequate rainfall across core producing areas continues to reinforce
expectations for Brazil’s record 178 mmt soybean crop, keeping Brazil firmly positioned as the preferred
origin early in the year

Argentina: Argentina’s export flows remain active but increasingly weather-sensitive. Up-River corn
values were quoted near $218/mt, while soymeal offers traded around $345/mt, supporting Argentina’s
role as a key supplier of feed ingredients. Wheat production is locked at a record 27.5 mmt, with exports
flowing steadily following harvest completion. Dryness in southern production areas remains a point of
monitoring for corn and soybeans, but export channels continue to function normally, aided by a weaker
peso and competitive FOB pricing relative to US origin.

China: Chinese buying behavior remains tactical rather than structural. Cumulative US soybean
purchases tied to China are estimated near 10 mmt, largely interpreted as state-directed procurement
rather than broad commercial restocking. Domestic futures reflected stable demand, with Dalian corn
trading near ¥2,395/mt, but no sustained arbitrage window has opened to materially accelerate US grain
imports. On corn and wheat, Chinese participation remains limited despite elevated domestic prices,
keeping US export opportunities episodic rather than persistent.

EU / Black Sea: Black Sea origins continue to set the global price ceiling. Russian wheat FOB values
were reported near $230–235/mt, maintaining a competitive edge in key import markets. Ukrainian corn
offers near $173–175/mt continue to pressure EU feed markets, while French wheat remains less
competitive in export tenders. With export corridors functioning and supplies ample, Black Sea flows
remain a central constraint on US and EU export competitiveness.

Other Regions: Other exporters remain steady contributors to global supply. Australia’s wheat crop,
while below recent peaks, continues to move into Asian markets, and Canada’s spring wheat exports
proceed on a routine basis. No material policy shifts or logistical disruptions were reported across
secondary origins during the period, leaving the global trade environment well supplied and competitive.

So What? Global trade flows remain well supplied and highly competitive, with Brazil and the Black Sea
continuing to dictate price ceilings rather than react to US values. Brazil’s early-year dominance is firmly
established as harvest advances without logistical friction, limiting near-term reallocation toward US origin
despite episodic Chinese interest. Argentina adds a layer of weather-related uncertainty, but for now
remains a reliable supplier across corn, wheat, and feed products, with exports flowing normally. China’s
engagement remains tactical rather than transformational, offering intermittent support without altering the
broader trade balance. In this environment, US export competitiveness is unlikely to improve materially
without a change in FOB differentials or a demand shock, reinforcing that domestic pull and basis, not
global arbitrage, will continue to set the tone for nearby pricing.

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Jan 8 – Jan 13)

USDA Crop Production – Final 2025 (released Jan 12): USDA finalized the 2025 US corn crop at
17.021 bbu, driven by a 186.5 bpa national yield across 91.3 million harvested acres, confirming a record
outcome and exceeding late-year expectations. Soybean production was finalized at 4.262 bbu on a 53.0
bpa yield and 80.4 million harvested acres, while US wheat production held steady at 1.985 bbu with a
53.3 bpa yield on 37.2 million harvested acres. The final data removed residual uncertainty around yield
and acreage and set a firmer baseline for January balance-sheet revisions across the complex.

USDA Grain Stocks – December 1, 2025 (released Jan 12): December 1 stocks confirmed ample on-
hand supplies entering the first quarter. US corn stocks were reported at 13.28 bbu, up 10 percent year
over year, implying stronger early-season disappearance but also larger available supply. Soybean
stocks totaled 3.29 bbu, up six percent y/y, while wheat stocks reached 1.675 bbu, up 7 percent y/y. The
stocks data played a key role in shaping January WASDE feed/residual and use assumptions, particularly
for corn and wheat.

USDA WASDE – January 2026: January WASDE absorbed the final production and stocks data,
delivering a clear supply-side reset. For corn, beginning stocks were raised to 1.551 bbu, production
increased by 268 mbu to 17.021 bbu, feed and residual use was lifted to 6.200 bbu, and ending stocks
rose to 2.227 bbu, pushing stocks-to-use to 13.6 percent. Soybeans saw exports cut to 1.575 bbu, crush
raised to 2.570 bbu, and ending stocks lifted to 350 mbu (stocks-to-use 8.2 percent). Wheat adjustments
were more modest, with feed and residual lowered to 100 mbu and US ending stocks increased to 926
mbu, keeping stocks-to-use elevated at 45.6 percent. Globally, WASDE raised world ending stocks
across all three commodities, reinforcing a looser supply backdrop.

Export Inspections (USDA FGIS – week ending Jan 8): Export inspections provided a counterweight to
the heavier balance sheets. Corn inspections totaled 1.49 mmt, lifting cumulative shipments to roughly
950 mbu, approximately 60 percent ahead of last year. Soybean inspections reached 1.53 mmt, but
cumulative loadings remain near 19.1 mmt, roughly 40 percent behind last year, reinforcing USDA’s
export downgrade. Wheat inspections totaled 0.32 mmt, bringing season-to-date shipments to
approximately 16 mmt, about 8 percent ahead of last year, keeping the 900 mbu export forecast
defensible for now.

Export Sales & Daily Announcements (USDA FAS – latest through week ending Jan 1): Weekly export
sales reflected a mixed demand picture. Corn net sales totaled 377,600 mt, a slower pace but consistent
with strong execution. Soybean net sales reached 877,900 mt, while wheat sales totaled 118,700 mt.

Daily sales announcements during the period included 310,000 mt of corn to unknown destinations and
204,000 mt to South Korea, underscoring that demand continues to surface on price breaks even as
weekly totals moderate.

Ethanol Production & Stocks (EIA – latest available): US ethanol production remained supportive
through early January, with output averaging 1.098 mbpd in the week ending January 2, alongside stocks
of 23.652 million barrels, implying weekly corn use near 98 mbu during the holiday period. More recent
data for the week ending January 9 showed production rebounding to 1.196 mbpd, with stocks rising to
24.473 million barrels, signaling a return toward normal run rates following seasonal slowdown. While
ethanol use is not explicitly separated in WASDE, the sustained grind profile is consistent with the
January report’s upward revision to feed and residual use, reinforcing ethanol’s role as a stabilizing
demand component even as overall corn supply expanded.

CFTC Positioning (latest available – week ending January 6): Managed money positioning remains
mixed across the grain complex following the January data release. In corn, funds are modestly net short
at roughly –13k futures-only contracts (225k long vs 238k short), leaving positioning light and not a clear
driver unless cash signals force covering. In soybeans, managed money remains net long near +66k
contracts (123k long vs 58k short), but the long is no longer crowded, keeping the market balanced
between incremental buying and renewed liquidation risk. Wheat remains the most asymmetric market,
with managed money heavily net short near –109k SRW contracts (90k long vs 200k short), leaving the
board vulnerable to short-covering rallies on headline risk even as the global balance sheet stays heavy.

So What? With January’s USDA data now fully absorbed, markets are shifting back toward real-time
commercial signals. Corn demand continues to stand out, with inspections and ethanol grind validating
board levels despite a clearly looser balance sheet. Soybeans remain supported by record domestic
crush but constrained by export underperformance as Brazil moves into peak availability. Wheat’s
shipment pace remains quietly constructive, but global supply continues to cap rallies. Until new
information emerges, either through South American weather confirmation or a change in demand
behavior, basis, inspections, and spreads remain the most reliable guideposts for price discovery.

International Reports

Brazil: Brazil continues to set the tone for global grain trade early in the year. ANEC estimates January
soybean exports near 3.7 mmt, with corn shipments projected around 3.27 mmt, reflecting strong
carryover from the prior safrinha cycle. FOB soybean values near $420/mt and corn FOB near $220/mt
keep Brazil competitively positioned into Asia and the Middle East. Harvest progress and logistics remain
orderly, reinforcing Brazil’s role as the primary price-setter for nearby export flows.

Argentina: Argentina remains active in export channels, particularly on the feed side. Up-River corn
values near $218/mt and soymeal offers around $345/mt continue to support Argentina’s presence in
global feed markets. Wheat exports are flowing following confirmation of a record 27.5 mmt crop. While
dryness in southern regions is being monitored for corn and soybeans, trade flows have not yet been
disrupted, and Argentina remains a reliable supplier into early 2026.

China: Chinese participation remains selective. Confirmed US soybean purchases near 10 mmt are still
interpreted as largely state-directed rather than broad commercial restocking. Domestic pricing remains
elevated, with Dalian corn near ¥2,395/mt, but no sustained arbitrage has opened to materially accelerate
US corn or wheat imports. Buying behavior continues to be tactical, limiting China’s role as a consistent
demand catalyst.

EU / Black Sea: Black Sea origins continue to anchor global wheat pricing. Russian wheat FOB values

near $230–235/mt preserve a clear cost advantage in key import markets, while Ukrainian corn offers
near $173–175/mt pressure EU feed grain demand. With export corridors functioning and supply ample,
Black Sea flows remain the primary constraint on higher global prices and on US export competitiveness.

Global: Across other origins, supply conditions remain comfortable. Australia continues to ship wheat into
Asia without logistical friction, and Canada’s spring wheat exports proceed routinely. No material policy
shifts or trade disruptions were reported during the week, leaving the international trade environment well
supplied and highly competitive.

So What? Global trade dynamics remain supply-led. Brazil continues to dominate nearby oilseed and
corn flows, the Black Sea sets the ceiling for wheat prices, and Argentina fills feed demand where
competitive. China’s engagement remains episodic rather than structural. In this environment, US exports
must compete on execution and pricing rather than scarcity, keeping international trade flows neutral to
heavy following January’s supply reset.

Weather & Crop Conditions

United States
Weather remains a secondary input for US grains at this stage. Conditions across the Plains and Midwest
stayed warm and generally dry, keeping winterkill risk low and allowing logistics to operate without
interruption. With harvest complete and no active fieldwork underway, weather has not introduced new
supply or demand signals. River systems remained stable, and there were no weather-related constraints
on grain movement during the period. For the US, weather currently functions as a neutral backdrop
rather than a market driver.

Brazil
Brazilian weather continues to reinforce confidence in large production rather than introduce risk. Core
soybean areas across the Center-West maintained favorable moisture, supporting steady crop
development as harvest begins, with Mato Grosso progress estimated near 8 percent. Observed rainfall
totals in the 40–70 mm range across key producing regions helped stabilize crop conditions and logistics.
With no material disruptions reported and USDA maintaining a 178 mmt soybean estimate, weather in
Brazil remains supportive but no longer incremental to price discovery.

Argentina
Argentina remains the only region where weather carries optionality. Dryness intensified across southern
production areas, particularly in Buenos Aires and La Pampa, as soybeans approach sensitive
reproductive stages. While scattered rainfall of 15–30 mm has been noted in parts of the region, moisture
deficits persist and warrant monitoring. Wheat outcomes are already locked, but corn and soybeans
remain exposed if dryness extends. With soybeans entering pod-setting and early corn moving into
pollination windows, the next 10–15 days carry disproportionate yield sensitivity if dryness persists. At this
stage, weather introduces risk asymmetry rather than confirmed supply loss.

Global
Outside South America, global crop conditions remain broadly stable. Northern Hemisphere winter wheat
entered dormancy without widespread stress, and no major weather disruptions were reported across
secondary exporting regions. Australia’s wheat harvest concluded without logistical issues, and no new
weather-related threats emerged during the week.

So What?
Weather is no longer a uniform driver across markets. Brazil reinforces supply confidence, the US
remains neutral, and Argentina is the sole source of potential weather-related volatility. For now, weather

functions as a conditional risk rather than a catalyst, with only sustained Argentine dryness capable of
challenging the supply-heavy narrative established by January USDA data.

Synthesis & Outlook

January’s USDA data bundle decisively shifted the grain market narrative from late-2025 tightening
concerns to a supply-managed environment. Final crop production and December 1 stocks confirmed that
US corn and soybean availability is larger than previously assumed, while global balance sheets were
also revised higher. Futures adjusted lower to reflect that reality, but the reaction has been measured
rather than disorderly. Structure, basis, and export execution continue to signal that commercial demand
remains present, even as balance sheets loosen.

Corn sits at the center of that tension. Record production and a 2.227 bbu carryout cap upside, yet strong
inspections, steady ethanol grind, and firm Gulf replacement values continue to define a floor. The market
has repriced supply but has not lost its physical anchor. As long as export flow remains consistent,
downside extensions are likely to be incremental rather than impulsive.

Soybeans remain more internally divided. January WASDE shifted the burden of demand squarely toward
domestic crush, which continues to perform at historically strong levels, while export execution lags amid
Brazil’s advancing harvest. That split keeps soybeans range-bound: supported by processors,
constrained by global availability. Without a clear acceleration in exports or a material South American
disruption, price discovery is likely to remain defensive but orderly.

Wheat remains the heaviest balance sheet in the complex. Global production increases and rising stocks
continue to cap rallies, even as US shipment pace has quietly improved. Structure remains firmly in carry,
reinforcing storage rather than scarcity. Any near-term strength is likely to be positioning-driven rather
than fundamentally led, unless global supply assumptions are challenged.

Bullish triggers: Upside risk would require a meaningful shift in either demand execution or South
American supply. For corn, continued inspections at or above recent pace, combined with sustained
ethanol grind, would tighten the effective nearby balance despite a larger carryout. In soybeans, any
disruption to Argentina’s crop or a more persistent return of Chinese buying beyond tactical state
purchases would materially change the demand calculus. Wheat upside remains the most conditional,
relying on export flow surprises or supply friction in key exporting regions rather than US fundamentals
alone.

Bearish triggers: Further downside would likely emerge if global supply confidence increases rather than
erodes. For corn, a deceleration in export flow following the January repricing would expose the market to
wider carries and deeper storage economics. Soybeans remain vulnerable to Brazil’s harvest pressure if
logistics continue smoothly and export pace fails to improve. Wheat remains exposed to aggressive Black
Sea competition, with global stocks limiting the market’s ability to absorb additional supply without price
concession

In summary: With January’s supply reset now largely priced in, grain markets are transitioning back to a
phase where physical signals matter more than balance-sheet revisions. Basis behavior, spread
structure, and export execution will determine whether prices stabilize or drift. Risk remains two-sided, but
asymmetric: upside requires disruption, while downside depends on demand follow-through. Until one of
those conditions materializes, markets are likely to remain range-bound, disciplined, and driven by
commercial rather than speculative conviction.

Ethanol for America Act

Corn – Funds Press Shorts, but Cash and Logistics
Keep the Front End Anchored
March corn finished near $4.25/bu, little changed on
balance, as funds built their largest net short since October
(–90,658 contracts) following USDA’s upward revision to
production and carryout. The Mar/May spread widened
modestly to 7¢, still short of full carry and consistent with a
front end that remains supported by real-world movement
rather than pure storage economics. Export inspections
totaled 1.48 MMT for the week ending January 15, slightly
below the prior week’s level but still reinforcing strong
execution. Cumulative shipments now stand at 29.92 MMT,
keeping pace 55–60 percent ahead of last year, consistent with USDA’s 3.2 bbu forecast. CIF Gulf basis
softened to +88H, still within a firm +85–90H range, while interior river and rail basis held mostly steady.
Freight premiums rose amid colder weather, and barge movement slowed further as ice developed
across the Upper Mississippi. Despite a looser balance sheet, steady exports and replacement costs
continued to prevent wider carries from emerging.

Wheat – SRW Stays Rangebound as Russian Flow Cements Ceiling

March SRW wheat settled near $5.10/bu, down about 7¢ from the prior week, with the Mar/May spread
steady at an 11¢ carry, reflecting ample stocks and a storage-led structure. USDA data confirmed global
and US ending stocks were higher year-over-year, with Russian FOB 12.5 percent wheat holding at
$225–227/MT and January exports expected near 3.4 MMT. US wheat inspections totaled 0.39 MMT, up
modestly on the week and keeping cumulative shipments at 15.58 MMT, or 19 percent ahead of last
year, in line with USDA’s 900 mbu export projection. Speculative short positioning remained extreme,
with managed money holding a –108,247 contract net short. Broadly, the market remains capped by
global supply and Black Sea competitiveness, but cash flow and short saturation continue to support
structure.

Soybeans – Demand Splits Sharply as Export Book Cedes to Domestic Crush

March soybeans ended the week near $10.63/bu, firmer on balance, but demand remains bifurcated, with
export share continuing to cede to Brazil while domestic crush does the heavy lifting. The Mar/May
spread traded near 11¢, slightly wider but still reflecting a relatively supported front end given firm
processor pull. Weekly inspections totaled 1.34 MMT, down from the prior week’s 1.59 MMT, with
cumulative shipments at 17.93 MMT, or roughly 42 percent behind last year’s pace. While China
remained the top destination, the lag versus last year continues to underscore Brazil’s competitive edge.

In contrast, NOPA crush for December reached 225 mbu (second highest on record), and processors
held bids steady to firmer, particularly in the Eastern Corn Belt and Northern Plains. China booked at

Macro / Policy – Ethanol Print Hits Record; Argentina Cuts Export Taxes

The US dollar index ended the week near 98.62, slightly lower than reported earlier, while the Brazilian
real weakened modestly to R$5.37/USD, modestly supporting Brazilian exports. US ethanol output
surged to a record 1.196 million bbl/day in early January, boosting corn grind even as stocks rose to
24.47 million bbl. In Argentina, the Milei administration formalized export tax cuts, 24 percent on
soybeans, 8.5 percent on corn, and 7.5 percent on wheat, in a bid to accelerate farmer sales and FX
inflow. No new US biofuel or grain trade policies were reported during the week.

Weather – US Cold Snap Slows Logistics; Argentina Drier, Brazil Mixed

NOAA’s 6–10 day outlook showed below-normal temperatures across the Midwest, above-normal across
the Southern Plains, and dry conditions across the Delta and Pacific Northwest. River traffic slowed
further on ice buildup along the Illinois and Upper Mississippi, though no full closures were reported. In
Brazil, central and northern zones received 100–200 percent of normal rainfall, stabilizing soil moisture
and supporting early harvest (1 percent complete). In contrast, southern Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul,
Paraná) remained drier, raising localized stress concerns. In Argentina, subpar rainfall persisted across
Córdoba and Buenos Aires, placing early corn under yield pressure. While Santa Fe saw isolated relief,
the moisture gap remains wide and the window for crop recovery is narrowing.

What’s Next (Jan 22 – Jan 29):

Export Sales (Jan 25): Will corn momentum to Mexico/Japan hold? Is there follow-through from China in
soybeans?

Fund Flows: Watch if soybean length rebuilds after last week’s 46k contract liquidation.

Brazil Harvest: Track pace and potential pressure on FOBs and front-end spreads.

Argentina Weather: Dry bias into late January could escalate stress on corn and soy during key
reproductive stages.

River Logistics: Ice and low water conditions expected to constrain barge movement into early
February.
