Corn Market Deep Dive
Futures & Spreads: Corn drifted modestly lower through the holiday-shortened week, with March futures
settling near $4.27, down roughly five cents from the prior close. The March–May spread widened slightly
to around a 9.25-cent carry, representing roughly 61 percent of full carry under the Mar–May framework.
While the curve remains in carry, it is not pressing toward maximum storage economics. The structure
continues to reflect adequate supply but steady nearby demand, with no evidence of stress in either
direction. Volatility remained muted and price action contained, reinforcing a market that is consolidating
rather than trending.

Funds & Positioning: Managed Money maintained a net short near 57,493 contracts as of the February
10 CFTC report. The position remains meaningful but far from historical extremes and, importantly, is no
longer expanding. Gross shorts have stabilized while longs have edged modestly higher, suggesting a
defensive posture rather than an aggressive bearish build. With futures failing to break meaningfully lower
and spreads holding their ground, speculative pressure appears controlled. Absent a macro catalyst or
deterioration in export pace, funds appear comfortable maintaining exposure without increasing
conviction.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets held relatively steady. CIF Gulf values remained firm in the $5.26–$5.29
range, while interior river bids showed modest regional variation but no broad softening. Freight
conditions have improved from peak winter disruption, though draft limitations continue to influence barge
efficiency. Basis strength is not accelerating, but neither is it eroding. The nearby physical market remains
stable, signaling continued execution rather than liquidation.

Export Sales & Inspections: Export inspections for the week ending February 12 totaled approximately
1.49 million metric tons, maintaining a shipment pace ahead of last year and broadly consistent with
USDA expectations. Weekly export sales for the week ending February 5 totaled 2,105,500 metric tons,
reinforcing that forward commitments remain active. Cumulative shipments now account for roughly 60
percent of the USDA export forecast, indicating that the program remains on pace despite softer flat price
action. The export channel continues to provide structural support even as futures consolidate.

Global Context: Brazil’s export program remains active, though forward pressure has moderated relative
to peak harvest expectations. Argentine corn production remains stable on official estimates, with no new
material downgrade during the week. Russian and Ukrainian corn offers remain present but not
aggressively undercutting U.S. Gulf values into core destinations. U.S. origin retains a competitive
position into Mexico and select Latin American markets, though Brazil continues to anchor broader global
pricing expectations.

So What? Corn remains structurally stable. The board has softened, but spreads are holding near 60
percent of full carry, basis is steady, and export execution remains intact. Funds are short but not
pressing. Without a supply shock or demand deterioration, the market continues to oscillate within a
range defined more by carry economics than directional conviction. For now, structure remains firmer
than flat price suggests.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: Soybeans softened modestly through the week, with March futures settling near
$11.33, drifting lower in holiday-thinned trade. The March–May spread held near a 16 cent carry,
maintaining a clear contango structure that continues to reflect adequate nearby supply. On a full-carry
framework, the spread sits near 72 percent of full carry, signaling neither tightening stress nor
burdensome pressure. The curve remains stable, and price action suggests consolidation rather than
directional conviction. While flat price lacks urgency, the structure has not weakened materially.

Products & Crush: Crush fundamentals remain the anchor. January NOPA crush totaled 221.6 million
bushels, a record for the month and confirmation that domestic demand remains historically strong.
Soybean oil stocks rose to approximately 1.9 billion pounds, up sharply year over year, tempering
enthusiasm on the product side. The crush margin remains meal-driven, with soybean meal demand
providing the primary support for processing economics. USDA’s emphasis on domestic use as the key
demand pillar continues to be validated by execution data.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets held steady despite softer board tone. CIF Gulf values remained near
$12.36–$12.37, reflecting continued export coverage even as Brazil’s harvest advances. Interior
processor bids remained firm across the Midwest, with limited evidence of aggressive farmer selling.
Basis is not accelerating higher, but it is not retreating either. The nearby market remains supported by
crush pull rather than export urgency, reinforcing the divergence between domestic strength and global
supply weight.

Funds & Positioning: Managed Money maintained a sizable net long near 115,896 contracts as of the

February 10 report, elevated relative to recent historical averages. While not at record extremes, the
positioning profile leaves the market more vulnerable to long liquidation than short covering. Gross long
exposure remains substantial, and absent a fresh bullish catalyst, speculative conviction appears tactical
rather than structural. The positioning tilt is constructive, but extended.

Export Sales & Inspections: Weekly export inspections for the period ending February 12 totaled
1,202,617 metric tons. Cumulative inspections for the 2025/26 marketing year now stand at 24,348,735
metric tons, compared with 36,019,599 metric tons at the same time last year — a decline of roughly 32
percent year over year. While weekly flow remains functional, the broader export program continues to
lag materially behind last season due to Brazil’s dominant early-season presence.

Global Context: Brazil’s 2025/26 soybean production estimate remains near 178 million metric tons,
reinforcing expectations for a large exportable surplus. Harvest progress continues without major
disruption in central regions, and FOB offers remain competitive into Asia. Argentina’s production outlook
remains near 48.5 million metric tons, with localized stress but no material downgrade during the
reporting window. Brazil continues to set the global pricing ceiling, limiting U.S. upside absent a supply
disruption or shift in trade flow timing.

So What? Soybeans remain domestically supported but externally weak. Record crush continues to
anchor the nearby structure, yet cumulative export inspections are running roughly 32 percent behind last
year, underscoring Brazil’s dominance in early-season trade flows. The curve reflects comfortable supply,
and funds remain meaningfully long. Absent a shift in export momentum or a South American production
disruption, upside remains capped while domestic demand prevents structural deterioration.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: Wheat futures firmed through the holiday-shortened week, with March Chicago
SRW settling near $5.47, down roughly fifteen cents on the period. The March–May spread held near a
4.75-cent carry, maintaining a storage-led structure but without tightening. The curve remains comfortably
in contango, reflecting adequate supply and limited urgency from commercial buyers. Price action was
largely technical, with no fresh fundamental catalyst emerging. Kansas City and Minneapolis contracts
followed a similar tone, offering little structural divergence within the complex.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets remained broadly stable. CIF Gulf SRW values held near $6.23–$6.28 per
bushel, while interior basis levels showed regional variation but no meaningful tightening. Plains HRW
basis remained steady despite localized dryness concerns, and Pacific Northwest values were largely
unchanged. The absence of basis acceleration reinforces the view that end users remain covered. The
physical market continues to signal sufficiency rather than scarcity.

Export Sales & Inspections: Weekly export inspections for the period ending February 12 totaled
approximately 0.38 million metric tons, a moderate weekly pace. Export sales for the week ending
February 5 reached roughly 488,000 metric tons, consistent with routine demand but not indicative of
acceleration. Cumulative shipments remain aligned with USDA projections and modestly ahead of last
year’s pace, yet volumes remain insufficient to materially tighten the balance sheet. The export program
is functioning, but it lacks momentum capable of shifting broader sentiment.

Global Context: Global supply remains the defining feature. Russian wheat continues to anchor world
pricing, with export offers remaining competitive into North Africa and the Middle East. Ukrainian
shipments remain active through established corridors, and European origin has re-entered select

tenders where freight allows. Argentine supply remains available, adding incremental pressure. With no
logistical disruption or policy constraint emerging across major exporters, global availability continues to
cap rallies and limit speculative rebalancing.

Funds & Positioning: Managed Money maintains a substantial net short near 85,832 contracts as of
the February 10 CFTC report. While positioning is not expanding aggressively, it remains historically
large. Short covering has been limited, suggesting that funds remain comfortable leaning defensively in
the absence of a catalyst. The short profile provides latent upside risk, but without a supply disruption or
export acceleration, that positioning alone has not been sufficient to trigger sustained covering.

So What? February reaffirmed wheat as the loosest balance sheet within the grain complex. Domestic
stocks remain elevated, global inventories are comfortable, and structure continues to reward storage
over urgency. Export demand is steady but insufficient to tighten conditions, and cash markets show little
stress. Without disruption in a major exporting region or a material shift in global demand, wheat is likely
to remain rangebound, driven more by positioning and spread behavior than by fundamental tightening.

US Cash Market & Basis

Corn: Corn basis held steady across primary corridors despite softer futures. CIF Gulf values remained
near $5.26–$5.29 per bushel, reflecting continued export coverage. Interior river bids showed modest
regional variation but no broad deterioration. Freight conditions have improved from peak winter
disruption, though draft limitations still affect barge efficiency. Ethanol plant bids across the Midwest
remained firm, signaling consistent grind demand and limited farmer selling. The physical market remains
balanced, with no evidence of forced movement.

Soybeans: Soybean basis continues to reflect strong domestic crush pull. CIF Gulf values held near
$12.36–$12.37, indicating steady export coverage even as Brazil’s harvest advances. Interior processor
bids across key Midwest regions remained competitive, reinforcing spot demand. River logistics have
normalized relative to prior constraints, reducing transportation friction without materially loosening basis.
While the board softened, cash markets continue to reflect structural domestic demand.

Wheat: Wheat cash markets were largely unchanged. CIF Gulf SRW values remained near $6.23–$6.28
per bushel, while HRW basis across the Plains showed limited movement. Pacific Northwest bids were
steady, and interior markets lacked directional energy. With no export acceleration or logistical disruption,
basis remains stable but unresponsive. U.S. wheat continues to face competitive global pressure, limiting
tightening in nearby structure.

So What? Physical markets remain steadier than futures suggest. Corn basis reflects export execution
and ethanol demand, soybeans remain anchored by crush, and wheat signals sufficiency rather than
scarcity. Logistics have improved but have not altered structure. Absent a material shift in demand or
supply, cash markets are likely to remain balanced as futures consolidate.

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Brazil continues to anchor global trade flows through strong execution and competitive pricing.
ANEC projects robust soybean shipments through early 2026 as harvest advances. FOB offers out of
Santos and Paranaguá remain competitive into Asia, sustaining export momentum. Corn exports remain
supported by late-season availability and active vessel lineups across major ports. Brazil’s export
program remains the dominant structural force in global oilseed and coarse grain flow.

Argentina: Argentina remains the primary supply-side uncertainty. Soybean and late-planted corn

conditions show vulnerability amid uneven rainfall and soil moisture deficits, heightening sensitivity to
February precipitation during reproductive stages. FOB offers have adjusted modestly and remain
competitive where available. Export flow continues but lacks the scale to challenge Brazil’s dominance
absent a weather-driven disruption.

China: China’s import posture remains selective. Routine U.S. soybean cargoes have moved, but no
large new purchase announcements emerged during the window. Brazilian origin continues to be favored
due to pricing advantages and abundant supply. Domestic corn price support tempers incremental import
demand, while downstream feed margins remain pressured. China remains tactical rather than
expansionary.

EU / Black Sea: Black Sea origin continues to set the tone for wheat pricing. Russian 12.5 percent
protein wheat remains competitively offered on FOB terms, pressuring U.S. origin into price-sensitive
tenders. Ukrainian corn remains available through established corridors, while EU wheat export pace
trails last year. Lower-cost Black Sea supply remains the primary outlet for global wheat trade.

Other Regions: Australia continues to move wheat into Asian markets following a solid harvest, while
Canadian spring wheat exports proceed in line with seasonal norms. No material trade restrictions, quota
shifts, or policy disruptions have emerged across secondary exporters. The broader international
environment remains stable and well supplied.

So What? Global trade flows continue to reflect price leadership rather than disruption. Brazil dominates
soybeans and remains competitive in corn, Russia and Ukraine anchor wheat supply, and Argentina’s
role remains weather-dependent. China’s demand remains opportunistic. U.S. competitiveness is timing-
driven rather than structural, and absent supply shocks or narrowing FOB spreads, global flows are likely
to remain competitive rather than restrictive.

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Feb 12 – Feb 18)

Export Inspections (USDA FGIS – week ending Feb 12): Corn export inspections totaled 1,492,383
metric tons, bringing cumulative 2025/26 shipments to 35,726,976 metric tons, compared with 24,749,316
metric tons at the same point last year, an increase of approximately 44 percent year over year, keeping
the program ahead of the pace required to meet USDA’s projection. Soybean inspections reached
1,202,617 metric tons, with cumulative shipments at 24,348,735 metric tons versus 36,019,599 metric
tons last year, a decline of roughly 32 percent year over year, reflecting Brazil’s dominant early-season
export window. Wheat inspections totaled approximately 381,000 metric tons, with marketing-year
shipments modestly ahead of last season and broadly aligned with USDA expectations, though not at a
pace sufficient to materially tighten the balance sheet.

Export Sales (USDA FAS – latest through week ending Feb 5): Weekly export sales for the week
ending February 5 reflected continued forward activity. Corn net sales totaled 2,105,500 metric tons,
marking a strong weekly commitment. Soybean net sales totaled 377,600 metric tons, while wheat net
sales reached 498,000 metric tons. While soybean bookings remain moderate relative to prior seasonal
peaks, corn commitments continue to run firmly. No major daily flash sales were reported during the
window. Due to the Washington’s Birthday Federal holiday, the next U.S. Export Sales report will be
released Friday, February 20, 2026.

Ethanol Production & Stocks: Ethanol production for the week ending Feb 13 averaged 1.08 million
barrels per day (down from 1.11), while stocks remained high at 25.25 million barrels. This indicates a

slight seasonal dip in production while inventories continue to build, keeping a lid on immediate corn
demand upside.

NOPA Soybean Crush: January NOPA crush totaled 221.56 million bushels, a record for the month and
confirmation of historically strong domestic processing demand. Soybean oil stocks increased to
approximately 1.90 billion pounds, reflecting ample product availability even as crush margins remain
meal driven. The data reinforces domestic demand as the primary support within the soybean balance
sheet.

CFTC Positioning: As of February 10 (released February 13), Managed Money held a net short of
57,493 contracts in corn, reflecting stabilization rather than renewed bearish expansion. In soybeans,
funds maintained a sizable net long of 115,896 contracts, elevated relative to recent averages. Chicago
SRW wheat held a net short of 85,832 contracts, remaining the most structurally bearish position across
the grain complex. Positioning remains influential but is no longer accelerating in any single direction.

So What? Core U.S. fundamentals remain stable. Corn exports and ethanol grind continue to validate
steady demand. Soybeans are anchored by record crush despite competitive global supply. Wheat
execution remains routine but overshadowed by ample global availability. Speculative positioning remains
meaningful but is no longer expanding aggressively. Beneath the board’s consolidation, physical
execution remains intact as mid-February progresses.

International Reports

Brazil: Brazil remains the central driver of global oilseed and corn supply. CONAB maintains 2025/26
soybean production at 177.98 million metric tons, reinforcing expectations for a large exportable surplus.
Corn production under CONAB’s February update is estimated at 138.45 million metric tons, reflecting a
larger total supply outlook than earlier projections. The first crop remains steady, while the safrinha crop
accounts for the majority of the expected volume. This larger production profile reinforces expectations for
a significant second-half export presence and continued pressure on global FOB pricing once harvest
advances.

Argentina: Argentina’s production outlook remains stable on official estimates, with soybeans near 48.5
million metric tons and corn near 57 million metric tons. Weather variability persists, but no fresh
downward revisions emerged during the reporting window. Farmer selling remains measured, influenced
by currency dynamics and macro uncertainty, limiting aggressive forward flow. FOB values have adjusted
modestly but not sharply, indicating that export channels remain functional despite agronomic variability.
The market continues to monitor late-season rainfall, but risk has not yet translated into structural volume
constraints.

China: Chinese demand signals remained measured. No major new U.S. purchase announcements were
reported during the period, though routine soybean inflows continued. Domestic futures markets showed
modest firmness, suggesting stable crush economics, but downstream feed demand remains constrained
by livestock margin pressure. State support for domestic corn pricing continues to temper incremental
import demand. China remains active but tactical, providing support on breaks rather than driving
sustained upside.

EU / Black Sea: Black Sea origin continues to set the tone for global wheat pricing. Russian 12.5 percent
protein wheat remains competitively offered near $229 per metric ton FOB, reinforcing its role as the
global price leader. Ukrainian corn remains available through established export corridors, with offers
near $235 per metric ton FOB into select destinations. European Union wheat values remain elevated
relative to price-sensitive tenders, and EU export pace remains behind last year’s levels. With no new

policy or freight disruptions emerging, global wheat trade remains anchored by low-cost Black Sea
supply, limiting upside potential for alternative origins.

So What? International markets remain defined by availability rather than disruption. Brazil continues to
export aggressively, Argentina’s risk profile is monitored but not escalating, and Russia maintains pricing
leadership in wheat. China’s participation remains selective. Global supply remains ample on paper, and
until weather, logistics, or policy materially constrain exportable volume, international trade flows are likely
to remain competitive rather than restrictive.

Weather & Crop Conditions

United States
Weather remains a secondary driver for US grain markets, though short-term patterns have been
operationally supportive. Temperatures across much of the Midwest and Plains have trended near to
slightly above seasonal norms, limiting freeze-related logistics disruptions and allowing river systems to
function more consistently following earlier winter constraints. Snow cover across key HRW wheat areas
in Kansas, Oklahoma, and Colorado remains adequate, reducing immediate winterkill risk despite
intermittent cold shots. NOAA’s 6–10 and 8–14 day outlooks continue to favor moderation rather than
extreme cold, reinforcing dormancy stability for winter wheat and limiting headline-driven volatility. With
harvest complete and no active fieldwork underway, US weather remains neutral from a supply
standpoint, functioning primarily as a logistics variable rather than a production catalyst at this stage of
the calendar.

Brazil
Brazil’s weather profile remains broadly favorable for aggregate production. Central and northern regions
continue to receive adequate rainfall, supporting soybean development and sustaining expectations for a
large national crop near CONAB’s 177.98 million metric ton estimate. Harvest progress continues, though
fieldwork remains uneven in localized areas where rainfall has slowed operations. In southern Brazil,
moisture levels remain elevated in parts of Paraná and Rio Grande do Sul, contributing to localized
variability and increased disease pressure. However, no new national yield revision emerged during the
window, and export logistics continue to function normally. For now, Brazil’s weather remains a variability
story rather than a disruption narrative.

Argentina
Argentina’s crop profile remains the most weather-sensitive element globally. Soil moisture deficits persist
across key soybean and corn regions, and crop ratings remain below seasonal norms. However, during
the reporting window, no material downward revision to official production estimates was issued, with
soybeans near 48.5 million metric tons and corn near 57 million metric tons. Rainfall coverage remained
uneven, offering limited relief without reversing broader stress. With crops advancing through
reproductive stages, yield sensitivity remains elevated, but the market has not materially repriced supply
risk during the week. Weather risk remains present, though not intensifying.

Global
Outside South America, global weather risks remain limited. Winter wheat across Russia, Ukraine, and
the European Union remains in dormancy under generally stable conditions, with no new winterkill threats
reported. Black Sea logistics continue without disruption. Australia and Canada report no new production
concerns. The broader global weather profile remains stable.

So What?
Weather risk remains concentrated but contained. Argentina continues to face structural moisture stress,
while southern Brazil exhibits localized variability. Central Brazil remains productive, and U.S. conditions
remain neutral. At this stage, weather is being monitored rather than repriced. Until either Argentina sees

a measurable production downgrade or Brazilian harvest disruptions materially impact export flow,
weather remains a background variable rather than a directional catalyst.

Synthesis & Outlook

Futures softened through the holiday-shortened week, with corn settling at $4.27 per bushel, soybeans at
$11.33, and Chicago SRW wheat at $5.47. While flat price drifted lower, the underlying structure
remained stable. The March–May corn spread held near a 9-cent carry (60 percent of full carry),
soybeans near a 16 cent carry (72 percent of full carry), and wheat near a 4½–5 cent carry, confirming
adequate supply without structural stress. CIF Gulf and interior basis levels remained steady across all
three complexes. Managed money positioning remains meaningful, approximately –57,500 corn,
+115,900 soybeans, and –85,800 Chicago wheat as of February 10, but is no longer accelerating. The
divergence between flat price softness and steady physical execution remains intact.

Corn continues to reflect balance rather than stress. Export inspections totaled 1.49 million metric tons for
the week ending February 12, ethanol production held near 1.08 million barrels per day, and spreads are
holding near 60 percent of full carry. CIF Gulf values remain near $5.26–$5.29, and interior basis has
stabilized rather than strengthened. Futures remain capped by comfortable ending stocks, yet the front
end continues to resist disorderly widening. The market appears content trading carry economics while
awaiting a catalyst.

Soybeans remain structurally anchored by domestic crush. January NOPA crush totaled 221.6 million
bushels, a monthly record, reinforcing USDA’s emphasis on domestic use. Funds hold a sizable net long
near 115,900 contracts, introducing potential vulnerability to liquidation but also reflecting constructive
demand sentiment. Brazil’s soybean production estimate remains near 177.98 million metric tons,
keeping global supply expectations heavy, while Argentina’s production remains near 48.5 million metric
tons with weather risk present but not escalating. The structure remains firm at roughly 60 percent of full
carry, but flat price lacks urgency absent a shift in trade flow or supply outlook.

Wheat remains the most structurally heavy component of the complex. Export inspections totaled 0.38
million metric tons, consistent but not dynamic. Global supply continues to dictate pricing, with Russian
12.5 percent protein wheat offered near $229 per metric ton FOB. Spreads remain in carry near 5 cents,
basis is stable near $6.23–$6.28 CIF Gulf, and speculative positioning remains heavily short near 85,800
contracts without forced covering. Until global availability tightens or a weather event materializes, wheat
is likely to remain rangebound with rallies constrained.

Bullish triggers: Upside risk would likely require a measurable production downgrade in Argentina,
particularly if soybean output falls materially below 48.5 million metric tons or corn below 57 million metric
tons, or if harvest disruptions in southern Brazil begin to slow export execution. Additional support could
emerge from a sustained acceleration in U.S. corn export pace above the current 1.49 million metric ton
weekly trend, further strength in ethanol production above 1.08 million barrels per day, or meaningful
short covering in wheat triggered by a global supply disruption.

Bearish triggers: Downside pressure would build under a smooth Brazilian harvest with uninterrupted
export flow near 177.98 million metric tons, combined with stabilization or improvement in Argentine crop
conditions. Softening U.S. basis across interior corridors would signal weaker physical demand, while
long liquidation in soybeans, given the extended 115,900 contract net long, could amplify volatility.
Continued Black Sea pricing dominance near $229 per metric ton FOB would further cap wheat rallies
and reinforce the heavy global supply narrative.

Watchlist (Feb 19–Feb 26):

Argentina: Argentina rainfall distribution and crop ratings

Brazil: Brazil harvest progress and export lineups

Weekly exports: Weekly export inspections and sales consistency

Ethanol: Ethanol production and stocks trajectory

Positioning: Fund positioning shifts in corn and wheat

In summary: Corn remains supported by export execution and steady ethanol demand, with cumulative
shipments running 44 percent ahead of last year. Soybeans rely primarily on record domestic crush to
offset a materially weaker export program that is currently 32 percent behind last season. Wheat
continues to trade under the weight of ample global availability and persistent Black Sea competitiveness.
None of the complexes exhibit tightening stress, and until either demand accelerates or supply is
disrupted, price discovery is likely to remain governed by carry economics and incremental flow rather
than conviction-driven movement.

Ethanol for America Act

The major barrier to a higher Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) is the fuel versus food debate. Now is the
perfect time to move to E15. Corn prices are extremely low, and the latest USDA WASDE reported a record
crop and a record crop expansion.

USDA WASDE forecast corn production at 16.7 billion bushels, with the yield at 188.8 bushels per acre and
ending stocks at 2.1 billion. The season-average corn price dropped 30 cents to $3.90 a bushel. Most
importantly, 202526 crop year is expected to have 1.8 billion more bushels than 2024/25.

With current ethanol production consuming 5.6 billion bushels, a 10 percent increase in consumption would
consume an additional 560 million bushels. The reality is that year around E15 would add approximately
50 million bushels and regulatory streamlining would add another 50 million bushels. At some point over
the next ten years, the additional corn consumption could be 2.8 billion bushels minus lower fuel
consumption resulting from electric vehicles. The ethanol corn consumption increase is likely to be more
of a S curve as new compacity comes online.

With Brazil and the US corn and soybean production increasing, 100 million bushels of ethanol corn
consumption will barely move the needle. The ethanol production capacity expansion that would be three
to four years from now is when the corn consumption impact to the corn market would be felt.

Corn Market Deep Dive
Futures & Spreads: Corn futures firmed slightly this week, with March settling near $4.27 3/4, up 2 cents
from February 19. While flat price moved only marginally, the March–May spread widened to roughly an
11 cent carry, consistent with approximately 72 percent of full carry under the two-month storage
framework. The market remains comfortably in carry, signaling adequate nearby supply and stable
commercial coverage rather than tightening. Volatility remains contained, and price action continues to
reflect consolidation rather than directional momentum. The curve is stable even as the market continues
to weigh strong execution against an otherwise ample global supply backdrop.

Funds & Positioning: Managed Money holds a net short position near 42,313 contracts as of the
February 17 report, reflecting a defensive but not extreme speculative stance. The shift was driven
primarily by modest additions to gross shorts rather than aggressive long liquidation. While the net short
is meaningful, it remains below prior cycle extremes. Importantly, spreads have not collapsed in response
to the heavier positioning, suggesting that speculative pressure is being absorbed without structural
deterioration. Funds appear positioned defensively but not aggressively pressing the downside.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets strengthened modestly. CIF Gulf corn improved to +92H, reflecting firm
export demand and minor freight friction tied to draft constraints along portions of the river system. Interior

river bids firmed as well, while processor bids held steady. Basis is not surging, but the tone is
constructive. The physical market continues to signal steady movement rather than distress, with logistics
normalized enough to prevent bottlenecks but tight enough to keep freight supportive. Nearby commercial
flow remains orderly.

Export Sales & Inspections: Export inspections for the week ending February 19 accelerated to
approximately 2.01 MMT, a clear step higher from the prior week and reinforcing strong execution.
Cumulative shipments remain comfortably ahead of last year and continue tracking in line with USDA’s
export projection. Weekly export sales remain active, with forward commitments sustaining program
visibility into late winter. Shipments represent a large share of USDA’s export projection, underscoring
that demand performance remains the primary stabilizing force in the balance sheet. The export channel
continues to offset softer flat price dynamics.

Global Context: Brazil’s February corn export pace, while active, is running below last year’s level,
reducing immediate competitive pressure at the margin. Argentine production estimates remain steady,
though recent rainfall variability introduces localized uncertainty. Black Sea corn offers remain competitive
but not decisively undercutting U.S. Gulf into core Western Hemisphere destinations. Mexico continues to
anchor U.S. demand, and Latin American flows remain consistent. Global supply remains ample, but U.S.
origin retains competitive footing in key channels.

So What? Corn’s structure remains more stable than the board implies. Flat price has softened, and
speculative shorts remain meaningful, yet spreads hold near around 72 percent of full carry and basis has
firmed modestly. Export execution remains the anchor. Absent a deterioration in shipments or a renewed
surge in global competition, the market continues to trade within a carry-defined range. For now, structure
is steady, positioning is defensive, and downside momentum remains contained by physical flow.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: Soybeans softened modestly this week, with March settling near $11.34. The
March–May spread widened to roughly a 16 cent carry, near 70 percent of full carry. The structure
remains clearly in contango but not at full storage economics, suggesting adequate nearby supply without
signaling pressure. Price action reflects stabilization rather than momentum, with the front end supported
but not urgent.

Products & Crush: Domestic processing continues to anchor the complex. January NOPA crush at
221.56 million bushels reaffirmed historically strong throughput, even as soybean oil stocks remain
elevated near 1.9 billion pounds. Crush margins continue to lean meal-driven, with soybean meal demand
providing the bulk of processing support. The product complex has not accelerated meaningfully, but
neither has it deteriorated. Domestic use remains the primary structural pillar for U.S. soybeans as export
competitiveness fluctuates.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets softened slightly at the Gulf, with CIF values easing toward +95H as
Brazilian harvest pressure builds. Interior processor bids slipped modestly as well, reflecting reduced
urgency amid improving South American logistics. The nearby market remains supported by crush pull
rather than export-driven tightening. Basis tone is stable but not strengthening, underscoring the
divergence between steady domestic demand and heavier global supply availability.

Funds & Positioning: Managed Money holds a net long position near 92,000 contracts as of the
February 17 report. Positioning is constructive rather than defensive, which helps explain why breaks
have been absorbed even as Brazil dominates the export window. The tradeoff is that length introduces
liquidation risk if South American flow stays smooth and demand fails to re-accelerate. In short, soybeans

are not set up like a crowded short market; they are supported, but more vulnerable to sentiment shifts if
the fundamental tape softens.

Export Sales & Inspections: Weekly export inspections for the week ending February 19 totaled
approximately 0.67 MMT, a noticeable step down from the prior week. Cumulative inspections remain
materially behind last year’s pace, reflecting Brazil’s dominant early-season window. ANEC projects
February soybean exports near 11.4 MMT, well above last year’s February pace and reinforcing South
America’s pricing influence. U.S. export flow remains functional but secondary in the global trade rotation.
The export channel continues to operate, but it is not the primary demand driver at this stage of the
marketing year.

Global Context: Brazil’s soybean production estimate remains near 178 MMT, with harvest advancing
under broadly favorable conditions across central regions. FOB Santos values remain competitive into
Asia, effectively setting the ceiling for U.S. pricing absent a freight or currency shift. Argentina’s soybean
outlook holds near 48.5 MMT, though renewed dryness across second-crop areas reintroduces weather
sensitivity. For now, Brazil defines the global supply narrative, while Argentina remains the volatility
variable rather than a confirmed disruption.

So What? Soybeans remain supported by domestic processing but capped by Brazil’s seasonal export
dominance. The board finished slightly lower on the week and the March–May spread widened versus
last week, reinforcing a carry-driven tone as nearby coverage stays comfortable and South America sets
the external ceiling. Export flow remains functional but secondary, while crush continues to provide the
structural floor. With managed money net long near 92,000 contracts, the complex is more sensitive to an
upside surprise in demand or South American weather than to a liquidation-driven break. Absent a
material shift in export competitiveness or a realized supply disruption in South America, price discovery
is likely to remain anchored by carry economics and the pace of Brazilian flow.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: Wheat futures recovered modestly this week, with March Chicago SRW settling
near $5.63 1/2, up 4 cents from February 19. The March–May spread widened toward a 10 cent carry,
roughly 61 percent of full carry, reinforcing comfortable nearby supply without signaling a market fully
rewarding storage. The rally continues to read as more technical than fundamentally driven, with structure
remaining in carry and consistent with adequate coverage. Kansas City and Minneapolis followed a
similar tone, with no meaningful divergence within the complex.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets were largely steady. CIF Gulf SRW basis softened modestly toward +65H,
while interior levels showed little evidence of tightening. Plains HRW basis remained stable near -20H
despite localized weather variability, and Pacific Northwest values held firm, reflecting routine coverage
rather than scarcity. The absence of basis acceleration alongside widening carry underscores a market
that is adequately supplied. Physical flow remains orderly, and commercial coverage appears sufficient.

Export Sales & Inspections: Weekly export inspections for the week ending February 19 increased to
approximately 0.54 MMT, a firmer pace relative to the prior week. Export sales remain routine but not
accelerating, and cumulative shipments continue to track broadly in line with USDA projections. While
export flow is functioning, volumes remain insufficient to materially alter the broader balance sheet
narrative. The program is steady, but not dynamic.

Global Context: Russian 12.5 percent FOB values firmed toward $235/MT, offering modest support to

global pricing, and Euronext wheat rebounded nearly 3 percent on the week. However, Black Sea supply
remains structurally available, and competitive offers into North Africa and the Middle East continue to
anchor world values. Ukrainian exports remain active through established channels, and European origin
has re-entered select tenders. No logistical or policy disruption has emerged to materially tighten
availability. Global supply remains ample, even if short-term pricing has stabilized.

Funds & Positioning: Managed Money maintains a substantial net short position near 69,567 contracts
as of the February 17 report. While exposure is below prior extremes, it remains meaningful and
continues to reflect a defensive stance. The recent price recovery has not triggered meaningful short
covering, suggesting that speculative conviction remains intact. Positioning offers latent upside risk, but
absent a structural catalyst, funds appear comfortable maintaining exposure.

So What? Wheat’s structure has grown heavier even as flat price improved. The expansion deeper into
carry reinforces comfortable coverage, though still short of full storage economics. Export flow has
strengthened modestly, and global pricing has stabilized, but neither development has tightened the
balance sheet meaningfully. With funds still meaningfully short and spreads rewarding storage, the
market remains rangebound. Until a material production shock or export disruption emerges, wheat is
likely to trade within carry-defined boundaries rather than trend decisively higher.

US Cash Market & Basis

Corn: Corn basis strengthened modestly across primary corridors despite softer futures. CIF Gulf values
improved to approximately +92H, supported by strong export inspections and slight freight friction tied to
draft constraints along the Illinois River system. Interior river bids firmed toward +24H in St. Louis,
reflecting continued export execution and limited farmer selling. Midwest ethanol plant bids remained
stable, reinforcing steady grind demand. While flat price drifted lower on the board, the physical market
tone was constructive. The nearby cash market signals orderly movement rather than liquidation
pressure, with export demand continuing to underpin basis strength.

Soybeans: Soybean basis softened slightly at the Gulf as Brazilian harvest momentum increased. CIF
Gulf values eased toward +95H, reflecting steady but less urgent export demand relative to prior weeks.
Interior processor bids across the Midwest slipped modestly, indicating adequate nearby coverage amid
strong January crush but rising South American competition. River logistics remain normalized, reducing
transportation friction. The cash market remains supported by domestic processing, yet lacks the
tightening tone seen earlier in the month. Basis stability persists, though the directional bias has softened
marginally.

Wheat: Wheat cash markets were broadly steady. CIF Gulf SRW basis held near +65H, while HRW basis
across the Plains remained anchored near -20H. Pacific Northwest values were unchanged, reflecting
routine export coverage rather than incremental demand acceleration. Despite modest improvement in
futures, basis has not strengthened meaningfully, underscoring comfortable nearby availability. The
widening calendar spreads reinforce the view that inventory coverage is adequate. Physical wheat
markets continue to signal sufficiency rather than scarcity.

So What? Cash markets continue to trade with greater stability than flat price suggests. Corn basis has
firmed alongside strong export flow, soybeans show mild softening as Brazil accelerates harvest, and
wheat remains structurally comfortable. Logistics are functioning efficiently, and no corridor signals stress.
Physical markets remain balanced, with corn showing relative strength, soybeans steady but capped, and
wheat reflecting ample supply.

International Cash & Trade Flows

Brazil: Brazil’s export program continues to define global oilseed flow as harvest advances across central
regions. ANEC projects February soybean shipments near 11.4 MMT, materially above last year’s pace
and reinforcing South America’s seasonal dominance. FOB Santos values near $424/MT remain
competitive into Asia, effectively setting the ceiling for U.S. export participation. Corn exports are active
but trail last year’s February level, reflecting the seasonal transition between crop cycles. Interior basis
firmness and rising B3 values highlight domestic retention even as export channels remain functional.
Brazil remains the primary price-setter in soybeans and a stabilizing influence in global corn trade

Argentina: Argentina remains the principal weather-sensitive variable. Recent rainfall has been uneven,
with dryness returning across portions of the soybean belt entering critical grain-fill stages. Official
production estimates remain unchanged at 48.5 MMT for soybeans, though localized stress sustains
volatility risk. FOB offers remain present but lack the scale to materially disrupt Brazil’s leadership. Corn
harvest progress is underway in early-planted areas, with yield variability emerging regionally. Argentina’s
export flow continues, but its influence remains secondary unless weather conditions deteriorate further.

China: China’s import posture remains measured. Brazilian soybeans continue to dominate forward
coverage due to price advantage and harvest availability, while U.S. origin remains opportunistic rather
than primary. Dalian corn and soymeal futures softened modestly this week, reflecting adequate domestic
supply and limited feed margin expansion. No large new U.S. soybean purchase announcements
emerged during the window. China’s demand remains tactical and margin-sensitive rather than
expansionary.

EU / Black Sea: Black Sea origin continues to anchor global wheat pricing, though FOB values have
firmed modestly near $235/MT for Russian 12.5% wheat. Ukrainian corn remains competitively offered
near $232/MT, maintaining pressure on Atlantic Basin pricing. Euronext wheat rebounded nearly 3
percent this week, suggesting short-covering and stabilization rather than structural tightening. EU export
pace remains below last year’s level, and no major logistical disruption has emerged. Black Sea supply
continues to cap rallies even as pricing stabilizes.

Other Regions: Australia continues to move wheat into Asian markets following a solid harvest, while
Canadian spring wheat exports proceed in line with seasonal norms. No material trade restrictions, quota
shifts, or policy disruptions have emerged across secondary exporters. The broader international
environment remains stable and well supplied.

So What? Brazil is still the price-setter in soybeans, but this week the market’s attention shifted from
“crop size” to “how fast it can physically move,” with ANEC implying another front-loaded February
shipment pace. Argentina, meanwhile, is no longer just a volatility headline, deterioration is starting to
show up in the way estimates and ratings are being discussed. For wheat, Black Sea FOB values have
firmed a touch, yet they still define the ceiling for everyone else.

Key Fundamentals & Reports (Feb 12 – Feb 18)

Export Inspections (USDA FGIS – week ending Feb 19): Corn export inspections accelerated to
2,005,050 metric tons, lifting cumulative 2025/26 shipments to approximately 37.7 million metric tons,
maintaining a pace well ahead of last year and broadly consistent with USDA’s export projection. The
improvement reinforces corn’s position as the strongest executing program within the complex. Soybean
inspections totaled 669,865 metric tons, a noticeable slowdown from the prior week, with cumulative

shipments continuing to trail last season materially as Brazil dominates the early marketing window.
Wheat inspections reached 535,113 metric tons, a firmer weekly pace that keeps cumulative shipments
modestly ahead of last year but still insufficient to materially alter the balance sheet narrative.

Export Sales (USDA FAS – latest through week ending Feb 12): Weekly net sales reflected continued
forward engagement. Corn net sales totaled 1,482,300 metric tons, sustaining active commitment flow.
Soybean net sales reached 412,600 metric tons, steady but not indicative of acceleration amid strong
Brazilian competition. Wheat net sales totaled 348,200 metric tons, consistent with routine demand rather
than expansion. Cumulative commitments for corn now represent roughly three-quarters of USDA’s
export forecast, while soybeans and wheat remain broadly aligned with seasonal expectations. No
significant flash sales emerged during the window.

Ethanol Production & Stocks: Ethanol production for the week ending February 13 increased to 1.118
million barrels per day, up from the prior week’s 1.110 million. Stocks remain elevated near seasonal
highs, signaling steady grind but no acceleration in blending demand. Production remains supportive for
corn usage, though inventory levels temper enthusiasm for additional near-term upside in ethanol-driven
demand.

NOPA Soybean Crush: January NOPA crush at 221.56 million bushels remains the structural anchor for
soybeans, reaffirming historically strong domestic processing demand. Soybean oil stocks near 1.90
billion pounds continue to reflect ample product availability, reinforcing that crush margins remain meal-
driven. Domestic demand remains intact and continues to offset export weakness.

CFTC Positioning (as of February 17, released February 21): Managed Money positioning remains
broadly defensive across the grain complex. Corn funds held a net short of 42,313 contracts, soybeans a
net long of roughly 92,000, and Chicago SRW wheat a net short of 69,567. The key takeaway is that
speculative exposure is still positioned to fade rallies in corn and wheat, while soybeans carry a more
constructive long, but it is not stretched enough to imply forced liquidation without a catalyst. With
spreads holding in carry and cash markets largely steady, positioning looks more like “patience and
optionality” than a crowded bet. In practice, that keeps the complex vulnerable to event-driven volatility,
weather escalation in Argentina, a logistics hiccup in Brazil, or a shift in export competitiveness, but it
does not, by itself, signal a market on the edge of a structural unwind.

So What? The complex is getting more uneven. Corn is the only leg clearly outperforming on execution
(2.01 MMT inspections), yet funds are still leaning short. Soybeans keep leaning on crush for a floor, but
weekly inspections cooled again, which reinforces the seasonal Brazil cap. Wheat flow improved, but
carry rebuilt and basis stayed calm, a combination that usually reads as “stabilization,” not “tightening.

International Reports

Brazil: Brazil’s February production profile remains intact, with CONAB maintaining soybean output near
177.98 million metric tons and total corn production near 138.45 million metric tons. The safrinha crop
continues to account for the majority of projected corn supply, reinforcing expectations for substantial
second-half export availability. While harvest advances steadily across central regions, no official
downward revisions have emerged. The size of Brazil’s soybean crop continues to frame global oilseed
balance sheets, anchoring expectations for abundant exportable surplus into mid-year. Structurally, Brazil
remains the dominant supply reference point rather than a volatility driver at this stage.

Argentina: Argentina’s official production outlook remains stable, with soybeans near 48.5 million metric
tons and corn near 57 million metric tons. Rainfall variability persists across key regions, particularly in
second-crop soybeans entering critical reproductive stages, but no formal downgrade has been issued.

Farmer marketing remains measured amid currency dynamics and macro uncertainty, limiting aggressive
forward sales. While agronomic risk remains elevated relative to Brazil, it has not yet translated into a
measurable supply contraction. Argentina remains the primary weather-sensitive variable, but not yet a
confirmed structural shift.

China: China’s demand posture remains pragmatic. Routine soybean imports continue, largely supplied
by Brazil’s advancing harvest. No material policy changes or reserve interventions were announced
during the window. Domestic futures pricing suggests stable but not expanding crush economics, and
feed margins remain sensitive to livestock profitability. China’s role remains supportive but selective,
engaging opportunistically rather than driving expansionary demand.

EU / Black Sea: The broader European and Black Sea production outlook remains stable. No significant
revisions to wheat or coarse grain output were announced during the reporting window. Export corridors
from the Black Sea remain functional, and EU export pace continues to trail last year’s levels. The
absence of logistical disruption or policy intervention reinforces a supply environment defined by
continuity rather than constraint. At present, structural availability remains the dominant feature across
the region.

So What? International balance sheets remain defined by scale rather than shock. Brazil’s large soybean
and corn production frames global supply expectations, Argentina’s weather risk remains monitored but
not escalated, and China’s import behavior remains tactical. Across major exporting regions, no new
production revision or policy shift has emerged to materially alter global availability. The international
backdrop continues to reflect abundance, with volatility centered more on weather potential than realized
disruption.

Weather & Crop Conditions

United States
U.S. weather remains largely neutral from a production standpoint at this stage of the calendar. The
USDA national Crop Progress report remains on seasonal pause, with full updates resuming in April,
leaving the market to rely on state-level updates and winterkill monitoring. Snow cover across key HRW
wheat areas in Kansas, Oklahoma, and Colorado remains adequate, limiting immediate freeze risk
despite intermittent cold. NOAA’s 6–10 and 8–14 day outlooks continue to favor above-normal
temperatures across much of the central U.S., reducing logistical friction along river systems and allowing
freight conditions to function more consistently relative to earlier winter disruptions. With winter wheat still
in dormancy and no active fieldwork underway, U.S. weather remains an operational variable rather than
a balance-sheet catalyst.

Brazil
Brazil’s weather continues to reinforce production expectations, though logistics are beginning to feel the
pressure of record volume. National soybean harvest has advanced to roughly 25 percent complete, with
Mato Grosso leading near 47 percent and reporting strong early yields that sustain aggregate production
expectations near 178–180 million metric tons. Soil moisture remains favorable for safrinha corn
establishment across the Center-West, preserving the second-crop outlook. However, frequent rainfall in
Mato Grosso and Pará has narrowed loading windows along the Arco Norte corridor, extending barge
wait times along the Tapajós system. In the South and Southeast, heavy rainfall in Paraná and Santa
Catarina has introduced localized flood risk, potentially slowing loading operations at Paranaguá and
Santos. Logistics remain functional, but the system is stretched, and the risk has shifted from theoretical
to operational as export flows accelerate.

Argentina
Argentina has moved from monitored stress to measurable deterioration. Soybean conditions have fallen

to 40 percent rated Good/Excellent, down sharply in recent weeks, with the Rosario Grain Exchange
projecting production near 48 million metric tons and warning that losses in the most affected zones could
reach 20–60 percent. Corn conditions stand at 44 percent Good/Excellent, prompting the Buenos Aires
Grain Exchange to reduce its production estimate to 57 million metric tons amid persistent dryness and
thermal stress. Rainfall coverage has been uneven and insufficient to fully stabilize second-crop
soybeans entering grain fill, while late-planted corn remains highly sensitive to short-term precipitation.
Unlike Brazil, where weather variability has not altered aggregate expectations, Argentina’s production
profile is actively being trimmed, keeping downside supply risk elevated.

Global
Outside South America, global weather remains largely stable. Winter wheat across Russia, Ukraine, and
the European Union remains dormant under broadly normal conditions with no significant winterkill threat
reported. Black Sea logistics continue without disruption, and no secondary exporter has introduced
meaningful supply risk. As a result, global weather volatility remains geographically concentrated rather
than systemic.

So What?
Weather risk is no longer evenly distributed. Brazil continues to support global supply with strong harvest
progress despite tightening logistics, the United States remains neutral during dormancy, and Argentina
has become the primary volatility node with declining crop ratings and downward revisions underway.
Unless Argentine conditions deteriorate further or Brazilian port congestion materially disrupts export flow,
weather remains a developing driver rather than a confirmed balance-sheet shock, but the asymmetry
has increased meaningfully compared to prior weeks.

Synthesis & Outlook

The defining feature of this week was divergence beneath stable flat price. Corn finished modestly higher
with March near $4.27, soybeans edged lower with March near $11.34, and Chicago SRW wheat firmed
to roughly $5.63, yet the more important signal came from structure and flow rather than the closes
themselves. Calendar spreads across the complex widened week over week and remain in carry: corn’s
March–May spread sits near an 11-cent carry (roughly 72 percent of full carry), soybeans near a 16-cent
carry (about 70 percent), and wheat near a 10-cent carry (about 61 percent). That structure continues to
reflect adequate coverage and limited urgency, even as cash and export execution send more nuanced
signals underneath the board.

Corn continues to behave like a market in equilibrium, but this week the export channel did more of the
heavy lifting. Inspections surged to about 2.01 MMT for the week ending February 19, reinforcing a
shipment pace that remains comfortably ahead of last year and aligned with USDA’s forecast. Gulf basis
firmed toward +92H and interior river bids strengthened modestly, suggesting that physical demand
remains intact even as the curve stays comfortably in carry. Funds remain net short near 42,000
contracts, keeping a defensive speculative overlay in place, but the combination of stronger inspections
and firmer cash tone helped prevent the board from slipping despite a market structure that still pays
storage.

Soybeans remain bifurcated between domestic strength and global weight. January NOPA crush at
221.56 million bushels continues to validate the demand floor, even as soybean oil stocks remain
elevated and keep the product complex from driving a broader revaluation. On the export side,
inspections cooled to about 0.67 MMT for the week ending February 19 and cumulative shipments remain
materially behind last year as Brazil dominates the seasonal export window. With ANEC projecting
February soybean exports near 11.4 MMT and Brazil’s harvest advancing, the market continues to treat
South America as the pricing ceiling near-term. The March–May spread remains in a carry-driven posture
near 70 percent of full carry, consistent with comfortable nearby coverage. With managed money net long

near 92,000 contracts, the complex is positioned to react to either a weather-driven surprise in Argentina
or a clearer demand signal, but absent that, the export rotation keeps upside constrained even as crush
provides support.

Wheat remains the heaviest leg of the complex despite this week’s modest recovery. Export inspections
improved to roughly 0.54 MMT, but the market’s structure moved deeper into carry, with the March–May
spread widening toward 10 cents. That combination, firmer futures alongside a heavier carry, reads as
stabilization rather than tightening. Black Sea pricing remains the global anchor, with Russian 12.5
percent FOB values near $235/MT continuing to cap U.S. competitiveness into price-sensitive
destinations. Basis was steady to slightly softer across Gulf and interior markets, consistent with
adequate coverage rather than urgency. Managed money remains meaningfully net short near 69,500
contracts, creating latent upside risk through short covering, but that risk still requires a catalyst beyond
routine weekly flow.

Weather risk is increasingly asymmetrical. Brazil remains abundant but operationally stretched as harvest
advances and export systems absorb large volumes, while U.S. winter conditions remain neutral during
dormancy and logistics have improved relative to earlier winter constraints. Argentina, however, has re-
entered focus with renewed moisture stress during critical reproductive stages, and crop conditions have
deteriorated relative to earlier weeks. For now, the market is acknowledging that risk without fully
repricing it into balance sheets, but the distribution of weather risk has shifted meaningfully compared
with mid-February.

Bullish triggers: Upside momentum would likely require confirmation that Argentine deterioration is
balance-sheet relevant rather than localized, particularly if soybean production slips materially below
current estimates or corn losses expand beyond the latest trims. A move from “stretched” to disruptive in
Brazilian export logistics could tighten the near-term pipeline and force a short-term repricing of
availability. Additional support could come from continued strength in U.S. corn export execution, an
acceleration in ethanol grind beyond recent levels, or any disruption in Black Sea logistics that shifts
wheat competitiveness and triggers short covering in a structurally short market.

Bearish triggers: Downside pressure would build under a smooth, uninterrupted Brazilian harvest and
export program that reinforces South America as the seasonal pricing ceiling for soybeans and limits U.S.
participation into Asia. A meaningful stabilization in Argentine rainfall and crop conditions would deflate
the weather premium that is beginning to re-enter the narrative. Domestically, softening U.S. interior basis
would signal weaker nearby demand, while the complex remains vulnerable to renewed pressure if
spreads continue to widen and commercial coverage stays comfortable. In wheat, persistent Black Sea
competitiveness and the absence of a supply shock would keep structure rewarding storage and continue
to cap rallies.

In summary: the grain complex remains structurally comfortable but increasingly uneven beneath the
surface. Corn is outperforming on execution and cash tone even as the curve stays in carry, soybeans
remain supported by domestic processing but capped by Brazil’s export dominance, and wheat remains
rangebound under heavy global availability despite a modest rebound. Until supply is materially disrupted
or demand accelerates in a measurable way, price discovery is likely to remain governed by carry
economics, cash-market signals, and incremental flow rather than conviction-driven trend.

Ethanol for America Act

The major barrier to a higher Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) is the fuel versus food debate. Now is the
perfect time to move to E15. Corn prices are extremely low, and the latest USDA WASDE reported a record
crop and a record crop expansion.

Wheat – Front-End Flips as Funds Cover into Persistent Black Sea Pressure
Chicago SRW’s front end tightened sharply, with the March–May spread flipping into roughly a 4-cent

remain steady, the inversion appears more positioning-driven than fundamentally restrictive, and absent a

Soybeans – Structure Firms Slightly as Brazil Expands Its Window
Soybeans recovered, with May settling near $11.73, up roughly 15 cents on the week, though export flow
remains seasonally subdued as Brazil accelerates shipments. Weekly inspections improved to 1.14 MMT,
but cumulative shipments at 26.18 MMT remain 30 percent below last year, consistent with Brazil’s
expanding export program, with ANEC projecting March shipments near 15.7 MMT. The March–May
spread narrowed to roughly a 10-cent carry, about 46 percent of full carry, down from 70 percent last
week, suggesting stabilization in nearby structure rather than expanding storage incentives. CIF Gulf
barge basis firmed modestly to +90H, and interior processor bids remain steady, reflecting continued
domestic pull. Managed money remains net short, and while domestic demand continues to anchor the
complex, Brazil’s seasonal pricing ceiling remains firmly in place.

Corn Market Deep Dive
Futures & Spreads: Corn futures advanced modestly on the week, with May settling near $4.49 versus
roughly $4.43 last Wednesday, extending the recovery that began in late February. The more important
signal remains in the curve: the March–May spread holds near a 12-cent carry, roughly 80 percent of full
carry under the two-month storage framework. Carry widened slightly from last week’s 11 cents,
reinforcing that the market continues to reward storage and signal comfortable nearby coverage rather
than front-end stress, even as the board firms. Realized volatility remains moderate near 14 percent
annualized, consistent with a market grinding higher rather than breaking into a higher-beta trend, and
price action continues to reflect execution-driven support more than a structural tightening of supplies.

Funds & Positioning: Managed money remains net short in corn near -286,685 contracts as of the
February 24 report, but the week featured meaningful short covering with a +103,702 contract
improvement from the prior week. That shift matters because it confirms the rally is no longer only
commercial-led; some speculative pressure is being relieved as execution stays strong. At the same time,
open interest in May declined roughly 9,000 contracts from Feb 25 to Mar 3, suggesting the recent move
has leaned more toward liquidation than aggressive new length. In other words, positioning remains
defensive, but the market is starting to force risk reduction. Importantly, spreads have not collapsed
despite the large remaining net short, indicating the market is absorbing speculative flow without signaling

tightening physical availability.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets cooled modestly after last week’s strength but still read as constructive. CIF
Gulf barge basis eased to roughly +85H from +92H, suggesting demand remains active but nearby offers
are less urgent. Interior river bids are still running around 20 cents under May, and ethanol plants
continue to post supportive bids to maintain nearby coverage. Basis is neither flashing scarcity nor rolling
over; movement looks orderly, with barge economics still the main swing variable capable of quickly
resetting Gulf values if river conditions tighten again.

Export Sales & Inspections: Export execution remains the anchor. Weekly inspections eased from last
week’s surge but stayed strong at 1.86 MMT for the week ending Feb 26, lifting cumulative shipments to
39.6 MMT, now 45 percent ahead of last year. Commitments stand near 62.96 MMT, equivalent to
roughly 75 percent of USDA’s 83.83 MMT export forecast already sold. Just as important, the four-week
average shipment pace near 1.54 MMT sits well above the roughly 0.80 MMT required weekly pace to
meet USDA’s projection through August. That gap suggests the balance sheet has room for additional
tightening if execution persists, even if weekly sales remain choppy.

Global Context: Global supply remains ample, but U.S. origin continues to hold competitive footing in
core channels. Black Sea offers remain steady, and Argentine FOB values are currently cheaper into
some destinations, but U.S. execution continues to be supported by dependable Western Hemisphere
pull, particularly Mexico. Brazil remains focused on soybean logistics and safrinha development, limiting
immediate corn export pressure in the near term. The global environment still caps runaway rallies, but
the U.S. program is performing well enough that competition has not yet forced a structural deterioration
in spreads or basis.

So What? Corn is firming while still trading like a carry market. The curve continues to reward storage,
but export execution is running above what the balance sheet requires, and speculative shorts are being
reduced rather than added. With May open interest drifting lower and managed money still meaningfully
net short, the market retains a defensive overlay, yet downside pressure remains contained by physical
flow and shipment momentum. Unless inspections materially cool or global competition sharpens, corn is
increasingly set up to trade as a stable carry market with tightening risk skewed toward the USDA export
line rather than toward a collapse in structure.

Soybean Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: Soybean futures moved higher this week, with May settling near $11.73 compared
with roughly $11.58 last Wednesday. The more notable shift occurred in the structure of the curve: the
March–May spread tightened to roughly a 10 cent carry, equivalent to about 45 percent of full carry under
the two-month storage framework. Last week’s structure had widened toward 16 cents, so the
compression signals that the market is no longer expanding storage incentives in response to Brazilian
harvest pressure. Nearby coverage remains comfortable and the market is still clearly in contango, but
the tightening spread suggests that the board is beginning to absorb seasonal supply rather than discount
it further. Price action therefore reflects stabilization within a carry structure rather than a directional
breakout.

Products & Crush: Domestic processing remains the primary source of underlying demand support for
the soybean complex. Crushers remain well incentivized to operate at high utilization rates, though the
margin structure is increasingly concentrated on the meal side of the balance sheet rather than on oil.
Soybean oil inventories remain comfortable, limiting the contribution from the energy side of the complex,
while steady feed demand continues to support meal pricing. The result is a processing sector that is
maintaining throughput rather than accelerating it. In effect, crush demand is acting as a stabilizing force

that prevents Brazilian export pressure from translating into deeper weakness in the nearby market.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets remain stable and largely transactional rather than urgent. CIF Gulf barge
basis is holding near +90H, firmer than recent lows but still consistent with routine export loading rather
than a scramble for nearby coverage. Interior processor bids generally sit around 40 cents under May
futures, reflecting balanced crusher coverage as plants maintain solid run rates without needing to step
bids higher. With Brazil supplying the bulk of export demand during this window, basis behavior continues
to read as “steady domestic pull” instead of tightening pipeline signals.

Funds & Positioning: Speculative positioning has shifted toward a more defensive posture. Managed
Money is now net short roughly 171,000 contracts according to the February 24 CFTC report, a
significant reversal from the constructive long positioning seen earlier in the winter. The build in short
exposure reflects the market’s adjustment to Brazil’s dominant export window and the broader seasonal
increase in global supply availability. Importantly, spreads have tightened despite the heavier speculative
short exposure, suggesting that the market is absorbing positioning pressure without structural
deterioration. The current configuration indicates a market that is defensively positioned but not collapsing
under speculative weight.

Export Sales & Inspections: Export activity remains secondary while South America dominates global
shipments. Weekly U.S. soybean inspections reached approximately 1.14 MMT for the week ending
February 26, an improvement from earlier weeks but still leaving cumulative shipments near 26.18 MMT,
roughly 30 percent below last year’s pace. Total export commitments stand around 35.65 MMT, or
approximately 83 percent of USDA’s 42.87 MMT export projection. The remaining shipment requirement
is manageable, and the recent pace suggests the United States can still meet the current forecast, but the
trade rotation clearly favors Brazil during this portion of the marketing year. Export demand therefore
remains functional, though it is no longer the primary driver of price formation.

Global Context: Brazil remains the defining force in the global soybean balance sheet. CONAB’s latest
estimate places production near 178 MMT, confirming another record crop as harvest progresses across
the central producing states. ANEC projects March soybean exports near 15.7 MMT, underscoring the
scale of Brazilian logistics as export flows accelerate. FOB Santos offers remain competitively priced into
Asia relative to U.S. Gulf values, reinforcing Brazil’s dominance during the peak shipping window.
Argentina’s crop outlook remains closer to 47–48 MMT, though crop ratings remain historically weak after
earlier heat stress and keep the market sensitive to late-season weather developments. For now, Brazil
defines supply while Argentina represents the remaining weather variable.

So What? Soybeans appear to be transitioning from seasonal pressure toward stabilization. The board
moved higher on the week and the March–May spread tightened materially, signaling that the market is
beginning to absorb Brazilian harvest flow rather than expanding storage incentives. Domestic processing
continues to provide the structural demand floor, while export activity remains active but secondary during
South America’s peak shipping window. With managed money now positioned net short rather than long,
the market carries less liquidation risk but remains sensitive to shifts in global supply expectations. Unless
South American production expectations change materially or U.S. export competitiveness improves,
soybean price discovery is likely to remain anchored by steady domestic crush demand and the pace of
Brazilian export flow.

Wheat Market Deep Dive

Futures & Spreads: Chicago SRW wheat futures edged higher during the week, with May settling near
$5.80 compared with roughly $5.79 last Wednesday. The more meaningful development occurred in the
nearby structure: the March–May spread flipped from carry into a modest inversion near four cents. That
shift represents a notable change from the carry structure observed in recent weeks and indicates
tightening nearby availability rather than an expansion of storage incentives. Volatility also moved higher
relative to corn and soybeans, reflecting the market’s sensitivity to shifting trade flows and speculative
repositioning. While the flat price move itself was limited, the spread inversion signals that the front end of
the curve has become more responsive to short-term supply and logistics dynamics.

Cash & Basis: Cash markets showed a firmer tone across export corridors. CIF Gulf SRW values are
currently near +110H, indicating steady demand for nearby export slots despite limited improvement in
global competitiveness. Plains HRW basis remains defensive near 40 cents under May futures, reflecting
adequate regional coverage rather than aggressive commercial bidding. Pacific Northwest values were
largely unchanged, with export programs continuing to operate at routine levels. Overall basis behavior
suggests that the nearby inversion is being driven more by short-term positioning and logistics dynamics
than by a widespread tightening in underlying physical supply.

Export Sales & Inspections: U.S. wheat export activity slowed somewhat during the latest reporting
week. Export inspections for the week ending February 26 totaled roughly 0.34 MMT, below the prior
week’s pace but still leaving cumulative shipments near 18.62 MMT, roughly 19 percent ahead of last
year. Export commitments now stand near 93 percent of USDA’s marketing-year projection, meaning only
modest additional sales are required to reach the forecast before the May marketing-year close. While the
export program remains steady, shipment volumes alone are unlikely to materially tighten the U.S.
balance sheet without an improvement in global competitiveness.

Global Context: International wheat pricing continues to be shaped by Black Sea supply. Russian 12.5
percent FOB offers are currently near $234 per metric ton, maintaining a roughly $29 per ton discount to
comparable U.S. Gulf SRW values. That pricing advantage continues to anchor global trade flows into
traditional import markets across North Africa and the Middle East. European wheat values have firmed
modestly alongside the broader complex, but Black Sea origin remains the dominant pricing reference. As
long as Russian exports continue moving without disruption, the global wheat market remains structurally
well supplied despite short-term price fluctuations.

Funds & Positioning: Speculative positioning has shifted notably. Managed Money moved into a modest
net long position near 17,700 contracts in Chicago SRW wheat following several weeks of short covering.
The adjustment reflects the market’s sensitivity to spread tightening and volatility rather than a wholesale
shift in the global supply narrative. Even with the move into net long territory, speculative exposure
remains relatively small compared with prior cycles. The current positioning suggests that funds have
reduced downside conviction but have not yet established aggressive bullish exposure.

So What? Wheat’s tone has improved modestly, but the broader balance sheet remains heavy. The shift
of the March–May spread into inversion highlights tightening in the nearby structure and greater
sensitivity to short-term positioning and logistics flows. At the same time, export competitiveness remains
constrained by the persistent Black Sea pricing advantage, and global supply availability continues to limit
sustained upside. With speculative positioning shifting away from outright shorts and volatility elevated
relative to corn and soybeans, wheat may experience sharper short-term price swings. However, without
a meaningful disruption to global export flows or a production shock in a major origin, the market remains
fundamentally constrained by ample world supply.

US Cash Market & Basis

Corn: Corn basis held relatively firm across key export corridors even as futures edged higher during the
week. CIF Gulf barge values remained near +85H, reflecting consistent export loading and active river
movement. Interior river bids were roughly 20 cents under May futures, suggesting that elevators
continue to source grain without needing to aggressively lift bids. Ethanol plants also maintained
supportive bids as processors compete locally to secure supplies for steady grind rates. While basis has
cooled slightly from the stronger levels seen earlier in the winter, export shipments and ethanol demand
continue to provide the underlying support for the nearby cash market.

Soybeans: Soybean basis showed little directional change as global trade flows continue to rotate toward
South American origin. CIF Gulf barge bids are currently near +90H, indicating ongoing export movement
but below the stronger premiums observed earlier in the season. Interior processor bids around 40 cents
under May futures suggest crushers have sufficient nearby coverage while maintaining strong run rates.
With Brazilian exports ramping up rapidly during the harvest window, U.S. soybeans are moving into a
more secondary role in international trade, leaving the domestic cash market stable but lacking strong
upward pressure.

Wheat: Wheat cash markets leaned slightly firmer along export channels. CIF SRW basis near +110H
reflects consistent vessel demand at the Gulf despite the persistent price advantage held by Black Sea
